subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) relatng to taxation have not so far met with a great deal of favour from any quarter of this house. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) stated last Tuesday that he was glad to be able to congratulate his colleague on the statement of Canada's business which he had presented for the past year. But apart from such general remarks, there has not been very much favourable comment from either side of the house, especially from hon. members to your right, sir, with regard to the taxation proposals of the budget. In his reference to his colleague's statement of Canada's business, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) asked:
What percentage of this credit is due to the self-reliance and industry of our people, what percentage to the acts of a benign Providence, and what to the actions of the government seems, however, to be a matter for debate.
Without seeking to fix the percentage of credit, Mr. Speaker, I would say that Providence has been generous to us during the last three years; our people have been very industrious; and I think we will have to admit that the Minister of Finance is a careful administrator.	_	_
Now, as far as my time will allow, I wish to deal with the taxation proposals contained in the budget. We have four main sources of taxation revenue:	Customs, excise, sales
tax and income tax, and it is as the budget proposals affect the taxation levied that I am particularly interested. I have not heard much comment so far in this debate, especially from the government side, on these taxation proposals. We have discussed many things which in my judgment are not directly related to the budget or connected with budgeting, but there seems to be a tendency to avoid any reference to the actual changes in taxation as proposed. As one of the members of this group I have been very much interested in some of the kindly criticism that has been levelled against us in this corner and against our amendment. I was very much interested in the speech made by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). He stated that he had a hard job to understand just why we were sitting on this side of the house, and he came to the conclusion, after reading our amendment, that there was no reason at all why we should sit on this side and that even he himself

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
had stronger reasons for differing with the government than those set forth in our amendment.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) delivered a remarkable speech. He said in his closing words:
I intend to vote for honest and practical legislation-for the budget.
But what was his analysis of that budget which led him to that sublime conclusion? First:
The tariff resolutions which the Minister of Finance has presented to the house are confusing. I do not believe that all the lawyers in Philadelphia could understand them, and I am not going to discuss them because they are too confusing. I would point out, however, that there seems to be a joker in the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance, and that joker is in the changing of the numbers of the schedule. Let me cite just one example in order to make my point clear.
Then he cites items 526 and 575. He goes on:
In the new schedules which the minister has brought down that is changed to item No. 545, and in changing the item they have inserted the words, ' for use exclusively in the manufacture of",-
He asks that the words: "For use exclusively in the manufacture of," be struck out.
So that the general public of Canada will get the same advantages as the manufacturers when it comes to importing material. He objects to the reduction in the income tax:
The reduction in the income tax, I am frank to say, does not please me.
These are his references to the direct proposals of the budget. Then he goes on to discuss the amendments. He says that some of us over here are anxious to rock the boat as it is safe. I would remind him that some of us rocked the boat when it was not safe, and if the matter is urgent enough and important enough we are prepared to do it again. The only reference which the hon. member for Provencher makes to the proposals of the budget he makes in condemnation of or in opposition to them. But he sums up his remarks by stating that he is prepared to vote "for honest, practical legislation-for the budget." I would point out that the hon. gentleman is the only member of the group known as Liberal-Progressives in this house who has so far spoken on this budget. I should like to know whether we are to take his attitude on the budget as representing that of the Liberal-Progressives. I am interested in this because I have a great deal of respect for the Liberal-Progressives and I should be glad to hear more of them tell the house what they actually think of
these budget proposals before the division is called on the amendments and on the budget itself. We are not infallible. We have been criticizing the budget and we are anxious to hear from some of those gentlemen, who have very much the same point of view as ourselves with regard to matters of taxation, as to the ground on which they will justify voting for the budget and against our amendment.
We heard also from -the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). That hon. gentleman in his speech on Wednesday did not come any nearer discussing the actual taxation proposals or the change in them than to refer to the income tax and to the increase in the British preference. On the latter point he had this to say:
As to the criticism which has been uttered with respect to the intimation by the Minister of Finance that in future it was proposed to ask that all goods coming in, taking advantage of the British preference, should have a 50 per cent British or empire content, I desire to say just this: the Minister of Finance gave that intimation in no sense intending thereby to limit the British preference in the slightest degree.
Whatever the Minister of Finance's intention may have been, the change is bound to limit the goods that will come in, when we increase the rate from 25 to 50 per cent. It is just as sure as if you raised the standard of wheat. You will have less of that grade than if the standard were lower. I cannot understand why the Minister of Railways should have pursued that line of reasoning. Of course he took .a slap at the group system. This has nothing at all to do with the budget as a matter of fact, but as regards the statement made by the Minister of Railways on the floor of this house and in some parts of the country as well, if we are to believe the newspaper reports, that we in this comer of the house wanted and did attempt to bludgeon the government, I have this to say: If our efforts can be properly described as bludgeoning-I do not think they can be, but if so-then I declare, and I invite anyone to challenge the assertion, that the only attempt we have made in this house in that direction have been attempts to keep the Liberal (party true to the pledges which they made to the people of this Dominion. If bludgeoning is justified at all it is justified in a case of that kind. The minister said the other night that the hon. member for Southeast Grey had called that method democracy. Well, a betrayal of promises such as we have witnessed for a number of years in this country by the Liberal party is certainly something that is not in the best in-
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy

terests of democracy; and if we who have claimed to believe in the same principles that have been thus repudiated did not take every opportunity to keep the Liberal party true to its promises, we should also be untrue to democracy and to the people who sent us here.
I am not going to quote this time the Liberal or the Progressive platforms. When I was a youth I was once taken out to some evangelistic meetings in the north of Scotland and I remember an old evangelist stating there were some parts of Scotland he did not like to visit because the people were gospel-hardened. I wondered whether it is worth while quoting these, platforms any more. Are the people across the floor gospel-hardened so far as these promises are concerned? I hope that is not so.

speechtext:
The Minister of Railways said something about cooperation. I remember reading in the press after the last election that there had been a meeting of the Liberal-Progressive group in the west. They reported that they were willing that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) should enter the cabinet because the policies of the two groups, Liberals and Liberal-Progressives, were similar. The Minister of Railways stated the other night that we had co-operation in this house between the two groups. After all, he is in power because of that system; he is in power as a result of co-operation between the two groups. I was glad to hear the minister say he was pleased with the co-operation which has been received from that group, but I wish some of the members of that group would tell us whether they are also pleased with .the .cooperation they have received from the treasury benches in carrying out legislation based on the policies on which they were both elected. I believe they owe that to their constituents, to this house and to the country, because I do not think they are fair to themselves if they vote without giving some explanation. As I understand the ward " cooperate " it means to work together for a common object. What is the common object? Is it this budget, the budget of last year or both together? The views of the three prairie provinces on fiscal matters are well known; the farmers represent a large proportion of the population of those provinces, and if you find a group of farmers expressing themselves with regard to the income tax and the tariff you can be pretty sure of their sentiments.
I do not want to take time to quote resolutions from the Canadian Council of Agricul-
ture and other farm bodies, but I believe the people who sent their representatives here from the three prairie provinces hold the same opinions with regard to taxation and budgeting in this Dominion. They are opposed to the indirect system of tariff taxation as they are opposed to decreases in the income tax.
Some of the newspapers of Canada have stated that the farmers are opposed to any reduction in the income tax because they do not pay that tax. Well, Mr. Speaker, possibly some of us would have come under the income tax had it not been for the exemption we were allowed, but notwithstanding that exemption I want to say that most of us are very anxious to-day to reach the point where we will have to pay income tax. If the farmers have not been paying income tax it is because they do not receive the incomes in spite of their long hours of work, the hardships which they endure and the practical conscription of the labour of both their wives and families.
The Minister of Railways referred to the sales tax and said that on this point the Conservatives and ourselves agreed. That is not so, and I am surprised that the minister did not read the amendment more carefully. I am strongly opposed to wiping out entirely the sales tax, not because I believe it is a good tax but because I believe it is better than the tariff. Under the sales tax we have pyramiding; not all the revenue collected goes into the treasury, but the tariff also pyramids and in addition possibly two or three dollars go into the pockets of private individuals for every dollar which is received by the federal treasury. The sales tax, on the other hand, does not lend itself to that, evil.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien), asked the Minister of Finance, because he was a kindly gentleman, to strike out of the proposed tariff schedule the words " for use exclusively for the manufacture of ". I want to say to the hon. member for Provencher and to other members of this house who have beeh studying .the tariff ithiat we have not been tied down to a policy of protection in this country at all. No, indeed; we have had an arrangement of protection and free trade whereby the manufacturers get protection on their finished products and a low tariff or no tariff at all on the raw material they need to buy. They secure the benefits of both policies while we, on the other hand, suffer the disadvantages of both, and that is why we intend to fight until we get at least a more equitable arrangement. If the Minister of Finance in-

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
tends to strike out those words in these proposals he will need something more than a kindly heart to carry him through. The tariff schedules as proposed by the minister are planned in my judgment to help a few large manufacturers at the expense of the general public and the smaller manufacturers, especially those manufacturing hats and caps.
In the first place we have a reclassification; under the old items a certain rate of duty was provided on a certain line of goods, such as clothing or blankets. The old item would apply to cotton and woollen blankets, or to cotton handkerchiefs, linen handkerchiefs and silk handkerchiefs as the case might be. Now an attempt is made to divide those items as between cotton, flax, hemp and jute, wool, silk, and art silk. At the beginning of this schedule the tariff is changed on some articles of a general character to suit certain industries, and while some of these changes are not extensive others are very important. In the time at my disposal it would be impossible for me to go through all these items, but I intend to examine some of these proposals in some detail to show where the advantage lies. It may be dry work, but I believe it worth while to do at least enough of it to show the general way in which the tariff has been revised.
We have two concessions to the fruit and vegetable growers in the proposed budget changes. The first is in item 87b:
Small onion plants, grown from seeds and imported for bona fide transplanting or propagation purposes only.
The other concession is under item 219a:
Non-alcoholic preparations or chemicals for disinfecting, dipping or spraying.
Last night I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). He started out by approving of this reduction in connection with onion plants, but then he advocated protection when it came to the sale of the onions. That is another illustration of the desire to profit by both policies, and it shows that human nature is pretty much the same on both sides of the house. The onion growers last year were referred to by the Minister of Railways in a rather scornful fashion; I remember he said they wanted protection, and that there were only three hundred onion growers in the Dominion of Canada. However, I congratulate the Minister of Finance on taking this method of helping them instead of increasing the protection already afforded.
Item 192a is a concession to the paper mills, and here is a case where these mills are given tariff reductions in order to assist
them. We have made considerable sacrifices in this Dominion to help the paper industry, but these manufacturers are now anxious to benefit by a lower tariff or a lack of tariff when they want to buy anything which enters into the manufacture of their finished product. As the trade returns are made up it is impossible to find out just what the importation of these articles amounted to for the year 1926, the last year for which we have returns.
Now I come to item 267b which is a very important one. The old item 267a read as follows:
Crude petroleum in its natural state, .7900 specific gravity or heavier at 60 degrees temperature, when imported by oil refiners to be refined in their own factories:	British
preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
The new item in the tariff reads as follows:
267b: Crude petroleum not in its natural state .725 specific gravity or heavier at 60 degrees temperature, when imported by oil refineries to be refined in their own factories: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
On and after July 1, 1931, those rates will be per gallon: British preferential tariff A cent, intermediate tariff A cent, general tariff i cent. Of crude petroleum, gas oils other than naptha, benzine and gasoline lighter than .8235 but not less than .775 specific gravity at 60 degrees temperature, the imports for the year ending March 31, 1926 were 1,884,348 gallons, valued at 8118,181 on which a duty of $28,265.23 was collected under the general tariff. In the case of crude petroleum in its natural state, .7900 specific gravity or heavier at 60 degrees temperature, when imported by oil refiners to be refined in their own factories, the imports amounted to 470,574,100 gallons, valued at $25,672,481.
The budget proposals will now allow (to come in free until July 1, 1931, crude petroleum not in its natural state, .725 specific gravity or heavier at 60 degrees temperature, when imported by oil refiners, to be refined in their own factories. This will allow partial refinement of crude petroleum in the United States, Peru, or Mexico, countries from which it has been imported, and the importation to Canada without duty until July 1, 1931. This is a concession to oil companies without any reduction in ithe duty in the finished products. It is the first intimation I have had that the oil companies were in distress. It appears that we are going to allow them to refine not
1,884,000	gallons of oil, but 470,000,000, and to bring that amount of oil in annually without paying duty up to July 1, 1931. The protection on most of the finished products of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to what has been said in the
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

course of this debate, and it is rather difficult at this late stage to present to the house any thoughts that have not already been dealt with to some extent. Before proceeding with my remarks on the budget, let me say that my attention has been drawn to some observations made by the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Odette) last evening when he stated:
Last but not least the Canadian Steel Corporation, the Canadian branch of the United States Steel Corporation, have started the production of steel in two large factories in Ojibway.
An hon. member wired to the Canadian Steel Corporation as follows asking for confirmation :
Has Canadian Steel Corporation started the production of steel at Ojibway?
Eccles J. Gott.
The reply from the Canadian Steel Corporation reads:
Message received. No.
I have been listening to remarks from different comers of the house and I think I have at least solved one thing and that is that, when a man either comes into this country from the outside or graduates from college or school in Canada and is ambitious, energetic, thrifty, capable and accumulates a little money round about him at, say the age of fifty years, he is promptly classed as a capitalist to be fired at by tax collectors and certain groups of men who perhaps have not been quite so successful and who have not gathered this world's goods about them. Listening the other day to the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), when he drew that very blue picture of the farmers in Saskatchewan who he claimed had been "shot at" for a long time by the manufacturers and the capitalists, I could not help thinking of a number of these farmers who have appeared on the Pacific coast, having made enough money from their farms in Saskatchewan to retire for life and come out on the Pacific coast and enjoy themselves, spending their time fishing when the fish are willing, playing golf and generally having a good time. These men are welcomed by us in Victoria and along the Pacific coast. We are very glad indeed to see them, and we would like to have more of them. Glancing across the house, too, I notice that the representatives from Saskatchewan are a very prosperous looking lot of men and capable of holding up their end in this house, and I come to the conclusion that after all these people at the coast that I refer to and these gentlemen across the floor must be just a few who have got away from the manufac-
turer and the capitalist. I have heard the hon. member for Rosetown speaking along these lines on several occasions, and I have been living in hopes that some day I would have the pleasure of seeing him out on one of our golf courses, rigged up in plus fours and all the usual paraphernalia, chasing the elusive pill over the course and inhaling the ozone of the Pacific coast. After he had enjoyed himself out there for a week or two and mixed with these retired capitalists, farmers and manufacturers, I am sure he would think that they are not such a bad lot after all. We need all these classes in Canada. We need the farmer, and he should have all the advantages that we can give him. We need the manufacturer, and we also need the capitalist very badly indeed, and we want him to expend his capital within the confines of this country, and in British Columbia particularly, if we can induce him to come out there.
I was sorry to notice in some of the newspapers, after some remarks made in this house, an effort to give the impression that the Conservative party was opposed to the Canadian National Railways. This is absurd on the face of it, because the Canadian National Railways were brought into being by the action of the Conservative party, and this party has supported them through thick and thini until now the Canadian National is one of the most important organizations in the country. It has a great deal to do with the development of this country, just as has the Canadian Pacific, and in British Columbia we appreciate what they are doing there. They have a very fine lot of men in charge of the Canadian National railways-and they have improved their service very greatly as regards the handling of both freight and passengers. They can rest assured that the Conservative party will stand strongly behind them and see that they get fair play under all conditions.
The other day, listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) stressing the fact that there was seasonal unemployment in Canada, I could not help wondering just how he ever expected to have anything else under the Liberal policy. Why, in the matter of the attempt to have our northern dairymen produce butter on one cent protection as compared with a country where spring conditions exist, let me say that no less than 103,000 cows were shipped out of Ontario in 1927. Now to take care of that number of cows, at least 5,000 men would be employed. Where did they go when those cows left this country? Either they went to the cities and joined the unemployed, or

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
probably they went to the United States. While the minister stressed the fact that this unemployment was seasonal, he offered no remedies whatever. I want to say that British Columbia is very much interested in this question, for the reason that thousands of harvesters are shipped out to the prairies from the east during the harvest season, and a great many of these men drift across the mountains and to the Pacific coast, seriously interfering with the labour men who are there. The labour men on the Pacific coast are men who in many cases have their own homes and have to pay taxes, and yet they have to meet with this unfair competition. Those Who are unemployed and are needing support of some kind during the winter months have to be carried by our province, and by the municipalities and the cities. The minister in his remarks clearly indicated that thi3 was a Dominion-wide problem. The Conservatives, Mr. Speaker, have a lurking idea that if they could get into power and introduce their policy of running Canada for the benefit of Canadians, this situation would be alleviated to a very great extent. But if the Liberals are going to remain in power they should devise ways and means of taking care of those who are bound to be unemployed as a result of the Liberal policy.
The Home Bank legislation is another matter to which I would like to refer briefly in passing. The house will remember that this bank failed some time ago, and that certain sums were voted by this house for the purpose of relieving a certain number of the depositors to the extent of some 35 per cent of their loss. The bill passed this house but was thrown out by the Senate, and later an amended bill was put through, and the result has been that- the funds voted at that time have not proved sufficient for the purpose, that while some early applicants have received their 35 per cent, others have received much less, and some none at all, although they are just as deserving as those who have been paid. It is estimated that a further $450,000 will be necessary to carry out the intention of parliament in the act which was passed in 1925, and I would call the attention of the government to the necessity of taking action along this line at this present session if possible, in order to carry out the intention of parliament and act in good faith with these people.
While the government has been emphasizing the necessity of extended markets and the establishment of embassies in different parts of the world-certainly the extension of our markets is quite O.K.. and I endorse it to the fullest extent-still I feel that we are not
making the best use of the opportunities offered to us in Canada. I feel that we should make a very thorough survey of our opportunities for development in industry and also in agriculture, that we should carefully examine the list of imports coming in from the United) States and select those articles which we can produce here at a profit, and then concentrate on their .production with a view to keeping that money at home for the use of our Canadian people and alleviating the seasonal unemployment that was referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
There is another matter in connection with the development of our industries in Canada which is very important indeed. In a country like this, with a sparse population and long hauls, the freight bills which it is necessary to pay for the handling of these products is a very important factor indeed, and the nearer to the point of production we can get our goods consumed, the more there will be for the producer. We recognize that the farmer today is facing many disadvantages to which he was not subjected some years ago. He is facing greater costs, because labour has been sensible enough to form unions for its own protection, and it has raised the standards of living in this country, which is very much to be approved. By organizing in this way they have been able to provide themselves with comfortable homes which they were not able to possess some years ago. But all this has added to the cost of living for the farmer and the cost of carrying on his work. In addition, the farmer has experienced some increase in farm wages, but on the other hand he is in some cases receiving greater prices for his products. The buying power of the man who is working for wages has increased, and he is now paying bigger prices for the products he requires than he did before. The farmer, too, might help himself in this regard and vastly improve his condition. In the first place, the average dairy cow in Canada yields 150 pounds of butter fat per year. We have many cows that are producing very much more than that. The milk product alone of our average cow would be less than 3,000 pounds, while we have other cows that have produced over 30,000 pounds, showing the difference between the very good and the very bad. In addition to that, we find that thousands of our cattle in very thin condition are rushed to market in the various centres where stockyards are located, such as Calgary, Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, with the result that they lose a great deal through lack of weight, and fetch poor prices. The farmer by improving these conditions can place himself in a much more favourable posi-
9S8
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

tion. Of the average animals for beef that go through our inspection abattoirs, let me say that only ten per cent are good enough in quality to compete with the Argentine beef which is shipped to the London market, showing that we have yet to do a great deal in improving the quality of our product. The farmer might take a generous view of the situation and do this just as an act of mercy to the poor Canadian consumer.
We all recognize the fact that nothing is of more importance to Canada than to place agriculture on a good, sound, prosperous basis. To do that we must remove as far as possible the farmer's disabilities. The budget promises nothing in this direction. The Canadian farmer is faced by the competition of the farmer in the southern United States, Mexico and California, who ships his products much earlier in the season, and has the further advantage of cheap Mexican labour. Mexicans cross by the thousand every year to work in the vegetable and fruit growing districts of the southern states, so that the Canadian farmer has to face the competition of fruits and vegetables produced under peon labour conditions. Then again the man down there very often will have a few acres devoted' to a certain class of vegetables and sell the main portion of his crop to good advantage in his own market and rush the tail end of his crop to this country, to compete with the producer here who is just getting his first crop on the market. The same thing is true of fruit and eggs. We have prayed to the government for protection along these lines ever since the passing of the Fordney tariff, but without result. The very last failure on the part of this government to show its appreciation of agriculture and its importance to the country was to ask our farmers to produce butter with a protection of only one cent a pound, while butter is produced1 on the grass and brought up here at a season of the year when our winter production is at the highest peak of cost. Yet our farmers are asked to produce butter under those conditions with a protection of only one cent a pound, while their competitors in the United States receive twelve cents a pound protection for their goods.
One branch of our agriculture has been seriously neglected for many years. It is a very valuable branch of the industry and is essential to the development of this country.
I refer to the sheep industry. We know the value of sheep, the cleaning effect they have on the farm; for they consume weeds and everything good to eat in the form of green food. They are produced at a very low cost, and they save the farmer many a long trip 
to the country store for meat. Another point in their favour is that they yield two crops during the year-a crop of wool and a crop of lamb. Still another point in favour of the sheep .industry is that a farmer can go into it with very little outlay indeed. Sheep will do we'll in any part of Canada, for we are not affected 'by drought as they are iin Australia and some other countries. The achievements of our breeders at the various exhibitions are simply an index of what can be done here in raising sheep of the finest quality. We all know Colonel McEwen, of Ontario, who on several occasions has won the first prize at the Chicago International Exhibition for the best carload of lambs, produced in and shipped from Canada.
We have done very little in a real way to support the sheep industry, and the figures I am about to give the house will be very interesting in this connection. While we have given prizes at exhibitions to encourage our farmers to produce better sheep, while we have formed sheep clubs in various parts of the country, while we have distributed pure bred sires-and all this has had some effect, yet the general effect, taking the whole Dominion. into consideration, is seen in the fact that the development of the industry during the last fifty-six years is nothing to be proud of. For instance, our sheep population in 1871 was 3,155,509; in 1927 the estimated figure was only 3,262,706, indicating that there is something radically wrong with our sheep industry because we have had immense increases in our cattle, in our horses-so long as horses were in use-and in swine, poultry and so forth, but with regard to our sheep we are practically where we were fifty-seven years ago.
What is that something that is radically wrong? Apparently it is the fact that our wool has been unprotected for very many years-I think perhaps over the whole of this period. Let us compare this for a moment with conditions in the United States. They have had a tariff on wool since 1816, except for a short period during the war. They took off their tariff in 1913 because there was a great demand for wool probably anticipating what was going to happen, and by 1921 the United States was simply flooded with wool of all kinds. The tariff was put on again in 1921, running from 15 to 45 cents a pound. The sheep population of the United States now stands at 44,455,000, the increase being 6.5 per cent during last year, or nearly as much as the whole sheep population of Canada, while our sheep population is, as I have said, practically the same as it was

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
fifty-seven years ago with free trade in wool prevailing here. That fact alone should occasion a good deal of thought.
Now, this country is capable of carrying more sheep than t'he United States. We have a vast grazing area, and we can build dp a huge industry just as soon as the government comes to the conclusion that it must run this country for the benefit of the people |who live here and pay the taxes. While we can grow sheep in any part of the Dominion, and grow them to perfection, I think we have in the province of British Columbia one of the greatest potential sheep areas on the continent of North America. I make this statement without fear ;of contradiction, for I have been connected with agriculture all my life and have travelled over the greater part of this continent. In 1871 statements were made by prominent easterners that the Canadian Pacific Railway would never get enough traffic to pay for the axle grease used in the operation of the road. We were also told that all the capital in the British Empire could not complete the road and operate it after it was built. At that time the country west of the Alberta boundary was described as a "sea of mountains." Well that sea of mountains has proven to be a tremendous asset. In the first place, we have there a crop which we can reap every year-scenery. We are selling it to the tourists of the world to the extent of millions of dollars a year. And there is one very important feature about this crop: all you have to do is to reap it; it was sown years and years ago. It is there and will remain a valuable asset just as long as any of us are interested. Then we have in those mountains vast mineral deposits, having sold only last year over seventy million dollars' worth of minerals in the province of British Columbia. In addition to that, we have in the valleys and foothills a potential sheep country second to none anywhere. We have there about 160,000,000 acres of range land, about 100,000,000 acres of timber range, and 60,000,000 of open range, all ideal for live stock conditions, and much of it excellent for the production of sheep. Sheep there can not only graze on the grass but they can also browse under conditions that they enjoy so much and under which they thrive very well.
Let us glance for a moment at the United States by way of comparison. Their new range is about exhausted; they have about reached their peak in the production of sheep at present cost, and any increase in their flocks now will have to be carried out largely on the farms and consequently at added cost of production. Their present ranges have
been over-stocked to a considerable extent. The four states lying just south of British Columbia-Montana, Idaho, Washington and Oregon-a little larger in area than the province of British Columbia, are using about 69.75 per cent of their available range, while British Columbia, with 160,000,000 acres, is to-day using only 6.25. Government experts in British Columbia advise us that we have sufficient arable land in the country to winter feed all the live stock that could be raised on that 160,000,000 acres. What is the value of the live stock at present using the British Columbia ranges? Only $12,000,000; and if all that range were put into use the potential value would be $240,000,000. The feeding season in British Columbia has no very serious difficulties. We feed from three to four months, depending upon conditions. I am speaking of range sheep. The period is three or four months, the longer period when there is a severe winter. It requires from two to three pounds of good hay per day to carry sheep over the winter, and not so much when the range is open in a mild winter. At the present time there are less than 100,000 sheep in British Columbia. One farmer with whom I was speaking a short time before I left told me that his lambs had averaged last fall, 80 pounds each. Some of the flocks on the range clip as high as 10 pounds of wool per ewe. One rancher sold his lamb crop for $30,000 last year, and these were produced on grass in the province which has been going to waste for hundreds of years. We have millions of acres of land available for production of sheep.
Predatory animals are not a serious menace. The usual method of coping with them out there is to trap them, poison them, or employ other destructive methods; the plan during the winter season is to trap over the range which will be used the following year. By so doing, many of the predatory animals are got rid of. We have good dog laws, and they are so arranged that they can immediately be put into effect upon a district being designated a sheep district. There is a splendid opportunity for the production of pure bred sheep in Canada and good prices are obtained for Canadian sheep. One of our Ontario breeders two years ago sold a single animal for $1,000. Our sheep are now known throughout the world. We have been shipping across the Pacific and to the United States and other places for many years.
As regards the production of fine wool, it has been said that Canadians are unable to produce wool of as fine a quality as that produced in Australia. This is perhaps true in regard to some specially fine merino grades,
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

but I am sure that research and careful breeding and feeding would bring satisfactory results; and in a province like British Columbia, where we have a varied climate and varied soils and conditions, it would be quite possible by careful handling to produce wools of a fine quality. This presents an opportunity for our research bureau to carry out some investigation along these lines.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it not good business to develop our opportunities at home- just such opportunities as I have been describing? I am quite convinced that with a well organized effort, and going after it persistently and carefully on a well laid plan, we could add greatly to our agricultural wealth in Canada through the development of the sheep industry. We should encourage the manufacture of wool in this country. After all, our first business in carrying on the government of Canada is to care for the wants of this country; let us put our own business on a good sound basis and1 we can go further afield later on.
Besides the fact that our wool growers face world-wide competition without any protection, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in the very budget we have under consideration at the moment, has removed all restrictions on rags, waste and trash of various kinds coming into Canada. It is bad enough to use our own rags 'and trash and waste of every description, having such material made into shoddy to compete with the local producer. But why should we accommodate ourselves to the rest of the world? What have we to do with their rags and tradh? It would be better for us to produce wool from live sheep and make clothing than to use rags and trash coming from other countries.
Taking the budget as a whole, I must say that the Minister of Finance has certainly been very generous with other parts of the world; he has been more generous with foreign countries than with Canada, instead of building up Canada first.

In these debates, however, we are able to hear discussed in this house the many diversified problems of the country and to elicit the views of various members representing constituencies throughout Canada. In the past week, I fear, the members of this house have been bending their energies more in the direction of delivering fine campaign speeches than of giving constructive suggestions to the government of the day. In referring to speeches given by members of the opposition, I desire to congratulate the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton), on his very able and fluent address delivered last night, and in passing I would also compliment my good friend the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott), upon the efficient manner in which he read his speech to the house yesterday.

The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
Coming down to the four parties who sit in the southeast corner of the house, they consider themselves bound together by a common ideal and by an equal status, in no way subordinate one to the other. They are all obsessed with the one idea that they have no politics. Politics, Mr. Speaker, is defined as the science of government, and when they say they have no politics I have no quarrel with them. I do say, however, that we in this corner of the house have been subjected to severe arraignments, admonitions, charges of betrayal and insincerity, and if it were not for the fact that those charges go beyond this house I would consider it beneath my dignity to even reply. I feel, however, that if we allow them to go unanswered we will probably earn the contempt of hon. members opposite, and rightly so. On Tuesday last we were favoured with a very eloquent phillipic, if I may use the term, by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). on Monday charged this government with holding office by fraud and deception. Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that there are few of us in this house sufficiently versed in technical railway matters to dispute their word. I do no'. know whether this information was supplied by the hon. gentleman himself but if he-was the publicity man, he did his duty welll The sketch tells how the hon. gentleman once hired out as a river driver without any previous knowledge of what a peavey or what a pike pole was. speechtext:
I should like now to deal with the budget itself. I am going to vote against the amendment of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher) because I do not hold' his extreme views, and I have more in common with the budget itself than with his amendment, although he probably moved it in all sincerity.
I am not so partisan as to say that I swallow the budget in. its entirety. I do not think any budget could be brought down that would suit any party or any ten members. You have to take the thing in a broad aspect. You cannot disagree on some minor points and agree on others. You are either for it or against it. I have every reason to congratulate the government on their splendid administrative record. I say in all sincerity and I believe I voice the sentiments of the constituency of West Elgin that the people there are in entire accord with the good administration of this government. It is pleasing to see our trade expanding, our debt and taxes being reduced and our prosperity increasing. These are factors to be taken into consideration before anyone think^ of voting against this particular budget. Because of the financial blunders of the Union government and the Borden government which preceded it, the soldiers who left our shores and fought in France, came back to find the country in debt for practically 100 per cent of the war. In fact these men had to share their burden of the tax for the salary of 11.10 a day which they drew while in the trenches in France.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fight and pay both.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. During the war millionaires in Canada sprang up like mushrooms and there should not be any undue haste in endeavouring to depart entirely from the principle of the income tax. These men should be made to bear a portion of the taxes for some time to come. I realize that there are reasons in favour of the abolition of the income tax. We know that while we can tax capitalists in this country, there is a great country to the south where taxation is lower and as there is no way of keeping them in this country and as there is a multiplication of income taxation here, municipal, provincial and federal, we have every reason to believe many of these men will go out of the country and be out of our sphere of taxation forever. That must be taken into consideration, but before any further move is made in regard to a reduction of the income tax, the matter

should be carefully considered because I happen at the present time to be sitting on a special committee of this house investigating the problems of returned soldiers and my opinion is that we are only on the fringe of what our pension bill will ultimately be. I think the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) who sits across the floor will agree with me that it has been the history of most countries that they do not reach the peak of their pension costs until many years after the war is over. I am not a pessimist, but I would not be surprised t-o see the pension bill of this country mount up to double the present cost and that within the next fifteen or twenty years. There are in Canada thousands of returned men whose health has been undermined by the hardships which they endured in France, and the government of the day, whatever it happens to be, cannot escape the responsibility of taking care of those men.
I want to deal for a moment or two with our friends of the official opposition. The chief criticism of our Conservative friends that is levelled against the government is the bugaboo about the emigration of Canadians to the United States.
It is true that in years past Canadians did go to the United States, and they will continue to go in the years to come. Likewise Americans have come to Canada in years past; I believe that since 1921, 169,000 Americans have come to this country, and I presume they will keep on coming in the future. I do not think there is anything to be alarmed about, because there will always be this exchange of people between the two countries. It is obvious that when we are enjoying good times in Canada, such as we usually do under a Liberal government, there is less likelihood of our people emigrating, and more likelihood of people immigrating to this country. I think if our friends of the official opposition are really sincere in their efforts to stop the exodus to the United States they ought to see to it that this government is kept in power for a long time in order that good times may continue, and not be interrupted by the advent of the Conservative regime.
We who live near the American border feel that the United States has reached the peak of her development; with her great man power and immense gold reserves, she cannot remain neutral. Capital will seek new fields for investment and labour will follow. In this regard I think the proximity of the United States to Canada is a great asset to us. Already in northern Ontario, northern Quebec, and in the west, principally in Manitoba, the mining industry is feeling the bene-

The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
ficial results of the influx of Americans and American capital. The immigrant who comes here from the United States with capital of his own, who comes unsolicited, is a very desirable immigrant. Only the other day I read that in the American west there were thousands of American farmers with capital only awaiting the coming of spring to move to western Canada and buy farms. For that reason I think the very friendliest of relations should exist, as they have in the past, between Canada and the United States. The bright star on the horizon for Canadian agriculture is the prospective market in the United States for our high class products. The United States is rapidly changing from a food-exporting to a food-importing country. I have a press clipping here which I shall not read because I do not like to have my hon. friend from South Essex glaring at me when I am reading-

The Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario is what I consider a very candid Conservative, and I have a great deal of admiration and respect for him. He represents in the Ontario house the constituency next my own, and I value his friendship. Speaking in southern Ontario only a short time ago he said that he hoped the time would soon come when the tariff barriers between Canada and the United States would be swept aside because there was the future market for Canadian agriculture, and upon our ability to market our goods in the United States depended to a very great extent the prosperity of Canadian agriculture, fl rade figures show that we are becoming firmly established in that market despite the fact that we have the Fordney tariff applied against us because of the defeat of reciprocity in 1911. We are still suffering from the loss of that agreement. The question of improving trade relations between the two countries is of paramount importance, and for that reason I think it is of even greater importance that we should have in power in Canada a government which is on friendly terms with the American people and that we should see to it that our friends of the Conservative party who have been very prone to stir up international prejudice between the two countries are kept out of power. They coined a phrase in 1911, " No truck or trade with the Yankees." That jarred on American sensibilities. A few days ago we had a visit from Secretary Kellogg of the United States, and I was glad that while he was in the chamber no Conservative member was enunciating that part of the Winnipeg policy in favour of an all-Canadian waterway, in contravention of our international agreement established through one hundred years of common -usage. I was mighty pleased that the hon. member for Northwest Toronto (Mr. Church) was out of his seat at the time and was not delivering one of his usual orations in condemnation of our official representative at Washington. I was pleased also that a debate on the purchase of our legation at Washington such as we had last year was not taking place, because if anything ever cheapened the Conservative party in the minds of the American people it was the debate carried on here last year in opposition to the purchase of that legation. We all know that it was purely a business transaction which would have been carried out whatever government was in power, that even our friends across the floor would have done the same thing had they been in power The Conservatives used the purchase of that legation as a bit of propaganda, fanned the flame of opposition to white heat, and did not confine their opposition to this chamber, but broadcast their remarks all over the country.
A few nights ago we had a discussion in this house precipitated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) on the Chicago drainage canal. I am not allowed to read from Hansard, but I want to say that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on that occasion dived into past history for the benefit of the present generation, revived the words of ex-President Roosevelt in connection with the famous Alaskan boundary dispute, when Roosevelt stated that if necessary American troops would be used to draw the line if other methods failed. That I think was very poor policy on the part of the hon. gentleman because his words would be broadcast all over the United States the next day. The feeling is growing in that country that the Liberal party in Canada is more friendly towards the people of the United States than the Conservative party, which never loses an opportunity to jar on the sensibilities of the Americans. I am very sorry that I am not allowed to read the very eloquent reply that was made at that time by our admired leader the Prime Minister of Canada. The viewpoint is now generally held among many classes of people in this country that such Tory tactics are poor business; I refer to the retail merchants, the wholesalers, and even the manufacturers.
Coming as I do from southern Ontario I know the magnitude of the American tourist traffic.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I purpose dealing with only one question. I wish to deal for a while with the movement of Canadians to and from the United States, and particularly so because in the budget speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on February 16 he declared that Canadians were returning home and that Canada was once more building solidly for the future. He wished, I presume, to convey the impression to this house and to the country at large that Canadians were returning in increasing numbers, and that that condition, if such condition exists, was the result of the policies of this government.
Not only is Canada in a unique position because of her situation alongside the highly developed industrial, commercial and agricultural country to the south of us, but also on account of the immigration laws of the United States. Under the strict quota law of the United States, immigrants are not allowed to enter from any other country to a greater extent in one year than two per cent of that nationality resident in the United States, as revealed by their census of 1890, with the exception of two countries, Canada to the north and Mexico to the south; and if newspaper reports are any indication it would appear that that quota law may soon be applied to Mexico and perhaps to Canada. For I believe that at the present time, there is a bill before congress which proposes to make the people of all countries in this hemisphere subject to the quota conditions. The Toronto Globe, in an editorial in its issue of February 28 last, after pointing out that the inclusion of Canada under the quota provisions, would probably reduce to one-third the number of Canadian bom going to the United States, gives its opinion of the effect upon Canada of bringing this country under the quota. It says:
In the long run the result would be the cutting off of Boston's export of shoes to Canada, of the silks, cottons and dress fabrics of New England, and the motor cars of Detroit, and the making at home of the goods that young Canadians now go abroad to produce. I he readjustment might be painful for a time, but Canada has had similar economic problems to face under the operation of the McKinley, Dingley and Fordney tariffs. If Canadian workers, as well as Canadian goods, are to encounter laws of exclusion, we shall find ways of living comfortably in a more self-contained way at home, and of competing effectively against American products in the open markets of the world. David's chances in that form of warfare are quite as good as Goliath's.
Now, I am not expressing any opinion as to the advisability or otherwise of Canada being brought under the quota law. I am

simply referring to the condition which the Globe pictures would happen if this country were so affected. If that is the condition that would follow here, then I wonder why we do not unite now to bring about that condition as the law is to-day without waiting seemingly to be forced into the position forecast by the Globe. It is the condition that we on this side of the house have been contending for and believe should! be maintained here in order to counteract the effect of the present United States quota law in its relation to Canada. I cannot, however, agree that such a readjustment might be painful, nor can I subscribe to the inference contained in the editorial that boots, shoes, silks, cottons, dress fabrics, motor cars, and other products of the United States should be permitted to come into Canada in exchange for the easy entrance of our native-born into that country. If that is the inference to be drawn, or if that is the condition to-day, then I think the exchange is most unbalanced, unfair, and wholly one-sided. I think, however, that the Globe in its editorial now admits that it is much better to build up a nation in Canada than to try to build up a nation elsewhere.
Coming back to the condition in Canada, as a result of the United States quota law, and without wishing to discuss the reasons which prompted the United States government to enact that law, it must not be forgotten that it created for us a condition which I think we cannot afford to overlook; for I consider it constitutes one of the most serious problems with which we have to contend. In short, the United States decided that she would no longer attempt to absorb unrestricted immigration, and she practically closed her doors, but she left the door wide open with respect to our native-born; for the quota applies only to those of our people who have become Canadians by adoption or naturalization. The result is that the United States opens its doors to our Canadian-born, the very type of citizens we must retain, if we are to maintain that strong British-Canadian sentiment that we so much admire and that is so essential to the full development of the Dominion. In other words, the United States are getting from this country the highest type of immigrant that it is possible to obtain-those bom on the North American continent, speaking the same language, and for the most part holding the same traditions and used to freedom of political thought and action along constitutional lines. In short, they are the most easily assimilated and the very highest type of citizen that any country could wish to

The Budget-Mr. Tummon
have. I repeat, sir, that this is one of the most serious problems with which Canada has to deal.
What is the government doing to cope with the situation? I have sat in this house going on three sessions, and I have yet to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or any member of his cabinet say that they are doing anything to meet this problem-; a problem so grave that it demands the most serious attention not only of the government but of every member of this house. I do not believe the time will ever come when there will not be a certain degree of coming and going between the people of the two countries, but I do believe the number of native-born citizens that Canada has been called upon to lose to the United States during the past few years is out of all proportion to the number that one might reasonably expect to leave this country. At page 8 of the report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization will be found some figures of the number of Canadian citizens who, the department claims, have returned from the United States during the past three fiscal years. I have heard some comment outside this house as to just how much value should be attached to those figures, but they are the only records we have, and I am willing to take them for what they are worth. We are told that for the fiscal years 1925, 1926 and 1927 there have returned to Canada 125,971 Canadian-born, 13,915 British subjects who had acquired Canadian domicile before going to the United States, and 8,064 naturalized Canadian citizens-the total returning to Canada during that period being 147,953. We are glad to know that some have returned, but the trouble is that for every one that returns, from two to three are going to the United States. Wishing to know what the first ten months of this fiscal year would show, I made inquiries at the Department of Immigration and Colonization. I am told that for the ten months of this fiscal year, April 1 to January 30, a total of 35,405 Canadian citizens of all classes have returned. Knowing these figures, let us compare the first ten months of this fiscal year, 1927-28, with the corresponding ten months of the three previous fiscal years. In the first ten months of the fiscal year 1924-25 there returned 39,032; in 1925-26, 37,863; in 1926-27, 50,898; and in the first ten months of 1927-28, as I have stated, 35,405. This statement of the department shows that fewer Canadians of all classes returned to Canada from the United States during the first ten months of the fiscal year ending 1928 than in the corresponding ten months of any of the three
previous years: less than the corresponding ten months of 1924-25 by 3,527; less than the corresponding ten months of 1925-26, by 2,458; and less than the corresponding ten months of 1926-27, by 15,493.
Let us make a further comparison. In the absence of figures for February and March to complete the year 1927-28, let us take the average number who have returned in these two months during the three previous years and apply them to this year. We find it gives a total of 42,125. When all the figures for the year are available I think it will be found, indeed, that 42,125 will be more than the number who will have returned, for in the month of January just past there came back only 1,683, the smallest number to return in any one month since the Department of Immigration and Colonization undertook in April, 1924, to keep records. However, taking the estimate for the twelve months as 42,125, the comparison may be made as follows:	This year there will be less than
1924-25 by 1,650; less than in 1925-26 by 5,096; and less than in 1926-27 by 14,835.
This does not seem to indicate that Canadians are returning in increasing numbers, But these figures of the Department of Immigration furnish some further very interesting information. We find that, over the entire 46 months of which we have record, the months which show the largest numbers returning from the United States were the months from November, 1925, to September, 1926. You will recall that those were the months following the election of 1925, that election from which emerged the Conservative party with 116 members. In that parliament the Conservative party had the largest group and the indications were that before very long -it was only a matter of time-the party would be afforded an opportunity of putting its policies into effect. Canadians, therefore, began to return immediately thereafter, in increasing numbers and continued to return in large numbers up until the election of 1926, immediately after which they began to fall off. The election of 1925 took place on October 29 and in the first month following the election, November, 4,331 returned in comparison with 2,993 for October, while in December, the second month after the election, the number returning was 7,923. The records of the department show that out of a total number of Canadians who have returned to Canada during the past forty-five months about 35 per cent returned in the eleven months that separated the elections of 1925 and 1926.

Mr. Speaker, in my contribution to this debate I wish to speak particularly with regard to the tariff changes which have been made at various times, and I desire also to make some comparisons of the results of these changes over a rather extended period. I was very much interested in the passages between the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott), the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Odette), and the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) with regard1 to the steel industry, because I have also something to say in that regard. The differences of opinion which arose between the hon. members evidently had their foundation in the policy adopted by the United States Steel Corporation with regard to the question of manufacturing in Canada. I have here a copy of Hardware and Metal, a trade publication under date of February 25, 1928, and without comment I will read a news item which appears as coming from New York:
James A. Farrel, president United States Steel Corporation, commenting on Montreal despatches indicating that the corporation was establishing branches to make all their present products in Canada, said that such plans were not contemplated. The wire plant now being finished at Ojibway, Ontario, near Windsor, merely represents the removal of machinery from, and abandonment of the Hamilton, Ontario, wire plant.
Since 1922, when the present government assumed office, we have had seven budgets presented to this house. In each of these budgets changes were made in the customs tariff, the most notable being the changes in the textile items this year, the changes in the automobile item's of 1926 and the changes in the agricultural implement items of 1924. In all of these changes the tendency has been to lower the duty on the manufactured article and then to compensate the manufacturer by passing on the reduction to the makers of the raw materials entering into the finished article. In other words, the primary producers are

The Budget-Mr. White (London)
penalized. This year the change has been made in the textile group, and it is rather hard to say just what the result will be; I suppose time alone will tell. As far as I can judge, some kinds of cotton products have received an increased protection, while wool, which was reduced some years ago, has suffered a further reduction, this year. It would appear that these changes will make it harder for Canadians to carry on business and will perhaps restrict the spinning of yam, since yarn is on the free list. If the production of spun yarn declines, of course it means the curtailment of labour and additional unemployment, and the Canadian farmer also loses part of the market for his wool and his foodstuffs in industrial centres. Thus, Mr. Speaker, the need for wider markets becomes apparent, and it is questionable whether the consumer will benefit in the long run by these changes. I am unable to say, and I do not believe anyone in this house can say, how it will work out.
Now I wish to refer to the changes which were made in 1926. In that year the automobile duties were reduced on cars valued at SI ,200 and less by 15 per cent and on cars over that figure by 7J per cent. Then, meeting with much opposition from the manufacturers of automobiles and also from labour, the government softened the effect of the change by a 25 per cent drawback on all material entering into the manufacture of cars, also abolishing the 5 per cent luxury tax. The net result was that the automobile manufacturers were left in almost the same position, with the duty reduced by perhaps 5 per cent, and the blow fell on the producer of the raw material, as in other cases which I will cite later. The loss of the luxury tax affected the public treasury also, of course. This is just another case of passing the loss on to the primary producer, but in spite. of all this our production of automobiles fell off by 13 per cent last year, while our importations increased by 28 per cent and our exports declined by 23 per cent. It has been said that the decline in the production of automobiles last year was due to the fact that the Ford Motor Company was not producing automobiles. That is a very interesting explanation of the case but it hardly stands inspection, because in 1925, before the reduction in the duty, there were 8,800 automobiles imported into Canada, while in 1926, eight months of which came after the budget of 1926 was brought down, reducing the duty, our importation increased to 14,900 automobiles, or an increase of 70 per cent. There is no doubt that in the history of nearly every industrial activity there comes a time, after it becomes firmly established, when duties may be reduced, and it may be that in time the reduction in the duty on automobiles will be a benefit to the industry and to the consumers generally. Our short experience, however, from the date of the budget which reduced the duty on automobiles until the present, is not very reassuring.
Hon. members on the other side of the house refer with a great deal of satisfaction to the reduction in duty on automobiles. One of them, in his enthusiasm, said the duties had been reduced and there were now more cars in Canada than ever before, but he did not say where the cars came from. The questions for Canadians to consider are where the automobiles come from; whether Canadian materials entered into their production; how many Canadians earned a livelihood from their manufacture and how many more Canadians might have been employed if this importation had not taken place. Other questions are whether the purchase of more cars abroad helped create an adverse financial balance; whether it built up foreign industries at the expense of our Canadian industries, and whether it tended to restrict the demand for foodstuffs in Canadian cities. There is still another question; did the purchase of these automobiles abroad create a reciprocal market in the country from which they were purchased? .No, Mr. Speaker; the market was largely closed to us by the Fordney-McCumber tariff, and by more recent increases, so that at present Canadian farm products are to a great extent refused entry into the United States, and the amount marketed there is but a fraction of what it was in 1921. I would refer the house to the Commercial Intelligence Journal of February 25 of this year, a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which shows, in a long list of products of the farm, our loss dm this market. In the month of January, 1921 our exports Of farm products to the United States were valued at $12,650,000, while in January, 1928, that figure had dropped to $2,870,000. It also shows that in the year 1921 our sales to the United States were $108,346,000, and in the year 1928 they had dwindled to $30,701,000, or a loss of the market to the extent of 87.3 per cent. The Canadians take the rebuff without any apparent sign of protest, and they continue to buy in the United States, as they did last year, to the tune of an adverse balance of trade amounting to $232,000,000.
