Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had completed that part of my remarks in which I showed that notwithstanding the reduction of 5 to 12J per cent in duty and the abolition of the sales tax on agricultural implements by the budget of 1924, the price of implements to-day is higher	than it was	in	1922 when theLiberal	government took	office.	My purpose was to show that when duties are reduced beyond a certain point there is no benefit derived by the consumer, and also that it may and does do harm to many of the industries concerned.I wish to proceed a little further and consider the effect of the tariff reductions of 1924 on the manufacture of steel and goods of that sort used in	the	making	of implements.	Pig iron and	rolled steel,	of course,
are the principal raw materials for the manufacture of agricultural implements. There is also a long list of small items in which steel plays a very large part.
The ordinary general tariff on steel is $7 per ton. It is a specific duty; it doe's not vary with the price. Prior to 1924 many items had been reduced from time to time until the duty on steel for agricultural implements for domestic use had been reduced by drawbacks to 30, 40 and sometimes 50 per cent, to about $4 per ton. The steel used in making agricultural implements for export was subject to a drawback of 99 per cent. By the budget of 1924 all the steel used in agricultural implements was put on the free list, and all other materials such as bolts, rivets, canvas and things of that kind were put in an item covered by six per cent duty. From this side of the house we protested against that reduction, claiming that it was excessive, that there had been no comprehensive study made of the whole situation, and advising the ministry of the damage we thought would be done to the Canadian iron and steel industry.
974	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. White (London)
No claims had been made as to excessive profits being made, and there had been no complaints, so far as I know, as to there being any combination in restraint of trade in that industry. The government, however, at the instance of the Minister of Finance, swept away the small duties that still remained, with the result that thousands of tons of steel, which mills in Canada are equipped to make, came and are still coming into this country. In the fiscal year ending March, 1925, steel under tariff item 445a came into Canada to the amount of 14,460 tons; in 1926 that had increased to 43,700 tons, in 1927 about the same amount, and for the ten months ending January 31st of this year the imports were
39,000	tons, or at the rate of 47,000 tons for the year.
In addition to that, materials on the six per cent list, largely made of steel, have been coming into Canada during all these years at the rate of about $2,500,000 per year, and last year the figure was $2,600,000, if I remember correctly.
All this has had its effect upon the unemployment situation and its effect upon the migration of our people. The loss which has been suffered by the steel companies is another item which must be reckoned with.
The maritime steel and coal situation has been pretty well discussed in this house and I think hon. gentlemen are fairly well conversant with it, but besides the companies in the maritime provinces there are two other large producers of steel in Canada, as well as many smaller mills scattered throughout the Dominion. One of those larger mills is the Lake Superior Corporation, which has been struggling for years, and last year showed a substantial loss. The other large producer, the Steel Company of Canada, is the only one in the industry in Canada which seems to be making progress. That company is a combination of fourteen or fifteen different companies which before their amalgamation were competing with each other for the Canadian business. A merger or trust, if you like, was formed. Of course I know these words are anathema to Liberals and Progressives alike. We have heard them get up in this house and rail against combines, mergers and trusts, and yet they are quite ready, when the steel industry is concerned, to get up and quote the Steel Company of Canada as a reason why the steel business in this country needs no consideration.
The Steel Company of Canada manufactures many lines from pig iron through all the various operations, including steel ingots, bars, pipe, wire, horse shoes, bolts and nuts, nails, screws, tacks and lead pro-
ducts. Many of these lines have not been affected by the tariff changes. For example, wire nails still pay a duty of $12 per ton, pipe a duty of 30 per cent, and tacks 35 per cent. The Steel Company of Canada also have practically free entry for their fuel. It comes in subject to a drawback of 99 per cent 'under tariff item 1019 for the manufacture of coke to be used in the melting of metals. The company make coal into coke, and in the process gas, of course, is generated. This gas is used to reheat their steel for use in the finishing mills, consequently they get their fuel in free of duty. There is another thing possibly in their favour. They bring the iron ore down the lakes to Point Edward and then transport it by rail to Hamilton, a distance of about 140 miles, and in so doing I am told they have a very favourable freight rate, in fact the lowest freight rate per ton mile on the American continent. It is so low that even if anything like an approximate rate could be applied to Alberta coal the very optimistic computation of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) might be realized. And yet the Steel Company of Canada with all these advantages cannot stem the ever-increasing tide of imports, records of which appear in the government statistics.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just a word on the production of pig iron and steel in Canada. I will compare the production of last year with that of 1913, the year before the war, to show our relative position to-day. In 1913 our pig iron production was 1,015,000 tons; in 1927, 710,000-a decrease of 30 per cent. In the same period the United States increased their production by 27 per cent. In ingots and castings the figures are similar; our production declined 26 per cent while that of the United States increased 45 per cent. Our trade balance in iron and steel with our neighbours is distinctly and increasingly adverse. In 1925 there was an adverse balance of $53,000,000; in 1926, $87,000,000; in 1927, $175,000,000.
In view of this it is pertinent to ask, what solution has the government for this situation -a situation largely induced by its own ill-advised acts. So far as I can discover they offer no solution. They have treated the basic industry of manufacturing iron and steel to drawbacks of duty on automobile materials; 99 per cent drawback on spring steel for automobile springs, and 25 per cent on all other steel. They have also put agricultural implement steel on the free list. We on this side of the house have entered our protest repeatedly against this policy. The report of the Duncan commission, issued on September 23, 1926, urges action, and I should like to

The Budget-Mr. White (London)
quote section 25, which will be found at page 37 of the report. It is headed, Steel and Customs Tariff, and is as follows:
It was submitted that the tendency of the tariff, as affected by successive alterations, has been to lessen the protection upon the primary products of iron and steel and to encourage their importation from other countries as being the raw materials of iron and steel-fabricating and finishing industries in Canada.
In respect of this matter, we do not conceive it to be our duty to express any opinion, since the question is, as we were informed by the chairman of the Tariff Advisory Board, who met us at our request, at the present moment under the consideration of that board. But we do regard it as our duty to record that the significance of this industry to the maritime provinces was forcibly brought home to us, not only in the manufacturing towns we visited in the maritimes but also throughout the agricultural districts of the maritimes. We record this in order to emphasize the need for prompt action.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after the lapse of one and a half years from the date of that report the government have advanced no remedy for the situation, they have not even shown a disposition to retrace their steps, and in the nature of things it will be another year before any relief is in sight. It is quite possible that some of those interested in this basic industry will have passed out of the picture before any relief arrives. But perhaps I should make an exception in favour of one member of the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm). He has suggested that British manufacturers might establish branch plants in Canada. I should like to direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the case of one British company that made the experiment, At the close of the war the Baldwin Steel Company, who have been manufacturing steel sheets in Swansea, Wales, for half a century, installed a sheet mill in Toronto. They found on proceeding to manufacture and market their product that it was an unprofitable venture, on account of steel sheets for galvanizing being on the free list. Thereupon they shut down the plant, and it remained idle for about three years. In 1925, despairing of any tariff relief, they scrapped part of the plant, and last winter they took out the mills and shipped them to England. Now, if Canadians cannot make a success in this basic industry, it would appear from the experience of the Baldwin Company that an English branch factory has no better chance of success here.
I have previously referred to the fact that coal is allowed into Canada free of duty for making coke. This is not an advantage to Nova Scotia. There are only two steel mills concerned in this particular item, and they have the benefit of practically free entry for
their coal-a 99 per cent drawback. There are other smaller mills in Canada which compete with these two large concerns, and they have to pay duty on their coal. The fact is that no coke is used in their process, and so they cannot come under the drawback provided for in item 1019. One of these concerns is in my city, and the other is in Selkirk, Manitoba. Up to 1925 the duty on bituminous slack coal was 14 cents per ton. During that session it was increased to 50 cents per ton, and the Minister of Finance stated that he expected this would provide about a million dollars additional revenue. This, of course, was for the most part a burden put on Ontario, but Ontario accepted it without a murmur. Alberta coal has been tried out by the Manitoba concern and found to be unsuitable. They and the other smaller mills use United States coal, and so they have now to pay a duty of 50 cents per ton and compete in the market with the larger mills that have free entry for their coal. This is not just; it is a discrimination as between plants in the same lines of business. In company with hon. members from Winnipeg and the hon. member for Selkirk I have made representations to the Minister of Finance and urged him to bring down some measure to relieve the situation. I hope when the resolutions are being considered that an additional resolution will be introduced by the minister for the purpose.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government have expressed no concern as to unemployment. There are no items in the budget to provide any relief, and in the speech from the throne they were silent on this subject. It seems to me that proposed reductions in the tariff are about all the answer the government have given to the request for jobs on behalf of our unemployed Canadians. This, of course, brings the matter closely to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). It is becoming a by-word amongst the smaller communities and amongst industries, that as soon as the budgets of the present Minister of Finance are brought down these communities and industries which have not been interfered with breathe a sigh of relief.
I am sorry, sir, that my time is exhausted. I had other items to bring to the attention of the house, but I will deal with them on some other occasion.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I fear
I cannot compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the presentation of his fifth budget. When I listened to him as he delivered that budget I felt that it was a rather
976	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
innocent document, but on reading it over carefully I discovered that it had potentialities for good and evil, and after studying a little more carefully I decided that the evil predominated. Now the public of Canada are studying budgets a little bit more than they used to, and well they may, because the budget has become an instrument in the hands of the minister to make or break people in their struggle for a living.
The budgets of the present Minister of Finance have two striking characteristics that did not appear in the budgets of previous ministers in that office. They are characteristics that are very disturbing to business men, characteristics that drive capital into hiding and retard progress. The first to which I refer is the instability of the tariff. It has become proverbial that no longer have the business men of Canada any security or any idea what the budget may bring forth each year. In 1923 the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, in delivering his budget, pointed out how essential it was to have tariff stability. At page 2848 of Hansard of that year he is reported as follows: "It is desirable that an assurance of tariff stability should be given to business men ***** I think that the tariff as it now stands is fair and reasonable and business men should be able to carry on without the fear of further changes." That is not the condition to-day. It would appear to me that the Minister of Finance has lost his perspective in relation to budgets. He fails to visualize Canada as a whole and to make his budget in the interests of the country. The budget is in his case framed entirely for political effect in the interests of the present government, of which he is a member. Business men throughout Canada will not remain in business under present conditions. Men of ability and of business foresight prefer to watch and wait, to' put their capital in hiding in some safe place rather than to use it in expanding industry in this country.
The budget of the Minister of Finance reveals another characteristic, the second one, which to my mind is serious from the standpoint of Canadian industry. The minister has a peculiar habit of paying unwelcome compliments to the industries of Ontario every second year. In 1924 he attacked the agricultural implement industry, and one peculiar fact about that incident was the very docile manner in which the affected industry took the reductions in the tariff. They made no particular protest, which created in my mind the suspicion that they knew what was coming. Some engaged in that industry were very near to the government and it would

seem that they got an inkling of what was about to happen and therefore began preparing for the event from 1922 to 1924. Later on I will give my reasons for so thinking. In 1926 the blow came to the automobile industry; it came like a bolt from the blue. There was consternation and the automobile manufacturers came to Ottawa and made their peace with the Minister of Finance, a peace that was satisfactory to him and expensive to the industry. Now in 1928 the textile industry is attacked. In 1923 an increase of 10 per cent in the British preference was given, which had a serious effect on the textile industry of this country, and in 1928 this second attack will be injurious to certain sections of the business. I intend to show that these are largely Ontario industries that are receiving the unwelcome attention of the Minister of Finance and of the government.
Speaking of the attentions of the Minister of Finance to the province of Ontario, it would seem to me that statesmanship is at a rather low ebb in Canada if a province like Ontario or any other province is to be coerced in this manner and used for political purposes, merely because that province is not sending to this government the support which they think it ought to send. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), if he were in his seat, a gentleman who enjoys a protection of thirty per cent on his own industry-

No, thirty per cent, I think, on the manufacture of furniture. I say I would ask that gentleman how he can consistently remain in the present government and see other industries treated differently from his own. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) has spoken in this house on various occasions and he appears to be consistently in favour of protection, particularly on industries in his own constituency. I believe he is a protectionist. I would ask him also how he'can consistently stay in the government while reductions in duty on various industries in Ontario are being made for political reasons. I do not know how the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) feels about it; I do not know whether he is a free trader or not. He also, however, comes from the province of Ontario. I say therefore that these three men ought to raise their voice in protest against the treatment which the province of Ontario has been receiving.
I remember quite well, when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) came into this house in 1920 as Leader of the Opposition, how he raised his voice many a time

The Budget-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
declaring his ultra democracy, telling the house what a democrat he was. He believed that the people should rule. Yet in eight short years he brandies out as an autocrat, trying to coerce Ontario through the Minister of Finance. The Globe newspaper, for nearly fifty years, has carried on one of its pages this dictum of Junius:
The subject who is truly loyal to the chief magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures.
Yet we find the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance using arbitrary measures on the province of Ontario.
The reductions which we find in this budget contain nothing at all for the average man in this country. Any one fortunate enough to enjoy a personal income large enough to come under the provisions of the income tax act is quite willing to pay that tax, but as there are only comparatively few of these people in Canada that particular reduction helps no one who really needs help. We can say the same thing about the sales tax; the reduction of one cent on the dollar may help the retail trade but it will never reach the ultimate consumer and he will reap no benefit from it whatever. The labouring man, the artisan, the farmer and the professional man will not be helped in any way by this reduction in the sales tax. Therefore these two items are of no interest to the average Canadian. The Minister of Finance stressed the fact that he was reducing taxation in Canada, stating that $19,000,000 would be handed back to the people this year. Not a cent of that money will go back to the average man, who really needs the reductions. Those who will be benefited are those who do not need help.

Every time this government change the tariff they stimulate the importation of foreign goods into Canada and thus injure our own industry, while every reduction in duties is followed by a flow of emigrants from Canada to some other country, in search of work. This government appear to me to be implementing their tariff policy of 1919, in which they said they believed in a reduction of the British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff; I believe the Minister of Finance is at that point now, and in some instances is below the 50 per cent level. I believe he is going still further in the direction of the Progressive policy of free trade with England; at any rate, he is nearing the point where we shall have a tariff for revenue only, which appears to be the Liberal policy to-day. Not only is the minister making reductions in the general tariff; he is also going around to the back door and giving preferential treatment to certain favoured nations, something of which the people are scarcely aware.
In connection with this budget there are certain things which particularly affect my own county of Halton. There is a little item in the tariff which will have the effect of giving an 80 per cent drawback on certain papers used in the publication of magazines. In this province we have mills which manufacture coated paper suitable for magazine publications. This is largely an Ontario industry, and in 1925 the duty was 35 per cent. An 80 per cent drawback will reduce that protection to 7 per cent. Ontario produces 66.3 per cent of this material, the balance coming from Quebec and New Brunswick, so it is a matter of vital importance to this province. These mills are seriously affected by this budget; their protection is practically eliminated, and I would suggest that the government give very serious consideration to the representations which I understand these manufacturers are making. We have a coated paper mill in the county of Halton; it is an important industry there, with quite a large number of employees and having a considerable amount of capital invested in it, and if this budget goes into effect it is possible that that industry will go partly out of business. I believe the manufacturers of this product have presented their case to the tariff advisory board, but in spite of their representations that board has

The Budget-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
recommended this reduction, to the government. Probably that is only to be expected, when you consider that at the head of the tariff board is a man who has free trade ideas, and who probably thinks of nothing else.
We also have three woollen mills in my county, and one of these will be seriously affected by this budget. I have mislaid my notes and a letter in this regard, but the factory to which I have reference is a spinning mill in my own town. The reduction in the duty on dry spun yarn and the free importation of yarn will injuriously affect that industry. They manufacture yarns, woollens and worsted yarns for the manufacture of carpets and so forth. The manager claims that this will take away almost their total protection, that he is hampered under existing conditions, that he has lost two large orders for the present year because he could not meet the British price. Wages in that particular industry in England are about $5 per week, while in the same industry in Canada the wages are $10 per week. This is a very serious handicap and that industry is unable to meet the competition coming from the old land. This loss of business is going to be seriously felt. Quite a number of families will have no means of earning a living; they depend for a livelihood upon that industry in that particular town. It is a very serious matter for them and I too would ask the government to take into their earnest consideration the representations made on behalf of that industry before the tariff advisory board showing the conditions under which they are operating in Canada. It is worth while for the government to consider these representations, because although the industry is in the province of Ontario it represents 82 per cent of the business in the whole of Canada.
Then we have another industry in the province of Ontario with which I intend to deal, although the conditions with respect to it were very fully explained by the hon.
member for London (Mr. White). My hon. friend is an expert in regard to the iron and steel industry and so was able to speak with authority upon this subject, but I will present the view of the man on the street who does not understand the industry, and I will try to show how the conditions affect the average farmer who buys the implements made by the agricultural implement industry, which is largely an Ontario industry. The capital employed in this industry in Canada in 1921 was $100,285,000, and in 1925, $81,861,000, a decrease of $18,424,000, as a result of the tariff policy of this government. The number of factories operated in Canada in 1921 was 90. The number operated in 1925 was 61, a reduction of 29. In 1921 the employees numbered 9,198 as against 7,669 in 1925, a decrease of 1,529. In 1921 the amount paid wages was $11,805,000 as against $9,089,000, a reduction of $2,716,000, largely in the province of Ontario.
Taking up the matter of production in Canada-and I am taking this from page 102 of the iron and steel report of the bureau of statistics for 1925-the production in Canada in 1920 amounted to $50,301,000. In 1925 the value had dropped to $24,770,000, quite a large reduction. The capital invested in 1925 amounted to $81,861,000. speakeroldname: Mr. D. J. COWAN (Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to the debate on this occasion will perhaps be somewhat coloured by my residence in northern Ontario in the heart of the mineral area which is now producing practically untold wealth for the people of this country. Hon. members who have had an opportunity of travelling across Canada will no doubt have noticed that large extensive territory apparently barren

The Budget-Mr. Cowan
and forbidding in appearance but most inviting to those who live there, in the northern part of Ontario from North Bay across country to the boundary of Manitoba. Hon. members and delegates Who attended the Winnipeg convention would have an opportunity of seeing that territory. I refer by the way to that great convention where we selected not only our leader but the gentleman who will be the next prime minister of Canada.
The scarcity of ideas on the budget, conjoined with the anaemic character of the speech from the throne, gives the opposition very little opiportumity to discuss to advantage the public questions of the day. Perhaps this government is in the rather unfortunate position of having applied to it the time-honoured saying of Hooker, "that even ministers of good things are like torches, light to others, but waste and destruction to themselves". It appears to me from my examination of the budget that this government is beginning to look backwards instead of forwards, and in a young country such as ours with the mineral and agricultural wealth we have to be developed, the government I think should have some suggestion which might be made use of in further developing and enriching this country. At the risk of repetition and being tedious I desire to offer some contribution to this debate in the course of which I shall make suggestions which I hope the government will see fit to adopt. I care not who gets the credit for it; I am only anxious that the mineral wealth of northern Ontario should be developed.
That northern country hon. members do know has come into prominence during the last few years. It is only a matter of a few years since even as wise and efficient an administrator as the late Sir James Whitney referred to that country as the land of the blasted ipine and stunted poplar. But that day, gentlemen, has long since passed. I know of no other country in the world that has such opportunities for young men, and I desire to address any self to that question with the idea of pointing out the opportunities for the young manhood of this country to find a means of livelihood and of acquiring wealth in that new area.
The stage is set by nature for a development of mineral wealth in Canada unparal-lelel in world history, Whether for magnitude or rapidity. We live in a country more lavishly endowed with undeveloped riches than any other in the world. Where can you point to a natural treasure house, still substantially unexplored, to equal the Laurentian plateau, that area of over 2,000,000 square miles, all
underlain by a Preoambrian formation; found wherever its surface has been scratched "to be rich in all the minerals, common or rare that are used' in -the arts,"-I am quoting from the Department of Mines report, 1924- and proven capable, from the few odd spots which have been developed, of yielding gold alone to the value of two and a half million dollars a month? Truly there is no country in the world that can approach Canada in undeveloped natural resources. In water power, in minerals, in agriculture, in pulpwood, four of the greatest assets a country can possess, Canada leads the world.
I have not the time to discuss this budget from the point of view of the agriculturist. That point of view has been ably and vigorously championed by all parties in this house depending, somewhat of course, upon the political party to which the speaker belonged. I do say, however, that I think the agricultural members of this house and the farmers of this country are taking a very short sighted view when they do not assist in the development of our industrial plants and in the development of our mineral wealth, which would provide them with a home market in Canada for their products.
I have not the time to discuss the question of water powers. Everyone knows the tremendous progress that has been made along the line of developing the white coal that never burns up. There are other features that I have not the time to deal with, but I intend to devote a few minutes to a discussion of the mineral wealth of this northern country.
History shows that continued and increasing prosperity has never come to a country save through pre-eminence in sources of industrial power, in precious metals, or in agriculture. Equally true is it that great natural resources, once adequately and energetically developed, have never failed to bring great wealth to their possessors.
Europe has already developed most of her resources; some of her minerals were exhausted a thousand years ago; even her coal is nearing its limit. Our neighbour across the border is developing fast, and with what profit to her citizens! Canada, far richer than any other country in the beginning, is still virtually undeveloped. For Canada is young. Only forty-one years ago the last spike was driven in her first transcontinental railroad. Only thirty years ago the first gold was found in Klondyke. Only twenty years ago two of her great provinces west of the area I have been speaking of were marked out and given the status of provinces in this Dominion.
We realize to-day the significance of the statement that this north country now
The Budget-Mr. Cowan

possesses a purchasing power of nearly a hundred million dollars annually. The government railway which traverses this strip is, along the Quebec-Cochrane section, now paying 90 per cent of its operating costs Think of the possibilities when real development begins! A billion dollars has come out of the four leading mining camps in this area already. Mining is closing the gap. To-day there is activity almost all along that thin red line of communication. Prominent authorities expect that the next twenty-five years will see this thin line broadened out into a strip at least one hundred miles deep-well populated, and continually pouring out riches to our country and providing work for our smelters, our furnaces and our workshops.
Look at the map. Trace the line of present activity, from the Flin Flon mine in Manitoba, to the deposits near Bulldog lake, Red lake, Woman lake, Narrow lake, Savant lake, Armstrong, Beardmore, Jellicoe, Tashota, Kashabowie, where the old Huronian is reopening Macqua-through the great established camps of Cobalt, Kirkland lake, and Porcupine-on through Rouyn to lake St. John. The gap is closing. It is symptomatic of the part that our buried wealth has played, and will play to an increasing extent, in the economic consolidation of the country.
The digging of new wealth from the earth is a fundamental industry. The recovery of mineral wealth rounds out our ability to prosper. It goes on winter, spring, summer and fall, producing regular national income, paying regular wages, offering full time occupation supplying raw materials to our other industries, independent of season and of weather. There is little marketing effort needed to sell gold or silver; they possess an intrinsic value, whether sold or held. The world demands our minerals; and the demand is growing. It is Canada's opportunity and duty to meet that demand.
Mining is now the third largest of our primary industries; but it would have been difficult to persuade the average man thirty years ago that, apart from the placer (surface) mines in the Yukon and British Columbia, and a little copper in the eastern townships of Quebec, and some gold in Nova Scotia, Canada contained any worth while deposits of gold, silver, or other precious metals. Even as late as 1910 hon. members will recall with what distrust the Hollinger, the McIntyre and other mines in northern Ontario were regarded. Do we really appreciate these great mineral resources? Our ores will undoubtedly prove phenomenally rich and abundant. As a matter of fact we possess the greatest

single exposure in the Precambrian formation in the world.
As I have stated, there is abundant mineral wealth there. In 1923, when Mr. Drury was premier, the Ontario government appointed a commission to inquire into and report upon the development of the iron ore industry of the province. On the basis of that report the provincial government took measures to develop the industry. But before I go into that question may I say that in 1913 there were in Canada twenty-two blast furnaces, but in the autumn of 1927 these had dwindled to four. What has been the situation? It seemed for a time as if the iron ore industry was on a sound basis. That was due to the legislation passed by the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier putting in force a bounty system, under which up to 1921 there was paid out in subsidies a total of eighteen million dollars. Apparently that aid enabled the industry to carry on successfully, but from 1921 the bounty ceased.
I was very glad to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) delivered in the course of this debate, for he is an authority on the subject. While formerly we had to import only $143,000,000 of iron ore and its products, last year we brought in $240,000,000 worth, and we did not mine an ounce of iron ore. Now, hon. members will recognize that that is not a healthy situation. We spent $240,000,000 to import mineral although we have abundant deposits. As I said a moment ago, in 1913 we had twenty-two blast furnaces in operation, while to-day there are only four. Of these two are at Sydney, one at Hamilton and the other at Sault Ste. Marie. This decline, of course, reflects itself in the number of men employed, and whereas in 1913 there were 1,589 men at work in our blast furnaces, in 1925 the average number was down to 656, and it is still less this year.
When I spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I urged that the government should supplement the legislation enacted by the legislature of Ontario, and I now propose to give the house a quotation from the provincial statute. It is known as the Iron Ore Bounty Act, 1924, and its purpose is set out in section 3, as follows:
3. Now, as to the imposition of an import duty. It is apparent that the $242,000,000 which in 1926 was added to the value of iron and steel products by the manufacturing activities in Canada was gained chiefly by the fabrication and finishing of imported materials, and that the contribution of materials of Canadian origin is becoming smaller by degrees and beautifully less to an extent that, if continued a few years longer, will render any Canadian contribution nonexistent. I think, too, it has been fairly well established that the importation of these raw or semi-finished materials has been aided by the lowering or complete omission of import duties in the most important instances of usage; but it is not true, as has been stated, that this favouring of importations from outside-so far as the products of blast furnaces and rolling mills is concerned-is required because of the inability of Canadian plants to furnish them. The record of idle blast furnaces, of unemployed men, and of declining production of primary products within Canada, are sufficient proof to the contrary.
I am not wedded to either scheme, whether an import duty should be placed on raw materials coming in from the United States, whether a bounty should be paid whereby our own iron mines would be developed, or whether a bounty should be paid to our blast furnaces; but I do suspect that the free importation of raw material has conduced to the destruction of this industry.
Including coal?
That brings up another phase of the subject. I understand this to be the fact, that the furnaces at Sydney, Hamilton and the Soo bring in American coal.
Not Sydney.
Well, the other two bring in American coal, on which they have a drawback of 99 per cent.
The hon. gentleman does not suggest that the drawback on coal used in the smelting and melting of metals causes injury so far as Ontario is concerned?

I think my hon. friend is right, provided Canadian coal cannot be used; but if Canadian coal is adapted for that purpose, then without doubt it should be used, and the miners either in Alberta or Nova Scotia benefited to that extent.
Now it is impossible to develop these mines properly without the aid of capital. Some hon. members may believe that labour is the important feature. I am more interested in the immigration of capital than of labour at the present time. We see the curious spectacle of men of Canadian origin living in Canada using their money to develop industries in Mexico and South America and other foreign countries, when there are plenty of opportunities for the investment of their capital in Canadian industry. And in the getting in of capital that provides jobs for immigrants in pulp and paper and mining and power development, what we get is this: we get labour into industries which, unlike farming, are not seasonable industries. Mining has three eight-hour shifts a day and pulp and paper three, and for that reason there is a large quantity of work, but best of all, twelve months of the year round. Most of us know that if labour is going to keep the flour barrel full in the corner of the kitchen, it must have twelve months' employment. That is what the development of our natural resources does, and that is not saying anything detrimental to our wonderful farming industry. I believe if Canada, without losing one bushel of her wonderful western wheat crop, can continue to develop her mining industry, now more than half the annual value of the wheat crop; if she can continue to develop her pulp and paper industry, now more than half the annual value of the wheat crop, to the limit of the market to absorb that paper; if she can continue to develop her white coal that never goes on strike, then I say to you she is marching along the lines towards that destiny that these rich natural resources entitle her to among the nations of the world.

The Budget-Mr. Cowan
What would be the effect so far as the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific are concerned? As I stated a moment ago, the area to which I refer is that barren stretch extending along northern Ontario. In the United States, we find, forty per cent of the revenue derived by class A railway is obtained from the haulage of mineral products. That is a feature not to be overlooked in this country. Now, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways are our two largest single employers of labour. They also use a considerable quantity of coal. I believe that thirty per cent of the coal used in Canada is consumed by these two systems. I do not know this as a fact, but I sincerely trust that our Canadian railways are using Canadian coal wherever possible. As regards the Canadian National Railways, I must say that, so far as I have been able to observe in our community, the system is well managed. There has been development in that railway-something of which we are all glad: the esprit de corps among the employees and the desire to give good service to the public are commendable. There is evidently a desire on the part of the employees to have the system become a nation-making entity, binding east and west together. I do not know the president, but I understand that those in the service of the company, from the officers down, are endeavouring to give satisfactory service.
I do not intend to enlarge on the question of our immigration, but I am concerned about the conservation of our population. It is far better to provide jobs in Canada for those men whom we now have here rather than to seek, at great expenditure, to bring in people from the older lands and from continental Europe. It would be far better for us to develop our mining industries in this country with a view to providing employment for our own people, who would be paid in Canadian money and who would live in Canada.
Reverting to the question of capital, is it not capital going into this north country development which alone can widen out the thin red line along the two transcontinentals north of lake Superior, heretofore, a barrier between east and west? Is it not resources development in Alberta and British Columbia we require on the one side of the prairie and is it not resources development in northeastern Saskatchewan and Manitoba on the other side of the prairie? Is it not more smelters and oil fields? Is it not more zinc development which exists in immense deposits in the Precambrian north of Saskatchewan and gold and copper in Manitoba, all allied with cheap power development? Is it not these we require to create home markets

on the prairies and diversified industry, which embraces mining, farming and manufacturing? Is it not research benefiting both the farmer and the manufacturer? Is it not resources development that all Canadians can meet on common ground? Is it not, after all, the building of Canada basically level through these sound economic methods that will meet the complex needs of this, a complex age? It certainly is, sir, as surely as the needle points to the pole.
The policy of this or any other government in power should be to grapple with these difficulties and to consider the suggestions that have been put forward, and not a policy of evading the question and postponing consideration. We should have a general policy for the whole of Canada, a policy of activity to promote our national welfare, with zeal for imperial relations.
I want to refer to the act in regard to bounties in order to show that this is not a new system so far as Canada is concerned. In 1923 this parliament passed what is known as the Copper Bounties Act, which contains the following provision:
The governor in council may authorize the Payment, out of the consolidated revenue fund of the following bounties on copper bars or rods manufactured in Canada and sold for consumption therein, from copper produced in Canada from ore mined in Canada, during the periods and at the rates following, that is to Bay:
From the 12th day of May, 1923, to the 30th day of June 1924, both inclusive, one and one-half cents per pound.
I will not give the other dates; they vary from year to year. The last, however, are:
From the 1st day of July 1927 to the 30th day of June 1928, both inclusive, one-half of one cent per pound.
It is to be observed in this connection that the provisions of the act will expire on the first day of July of this year. I do not quote the act for the purpose of suggesting whether it be continued or not, but I do believe that it has conduced to the building up of one of the largest smelters in British Columbia. I quote it simply to show that the principle is not new and that where it has been adopted it has proved of great service in the development of our mineral wealth. I trust, therefore, that these suggestions, which mean so much to that northern country and incidentally to the Dominion at large, will be adopted by this government. As I say, the system is not new, but even if it were new surely this government, which has displayed such a total lack of leadership in other things, might be induced to take up the question and deal with it at the present session.

The budget as brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is to a large extent but a repetition of former budgets brought down by him, in that whilst no very radical change is made in the tariff it still pursues the old policy of tariff tinkering, hitting one industry here, hitting another there, and creating in the manufacturing world a feeling of unrest, dissatisfaction and instability. One of the manufacturers in my riding has written me that as a result of the tariff changes brought down by the Minister of Finance there will be a decrease in the spinning of worsted yams in his plant of about 40 per cent, thereby throwing out of employment a certain number of men and women. In addition to that I believe when .one industry is affected it hurts other industries, thus reducing the market for Canadian products. I make this statement, sir, that in the past few years this government has done absolutely nothing for the development of the manufacturing industries of our country.
In common with the other speakers who have preceded me on this side of the house I desire to express my regret that no provision has been made for the abolition of the sales tax within the calendar year. This tax falls equally upon the rich and the poor and is in defiance of that well known principle of taxation, that the taxes should be paid by those who have the ability and the means to pay them.
Having in my riding of East Sirncoe the two important lake ports of Midland and Port MoNicoll, I should like to bring to the attention of this government the opportunity which exists for the building up of great industries in that portion of the country which will mean increased freights for our railways, larger cargoes for our freight boats, employment for a large number of men, larger payrolls throughout the country and in addition the return to this country of many thousands of Canadians who have been forced to a foreign country to earn that livelihood which has been denied them in Canada.
In the Georgian bay district, until a few years ago the lumbering industry was large and flourishing, giving employment to many thousands of men, paying in wages hundreds of thousands of dollars and giving in its industrial centres a splendid market to the farmer for his products. But, sir, I regret to say that that industry is rapidly vanishing, and that places which a few years ago were centres of activity are to-day scenes of enforced idleness. If this government can bring about a change which will result in renewed activity in these and other districts similarly affected I consider it their duty to do so.
The remedy is so simple that one wonders at the delay in applying it; perhaps its very simplicity is the reason for this neglect. To-da}'', Mr. Speaker, Canada is a large contributor to the building up of Buffalo and other United States lake ports, to the detriment of the lake ports of our own country. Large flour mills and storage warehouses are being built in Buffalo, involving the expenditure of millions of dollars, and this industry largely owes its existence to Canadian wheat. If a national Canadian policy were adopted, all this activity would be carried on in the lake ports of our own country. To-day Buffalo is producing more flour than any other city in the world, and one-half the wheat received at that port comes from Canada. The United States imposes a duty of 42 cents per bushel on Canadian wheat; if Buffalo had to pay 42 cents per bushel on the wheat it gets from Canada that wheat would soon be turned back into Canadian channels, but the United States are very clever; they take great care in looking after the interests of their own people. The United States made an agreement with Buffalo and other lake ports permitting them to mill all the Canadian wheat they desired in bond, without paying a cent of duty so long as the flour was exported. Canadian wheat going through Buffalo is not dutiable if passed on to. the seaboard for the purpose of export to fereign lands, but Buffalo and other United States cities may buy all the Canadian wheat they desire, manufacture it into flour and sell it abroad in competition with Canadian export flour. That is a splendid arrangement for the United States. The American duty prevents Canadian wheat from competing with American wheat but it does not prevent Canadian wheat, transformed into American flour, from competing with Canadian flour in the markets of the world.
What is the remedy? What means can we employ to keep Canadian wheat in our own country for transportation and for milling? The answer is simple; we should impose in export duty on that wheat, making it sufficiently high to protect our own industry. The United States duty against Canadian wheat is 42 cents a bushel, while our duty against American wheat is 12 cents a bushel.

The Budget-Mr. Thompson
Make the export duty 30 cents what will be the result? We shall have much more freight for our railways; larger cargoes for our vessels; an increased manufacture of flour in our mills; much more work for Canadians in our own country; increased payrolls and the retention in Canada for our farmers, live stock breeders and dairymen of the bran and shorts so much needed in these industries. It is estimated that during the last year Buffalo received 15,000)000 bushels of Canadian wheat for the purpose of milling in bond. Fifteen million bushels of wheat will produce 3,200,000 barrels of flour and 118,000 tons of offal, bran and shorts. The cost of converting wheat into flour, including overhead, is figured at 65 cents a barrel. Now 3,200,000 barrels at 65 cents per barrel amounts to $2,080,000, which represents the amount of wages paid to labour in the United States instead of in Canada. The loss to our railway companies in moving 15,000,000 bushels of wheat to Canadian mills and 3,200,000 barrels of flour to the seaboard is in excess of $1,500,000. Furthermore the sum lost through our transportation agencies not moving the 118,000 tons of bran and shorts referred to, would if distributed over Canada, represent a total of $675,000. If these products were shipped to the seaboard for export the earnings would represent some $550,000. The wheat milled in Buffalo is moved there from Port Arthur and Fort William, and no part of the product subsequently is carried by Canadian railways. A large part of our Canadian wheat instead of coming down to Midland and Port McNicoll for transhipment to our seaboard goes to Buffalo. That wheat is carried by United States boats and routed through American ports instead of Canadian ports, with the result that our railways lose a considerable amount of freight. Now, sir, if these advantages can be secured for Canada by the imposition of an export duty on our wheat, as I believe they can, surely we should not hesitate to adopt that policy. I trust, therefore, that the government will consider the advisability of imposing an export duty on wheat in view of the beneficial results which such a duty will bring to this country.
Before taking my seat I should like to say a word on behalf of the sailors who man the boats which carry grain from Fort William and Port Arthur to the southern lake ports. We all remember the loss of four fine freighters last fall with a sad loss of life in two cases. I have spoken with one of the officers of the wrecked ship Agawa, and as one listened to the tale of the hardships endured by the crews of these vessels

and the daring resourcefulness they displayed in saving themselves from drowning or perishing from the cold, one could not but admire the courage and heroism of those men and be proud of them as true Canadians. 1 would appeal to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) to see to it that every possible means is taken to protect the lives *of our sailors engaged in this hazardous occupation. In my opinion no work is so important as that. During the late fall the navigation of the great lakes is both difficult and dangerous-dangerous because of the storms that generally prevail in the late weeks of November and the early weeks of December, and difficult because the decks of vessels are covered with ice, the hatches are frozen down and the equipment largely disabled owing to ice conditions. On behalf of these men and their wives and children 7 would urge the minister to see that every possible precaution is taken by the establishment of life-saving stations, the installing of direction finders, and the adoption of other safeguards whereby the occupation of these men may be rendered less hazardous than it is at present.

The Budget-Mr. Fraser
It is the trend of business throughout the whole Dominion as far as I have been able to discover.
Having taken the minister's bubble of increasing imports of raw materials and burst it, I want now to deal with his attempted explanation of the increase of $30,000,000 in the importation of iron and its products. In this connection let me read from the article in Saturday Night to which I have just referred, in so far as it pertains to his explanation and his attempt to convince our people how little they should be alarmed about this importation. Here it is:
The remaining issue is that of the importation of industrial equipment, an issue intimately bound up with the increase of 30 million dollars in the imports of iron and its products. In a community like Canada it is of the utmost importance that iron and its products, the chief articles of industrial equipment, should be available as freely and as quickly as possible. In view of our great variety of manufacturing industries and the manifold types of machinery which they use as their industrial equipment, it is impossible to expect that all this varied machinery should be produced within the country in the early stages of its development.
Conceivably many industries might be compelled to use equipment made in Canada, but the desirability of enabling the producers of this country to secure their machinery at the lowest possible cost has been recognized by many governments. In 1918 the then government placed low-priced farm tractors on the free list.
That is, if you steal a sheep I can do the same.
The present government since its formation has lowered the duty on agricultural implements, many other implements of production and motor cars. This importation of machinery and industrial equipment on easy terms is of enormous advantage to the bulk of our producers and has been shown to be so by the general prosperity which has followed, the adoption of this policy, as is reflected in the financial standing of the industries affected in each case.
Will those hon. members who are particularly interested in our iron and steel industry please listen to this:
Are we now to delay or to retard the accelerating industrial expansion of the Dominion by discouraging the importation of industrial equipment, when there is scarcely a large manufacturer in Canada who is not using equipment of such a specialized character that it would be impossible to produce it for our limited demand except at prohibitive cost? Far from it; the great increase in our imports of iron and its products will be the source of increased production in the near future, and to check it would be disastrous.
And again I ask hon. members who are interested in the iron and steel industry to note the minister's words:
There is enough demand in Canada at present for articles of iron and steel to keep

our existing domestic plants busy so that our additional demands must need be imported from other countries.
Now, let me take that up seriatim.
In a community like Canada it is of the utmost importance that iron and its products, the chief articles of industrial equipment, should be available as freely and as quickly as possible.
Well, why not encourage our people to provide them as freely and quickly as possible? When we required these things in the pressing time of war whom did we turn to? Did we bring these commodities in, or did we turn our own people loose to manufacture them? I submit that a policy which is good in war time is easily adaptable to peace time. Then the hon. minister proceeds:
In view of the great variety of manufacturing industries and the manifold types of machinery which they use as their industrial equipment, it is impossible to expect that all this varied machinery should be produced within the country in the early stages of its development.
I want to ask the hon. minister if we are really in the early stages of our development. I thought that we have had the national policy for fifty years, and that it had given a pretty good account of itself during our expansive period in the eighties, again from 1900 to 1910, and again during the war years. Did we not find it pretty handy to have this iron and steel industry in the years between 1913 and 1918? Did we not find it good business to turn to our own people to provide these products for us. Why not turn to them now? The hon. minister the other day admitted on the floor of this house that after all our own people are the best on earth to do business with. This being so, I should like to know why he does not give them an opportunity to earn their living in their native country instead of importing this machinery because, as he suggests, "We are in the early stages of our development." And then he continues:
In 1918 the then government placed low-priced farm tractors on the free list.
Of course, it was not this government, it was the other government. Well, that is quite true, I believe a certain class of farm tractors was put on the free list by that government in 1918, and very likely for it they got the support of our free trade friends. But what has been the result? It is strange, Mr. Speaker, how the chickens come home to roost. Only two or three days ago I noticed in the press an article telling us that a trainload of fifty-three cars of farm tractors was being hauled to the prairie provinces. From where? From the works of the International Harvester Company in Chicago, if you please. Now, farm

The Budget-Mr. Fraser
tractors are required for the development of this country, and that being so, why not encourage our own people to build these tractors in Canada? Then he goes on:
The present government since its formation has lowered the duty on agricultural implements.
Yes, this government has reduced the duty on farm machinery-with what result? Our imports of farm implements in 1926 were
SI7,325,000	and in 1927 $25,782,000, or an increase of $8,457,000. That is to say, the increase in our imports in that period amounted to 48 per cent. What about exports, on the other hand? In 1926 our exports of farm implements totalled $17,318,700, whereas in 1927 they amounted to $16,701,500, or a decrease of $617,200-that is to say, 3i per cent. Here again we have an increase in imports of manufactured articles and a decrease in business when we attempt to sell these things abroad. Where is our agricultural implement business going to? Then take motor cars. It would make one weep, Mr. Speaker, to look into our motor car business and examine the returns of our imports and exports issued by this same Minister of Trade and Commerce. Let us take vehicles, for example. In 1926 we imported vehicles to the extent of $54,038.000-surely enough. That ought to be enough of imports of vehicles, embracing almost entirely motor cars. But apparently the government did not think these imports were large enough, and so we find in 1927 that they had increased to $65,431,000, or an increase of $11,392,000, or 21 per cent. And what do we find in the matter of exports so far as vehicles are concerned? In 1926 our exports of vehicles amounted to $39,-
430,000	whereas in 1927 they had declined to $33,758,000, a decrease of $5,672,000, or 16 per cent. In imports we find an increase of 21 per cent and in exports a decrease of 16 per cent. Surely that is providing work for the people of this country.
The writer of the article from which I have been quoting goes on to say:
There is enough demand in Canada at present for articles of iron and steel to keep our existing domestic plants busy so that our additional demands must need be imported from other countries.
Well, that is the final blow to the industry. There we have a straight-cut declaration of policy on the part of the government, a positive intimation that they have absolutely no consideration for the iron and steel industry of this country. We must get our supplies from outside because we are not capable of producing them here. That is an unequivocal indication of the intention of the
government to destroy the iron and steel industry in all its branches, lock, stock and barrel. Hon. gentlemen from the maritimes and from Ontario who are asking for more protection for iron and steel so that the industry may be built up in order to provide work for the people of this country may just as well kiss the business good-bye and forget all about it until we get a new government, one upon whom we can count.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is taking a hand in this affair also.
Just looking on.

He gets excited about imports and exports; once in a while he is much exercised in this regard. An important delegation from the National Dairy Council of Saskatchewan a short time ago presented to him certain facts in regard to the cream and butter industry, and now I am giving him information concerning other industries. All these industries are going in the same direction; they are all going to the bow-wows on account of this government's policy. The Minister of Agriculture, good natured soul that he is, came to Ottawa after they had made this declaration, and when he realized that the dairymen were alarmed'at the state of the industry, he poured oil upon the troubled waters by giving these people exactly the same assurance as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been giving to the people of Toronto: " Don't be afraid. Our imports are increasing and our exports decreasing, it is true, but all is well with the industry." Yes, all will be well with the industry when the government succeeds in having the whole business transferred across the line to the other side. In the last two years the Minister of Agriculture has altered the basis of this industry from an export of 24,000,000 pounds to an import this year of 10,000,000 pounds.
And the same thing is true in regard to any other business you like to mention. Let us take boots and shoes, for example. In 1926 we imported 802,744 pairs as compared with 805,532 pairs in 1927, or an increase of 2,788; while our exports have dropped from 110,534 pairs in 1926 to 87,634 pairs in 1927, or a decrease of 22,900 pairs.
In the matter of fish, our imports in 1926 totalled $2,376,800 and in 1927, $2,995,500, or an increase of $618,700; and our exports of fish declined from $35,984,000 in 1926 to $33,109,000 in 1927, or a decrease of $2,875,000. Apparently there is no end to the trend of events which all point to the total disappearance of industry from this country. Is it any
The Budget-Mr. Fraser

wonder that there is an exodus of people from Canada and that we are looking for immigrants to take the place of the capable citizens we are losing?
Let me give you the figures relating to wood products. In 1926 our imports were 19,335.947 and in 1927 $10,571,878, or an increase of $1,235,931: that is to say, 13 per cent. And so far as exports of wood products are concerned, there has been a decline from $54,174,989 in 1926 to $4S,S17,326 in 1927, a decrease of $5,357,663, or 10 per cent.
Then we have the fruit industry; exactly the same state of affairs exists in this business. Our imports of fruits in 1926 totalled $29,550,000 and in 1927, $32,820,000, an increase of $3,270,000, or 11 per cent; while our exports in 1926 amounted to $8,512,000 as compared with $5,539,000 .in, 1927, a decrease of $2,973,000, or 34 per cent.
The same thing is true of butter, which I mentioned a few minutes ago. And as regards cheese, our imports have increased 48 per cent. Those who are interested in the dairy industry will note that fact-an increase of 48 per cent in our imports of cheese, notwithstanding the fact that this country used to be the leading cheese producer in the world. It will take just one year more of this government's administration to wipe out the industry, and there will be no cheese factories left. But while there has been an increase of 4S per cent in our imports of cheese, our exports of the same commodity have declined by 15.9 per cent. The same thing is true, again, of eggs: our imports have increased by 7 per cent while there has been a decrease in exports of 148 per cent. Is it any wonder at all that the people of this country are getting tired of the present government? How long will it take the government to put Canadians out of business entirely and force them to cross the line, whether they want to go or not?
I have almost finished, Mr. Speaker. I believe I have two minutes left and in that time I will try to discuss a more pleasing subject, one which the government probably would rather listen to. I want to call their attention to conditions in the Peace River country. There is no denying the fact that in the Peace River district there is presented a great opportunity to bring in a population which would very rapidly enhance the prosperity of that part of the Dominion, because we have there a very fertile and productive territory.

The hon. member's time is up.
On motion of Mr. Glen the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe the house adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
Monday, March 5, 1928
The house miet at three o'clock.
