subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb, (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Cahan, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Fansher (East Lambton).

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will expect no bouquets from me to-day for the proposals contained in his budget speech, but that need not prevent me from extending to him my sincere sympathy in the discharge of the high duties of his office. He is a somewhat paradoxical gentleman, and as he sits and listens to criticisms of his budget speech he must come to the conclusion that he is of all members of the house the despoiler and the destroyer of our economic system. Yet it is a peculiar and remarkable thing that of all the members of this house there is none more trusted and more fully respected; he is certainly one of the greatest assets of this government to-day.
I propose to address myself more particularly to the two amendments which have been moved, the first by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) which is as follows:
This house regrets that the measures proposed by the government do not tend to provide increased employment in Canada, nor to induce the return of Canadians to their native land, nor to prevent the continued emigration of our people to the United States; and that they make no provisions for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products, nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the 1st of January, 1929-
It will be noted that the hon. member makes no reference to the reduction in the 56103-63i
rate of income tax. He stated at the beginning of his speech that his was-
.	.	.	. the task of replying to that address
and of setting forth as best I can the Views and policy of the Conservative party in this house and in the country on the several matters enunciated by the Minister of Finance ....
In the course of his speech the hon. member made some slight and casual references to the income tax, in one of which he admitted that the reductions in the income and sales taxes were reductions of special war taxes, and from the lack of comment on these reductions in the amendment I assume, as this house is entitled to assume, that the Conservative party are in favour of the reductions proposed. I intend to deal with that proposal later on, in its proper place. By this amendment the hon. member deplores the fact that the proposed measures do not tend to promote increased employment in Canada, to induce the return of Canadians to this country or to prevent the emigration of our people and I assume from the phraseology employed that this is intended to cover three major proposals, the latter two of which are related and should really form one.
I have carefully read the speech of the hon. gentleman in order to ascertain the remedies proposed by his party to overcome these defects, and so far as I can ascertain he proposes to meet these difficulties by the application of certain principles which he enunciated in the course of his speech, and which will be found in Hansard of Monday, February 20. I have not time to read these nor do I think it necessary to deal with them seriatim; they are couched in the usual form of convention resolutions dealing with matters of policy. They are broad enough to cover the Dominon of Canada; they are wide enough to embrace every body, political, religious and social, and they are deep enough to justify their application by any party in whatever way is found most convenient. Unfortunately for the hon. gentleman, however, they were framed in a setting which portrayed a picture entirely different from that conveyed by their verbiage; I think there was no necessity for so many words, because I am satisfied that one word alone would have conveyed the whole meaning, and that word is "protection." If that is not the meaning of the resolutions, and if that is not the method by which the unemployment and the immigration problems are to be settled, then the hon. gentleman has missed the import of all the speeches made from his side of the house.
The Budget-Mr. Glen

With that principle I do not agree, nor do those who sit around me. Consider paragraph 4 of these principles, which is as follows:
The stabilization in Canada of the costs of living and the costs of implements of production on such comparatively low bases as will enable our people, in producing and selling our surplus of national products abroad, to compete advantageously with the products of foreign countries in our common markets abroad.
That is exactly what we in the west have been striving for during many years, and we have found that to be contrary to the policies adopted by the party to which the hon. .gentleman belongs. The west has advocated free trade on those articles which comprise the essentials of living and the means of production, at the same time not denying to the east the same advantages. So far as I know, no one denies the east the advantage of free trade; no one wishes to deprive the manufacturers of their right to the raw material which enters into their finished product.
Let me quote a few examples to show how the manufacturers have made use of this principle. You will find that they are entitled to a drawback of 99 per cent on rolled iron, rolled steel and pig iron when used in the manufacture of mowing machines, reapers, harvesters, binders and attachments for binders. They are also entitled to a drawback of 99 per cent on steel used in the manufacture of cutlery, files, augers, auger bits, bit braces, hammers, axes, hatchets, scythes, reaping hooks, hoes, hay or straw knives, agricultural forks, hand rakes, skates, stove trimmings, bicycle chains and windmills. Manufacturers who import malleable iron castings or steel shafting for use exclusively in the manufacture of mowing machines, harvesters, self binding or without binders, binding attachments, reapers and complete parts thereof, cultivators, harrows, horse rakes, seed drills, manure spreaders, weeders and complete parts thereof, ploughs and complete parts thereof, wind stackers and threshing machine separators including baggers, weighers and self feeders therefor and complete parts thereof, spraying machines, fruit or vegetable grinding machines, incubators, brooders, jimmy hooks, shears, hay grain cutters, fanning mills, milking machines and so on are entitled to a drawback of SO per cent. All materials entering into the cost of the manufacture of binder twine or twine for harvest binders, when imported for such use exclusively by manufacturers manufacturing such twine only are entitled to a drawback of 99 per cent.
These finished articles include many of the implements of production. Under our tariff 
laws the manufacturer is entitled to a drawback on the materials used by him in the manufacture of these implements; in many cases he pays a duty of only one per cent. This is a fundamental free trade policy; the manufacturer requires it and no one gainsays his right to it, but there is no known method by which the farmer can secure such a drawback, and consequently he can only work for relief by way of lower duties. Surely there is something inconsistent and illogical in the system which permits the manufacturer to accept a free trade policy in the initial processes of his business but to deny that policy when he imposes a duty on his finished article, which duty must be paid by the farmer who has no drawback and who cannot add to the price of his product. The consumer says that if it is necessary this should be done, but I am sure the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George will agree that it should not be done on the ex-parte statement of the manufacturers alone. We say to them: Prove your claim before the tribunal which has been constituted, namely, the tariff advisory board, and when it is proved then, and then only, shall the remedy be applied.
The latter part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) regrets that there are no provisions-
-for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the 1st of January, 1929.
The hon. member does not deal at any length with any of these propositions, and I shall follow his example. I will merely say that the arguments advanced by the hon. gentleman on the question of markets, if he will pardon me for saying so were not very convincing. I shall deal with the question of the sales tax later. In my view, therefore, there is nothing that I can hope for by supporting the amendment of the hon. member. It seems to me that its form and its enunciation are more academic than real. It may be good doctrine from the point of view of the hon. member, and he may believe it, but it is not sufficient to convince me, and I shall therefore oppose the amendment. I come now to the sub-amendment of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher), which reads as follows:
This house regrets that the government proposes further reductions in the income tax, thus making a serious departure from the principle of direct taxation; that the proposed revision of the customs tariff is inadequate to bring effective relief to the consuming public; and that the sales tax on the necessaries of life has not been eliminated.

The Budget-Mr. Glen
Now the subamendment is in a different class from the amendment in that it is categorical in its terms and concrete in its application. I will deal in the first instance with the second part of it as to the revision of the customs tariff. I am not convinced that the sweeping charge made has been proved either by the mover in his fair and able address, or by subsequent speakers fair or unfair. These schedules are still unintelligible to the ordinary member, and the extraordinary member who does understand them has not revealed himself. There is need of investigation before definite conclusions can be arrived at, but I think that some general conclusions can be stated on part at least of the schedules. Prior to the introduction of the budget I, like others, was struck by this fact, namely, the absolute lack of press or other propaganda for increased or higher duties; even Besco was unwontedly silent. There may have been other causes, but I feel that at least one of the causes was the demolition of the applications of the manufacturers before the tariff board. I have always said that this question of tariff reform could not and cannot be understood until the question has been properly presented and properly published. We are now in the position where evidence can be presented, and only at this session can it now be published. I am going to suggest to the Minister of Finance that the evidence of the tariff board should be published in the form of a daily Hansard for the information of members and the public generally. After all the tariff board is a public body maintained at public expense, and its work should certainly be available to the public. Its principal function I understand is to get facts. I can only get these facts when applications are made for a hearing. In view of this it seems to me that it is altogether too early to decry the work of the board. It is only beginning to function, and if the government wishes the board to function as it should, and if it wishes to remove the suspicion which has been voiced in this house that the board is only a smoke screen for the government, it can easily dispel that suspicion by the publication of the records of the board.
Now, sir, I have, like most hon. members, considered as carefully as I could1 the question of the proposed changes in the tariff schedules submitted by the Minister of Finance. I realize that a number of these proposals are for the purpose of reclassification and enumeration of different items, tending to give a more scientific and more understandable tariff schedule. To that idea no one
will take exception, and I do not think it would be unwise to suggest a revision of the whole of the customs schedule. I realize in some degree what that means but as, in the last analysis, the government must depend upon supplies for the carrying on of public business, and as the largest part of our revenue is derived from customs, the undertaking would only be what might be called in ordinary mercantile establishments good business. Now apart from this classification I think it can be shown that there are a number of items, affecting cottons and linens principally, on which reductions are made in the existing tariff; and I think there are one or two instances which show increases. But I will not presume definitely to pronounce upon these items in this forty minute speech; when the budget goes to committee I shall take whatever opportunity presents itself to ascertain precisely the truth of the statement I have just made. The Minister of Finance has stated on his authority as a member of the government that there have been downward revisions. That statement from one in his position must be accepted as correct, failing evidence to the contrary, and so far as I have heard or read no one as yet has endeavoured to prove the contrary.
I am further strengthened in my viewpoint by this fact, that if no downward revision has been made, then one would imagine that the industries affected would have no complaint, and hon. members opposite who support protection and the sheltered industries would have acquiesced. I took the trouble to search Hansard and learn what has been said by hon. members, and I find that the member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) said on the 23rd of February, as reported at page 731 of Hansard, referring to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler):
He is an able native son of our county. But with the influence which I presume he has with this government it seems to me that he might have been a little more successful in protecting some of the industries which are established in the southern part of the county and which have been very badly hit by this budget.	I refer more particularly to the
textile industries, those of woven cloths and worsteds.
And the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), an apostle of high protection, said on the 21st February, as reported at page 656 of Hansard:
While the tariff changes may seem minor when one looks at them first, already from reports coming in to members of this house who have in their constituencies mills which are affected by these tariff changes, it looks as if serious injury was once again going to be done by this government to the industrial life of this country.
The Budget-Mr. Glen

Further on he says:
As time goes on, the government and the people of this country will find that the reductions in the present tariff, though minor in appearance, will do more injury to the industrial life of our country-
That is the opinion of this hon. member, and what have the industries affected said or done? I have not asked for nor obtained any names, but I am informed that numerous representations have been made by the woollen industry against the changes in the customs tariff rates. Some of these have been made in person, others by letter or telegram, and the burden of the complaint is that the revision will mean that they will have to close up their plants. Various textile manufacturers have objected to the changes on the ground that they require more and more protection. Paper manufacturers have interviewed the Minister of Finance and have protested against the eighty per cent drawback on paper used in the production of magazines. Cordage manufacturers have sent delegations protesting against the reductions. Chemical industries have interviewed the Minister of Finance and protests have also been received from them.
In view of these gloomy anticipations which, in my judgment, are only a repetition of the honk of the automobile, it seems to me that the sub-amendment is inadequate on this point, and its real meaning is that the budget has not gone far enough in its downward revision. But I must assume in the light of present knowledge, that the manufacturers who ought to know their own business are convinced that the proposed alterations have a downward tendency and consequently that revision will have an effect on the price to the consumer. As I said at the beginning, I am not here to hand out any bouquets to the Minister of Finance and I do not think he would expect them from me. These revisions are not what I hoped for; they are considerably less than I expected, and I would certainly have been much more satisfied with greater cuts. I am not unmindful of the fact that the present Minister of Finance, in his budgets since 1922 and in his dealings with tariff, cannot surely be charged with serving the cause of protection, but that whatever revisions have been made have been consistently downward. Only on Saturday morning I happened to receive in the mail the February issue of the Journal of Commerce which somewhat goes to support what I have said. This Journal of Commerce is a review of industry, commerce and finance, published monthly from the Garden City Press at Gardenvale, Quebec.
{Mr. Glen.]

They know, as most people in the west know, that such a deal would be in the nature of that known as robbing Peter to pay Paul, Paul representing the proteictionsts. Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should commence my speech without expressing to my friends opposite my appreciation of the measure of applause which they have given me on this occasion-I suppose it is because I seldom trespass upon the good nature of the house.

The Budget-Mr. Boys
As I have said on previous occasions, during my years as chief whip of the Conservative party, I thought silence was golden, and I imagine my hon. friend the government whip (Mr. Casgrain) will probably agree with me in that.
My main purpose in rising to take part in the debate is to discuss the merits and demerits of free trade and protection in connection with certain Canadian industries. But before doing so I wish to say a word or two upon three or four matters which have been engaging the attention of the house. First, I shall touch on the question of the right of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) to issue permits under the provisions of the Immigration Act.
If I required any excuse, Mr. Speaker, for touching upon this subject, it would be found in the invitation given by the minister himself to the lawyer members to express their views. If the rules of the house permitted, I should be glad to read what was said during the dialogue which took place between the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) and the Minister of Immigration and the Minister of Health (Mr. King) last Tuesday, February 28. But I think my recollection is accurate when I say that the Minister of Immigration stated distinctly that he had not authority under the act to issue a permit in the case under discussion. If I am wrong in that I shall be glad to give him an opportunity of correcting me, for I can assure him that I have not the slightest desire to mis-state anything he said in the discussion. In this view he was supported by the Minister of Health, and evidently it was thought that what had then been said was insufficient, for two days afterwards the Minister of Health himself made a speech dealing with the matter. To summarize the position, both ministers are of opinion that under the act the Minister of Immigration has no right to issue a permit.
In the discussion last Tuesday nothing was said about section 18, but in his speech the Minister of Health says that is the controlling section, and because of it there is no right to issue a permit. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, we will all agree upon this, that if ever there was a case that merited the exercise of favourable discretion on the part of the Minister of Immigration-if he has that discretion-it certainly was the case in question. I do not think for one moment that the minister would want to separate a baby of fourteen months old from its mother, nor, on the other hand, the mother and baby from the father and the other four little
members of the family. I am sure the whole house is agreed upon that proposition. It therefore brings us to a direct discussion as to the power of the minister under the act. To properly consider the question it will be necessary for me to quote one or two sections. Under section 3 we find this provision :
No immigrant, passenger or other person, unless he is a Canadian citizen, or has Canadian domicile, shall be permitted to enter or land in Canada, or in case of having landed in or entered Canada, shall be permitted to remain therein, who belongs to any of the following classes, hereinafter called "prohibited classes":

Then follow the various classes, and the main class is found in subsection (a):
Idiots. imbeciles, feeble-minded persons, epileptics, insane persons, and persons who have been insane at any time previously;
Then follows a subsection with respect to diseased persons, and so on, which I need not trouble the house with. Now let me quote section 4:
The minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada, or having entered or landed in Canada to remain therein without being subject to the provisions of this act. Such permit shall be in the form A of the schedule to this act, and shall be expressed to be force for a specified period only, but it may at any time be extended or cancelled by the minister in writing; and such extension or cancellation shall be in the form B of the schedule to this act.
Then follows a subsection No. 2 providing for returns of such permits to parliament.
Now then, the Minister of Health, to whom up to date has fallen the lot of giving the house the benefit of the law on the subject, says that the controlling section is section 18. Any person who reads the act will see that this section has not the slightest bearing upon a case of this kind because it deal's with cases where an appeal is to be taken from the decision of the board of inquiry. There was no appeal in this case. The child never landed, but was compelled to return to Scotland with its mother. So section 18 has not the slightest bearing upon the case. I am ready to admit that had the parents of the child appealed from the decision of the board of inquiry to the minister, under that section the child could not have been admitted. But, sir, there was no appeal taken, and the section has no application whatsoever. Therefore we are driven to a consideration of section 3 and section 4. Let us again consider section 4:
The minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada, or having entered or landed in Canada to remain therein-

So far as I am concerned I benefit to some extent by a reduction in the income tax. But this benefit is not anything like as important as many people think. On an income of 810,000 it means $23; on an income of $5,000, half that sum, and above that income in proportion. I would much prefer to do without that benefit, and, speaking purely from a selfish standpoint, I am inclined to think I would benefit more by the abolition of the sales tax. But whether I would or would not, I am absolutely in favour of the total abolition of the sales tax at the earliest possible date, and I am in accord with the suggestion made on behalf of this policy in the amendment. And when the time comes and the revenues of the country permit a reduction in income tax, by all means let us have it; but let the first tax to be abolished be the sales tax, thereby benefiting not the few, who can afford to pay, but all the people of the land. I could not favour the middle portion of the subamendment because it would be contrary to the protective principle with which I agree. I could not support the subamendment for the further reason that it entirely abolishes the amendment of my own party and that in itself would be a sufficient justification for my voting against it.
A word as to the Home Bank. I will come now to the question of free trade and the tariff. I hold no brief whatever for the manufacturer; I am not interested in any manner whatsoever in any manufacturing industry in Canada. But so far as I am concerned I do favour adequate
protection. I repudiate the suggestion that the party to -which I belong are high protectionists, although I believe there are cases where a higher protection would result in lower prices, and in that respect I should think the principle would accord with the views of any hon. member. I feel I have a peculiar right to discuss the question of protection inasmuch as I was elected twice upon that issue and it fell to my lot to be opposed, both in 1925 and 1926 by no less a person, than the Hon. E. C. Drury, the leader of the Progressive party in the province of Ontario, exPrime Minister of Ontario, past master of the Ontario Grange, and, until a few days ago, president of the Progressive party itself. He is perhaps one of the ablest, and certainly one of the most outstanding free traders in the Dominion. The Hon. Mr. Drury challenged me to a joint debate and as a matter of fact we had two debates, one in the town of Barrie and one in Collingwood, the subject under discussion being the tariff.	We each had, all
told, an hour, and perhaps it is not amiss for me to say that I doubt whether in any country town there have ever been two more largely attended meetings. In my own town the armory was jammed; there were over 4,000 people present. And in the skating rink in the town of Collingwood the attendance was also exceptional, many being unable to gain admittance. I may add that a good many persons came from beyond the confines of the county of Simcoe,- expecting no doubt a scrap of some sort. We discussed the tariff, and I will take this opportunity of showing to the house some articles that played a very important part, particularly in the election of 1926. I made it my business to have a friend of mine attend the meetings of my opponent to find out just what he was saying to the people, and I ascertained that he was going about with a small general stock of merchandise comprising ladies' dresses, ladies' silk stockings and hardware of varied descriptions, including two hammers. These hammers are well known in the county of Simcoe and fairly well known in the province of Ontario, but I do not suppose they are quite so well known in other portions of the Dominion or in the House of Commons. I have these hammers here and I thought the house might be interested to have a look at them. They were utilized for the purpose of exterminating me politically in those two elections. They have a history and it is necessary that I should give that history if the house is fully to appreciate what took place. I noticed that during the last week of the campaign of 1925 they were not displayed. I really did not know at that time why their use was discontinued, but for some reason or other they were abandoned. Now
The Budget-Mr. Boys

Mr. Drury's argument was this:	"Here is a
hammer made in the United States, price $1.65; and here is another hammer made in St. Catharines, Canada, price 11.75". As I say, this is Mr. Drury's argument, which I am illustrating in my own humble way. He was much more dramatic than I can be. He said, "If it were not for the tariff you would be able to buy this American hammer for $1.35 instead of $1.65". Of course, he received warm applause; the argument created great satisfaction among the farming community then present. I heard no more about the hammers during the last week of the campaign but after the election I heard something about them. I found that they were available. Mr. Drury had not bought them; he had only borrowed them, and having had the full use of them for a month he returned them. Having ascertained that they had been restored to the place whence they had come, I inquired whether I could purchase them and was informed that, like any other article in the store, they were for sale. I promptly said, they are mine, and I bought and paid for them. That hon. gentleman went around for three or four weeks telling the people that this hammer was made in the United States, and if it were not for our tariff it could be bought for $1.35, while the other hammer was made in Canada. On both these hammers, however, stamped in the plainest possible lettering, we find the words, "Made in Canada." They are here for anyone to see, and they were there at the time to be seen. Mr. Drury's explanation, when finally cornered, was that he thought one was made in. the United States. To be fair to him, he was apparently deceived by that little tag, but how in the name of goodness he could carry these hammers around for two or three weeks, producing them in the well lighted halls of North Simcoe, and fail to observe those words "Made in Canada " is beyond me. I do not suggest for one moment that he did it deliberately; I cannot think Mr. Drury would do that, but it is in keeping with many other fallacious arguments advanced by Mr. Drury and those who think with him on the question of free trade.
In deciding to what particular industries I should direct my attention, I wanted to get some which affected the rural population as much as, if not more than, the urban population, and I wanted to get two on the free list and two on the protected list. I think the arguments I am about to advance can be applied to a great many other industries, but the ones I have selected, rightly or wrongly, are those two standard industries

with which all free traders deal and with which Mr. Drury dealt in the debates we had together. I refer to binder twine and cream separators. The other two articles, both highly protected with a duty of 30 per cent, are rubber and leather.
The stock argument of the free trader is that the tariff is a tax and invariably the tariff raises prices; that is the argument we have to meet. In the election of 1925, before I knew the story of these hammers, I answered Mr. Drury in this way:	If the
tariff is a tax and always raises prices, and since the United States of America is one of the most highly protected nations in the world, why do you want free entry of their goods into Canada? If your argument is right the prices would be high and you would only secure the free entry of high-priced goods. That is what I cannot understand about many free traders; they want to get United States products intol this country, while no one will dispute the fact that the United States is one of the most highly protected countries in the world. Therefore, if the tariff is a tax surely the articles produced in the United States under this high protection must be high priced, and how are the people of Canada to gain by their free admission?

That left three up until two years ago, namely the Consumers' Cordage Company of Montreal and Dartmouth; the Plymouth Cordage Company of Welland and the Brantford Cordage Company of Brantford, and the latest information is that in 1926 the Dartmouth plant of the Consumers' Cordage Company ceased to manufacture binder twine, while in July, 1927, the Montreal plant of that company also ceased the manufacture of this article. That leaves only two. I understand there has been something of a controversy during the last few months in the Ottawa Citizen on this very question, and in this connection I would like to quote in part from a letter which appears in the Ottawa Citizen under date of February 7, 1928, over the signature of the Brantford Cordage Company. It was suggested that this business was not as well managed as it might be, and this letter is the answer of the company:
The business is still under the active management of Mr. C. L. Messecar, under whose direction the business was built up from small beginnings until it has become the largest binder twine plant in the British Empire .	.	.	. the present difficult situation is
entirely the result of new competition that has arisen from Holland and Germany.
The closing paragraph of the letter is as follows:
We have spoken to many representatives of western farmers' organizations and wherever the matter has been explained to them, they have agreed with us that some action should be taken and we trust this explanation will make our position clear. We can assure you there is nothing in the way of good management or handling of the business that can overcome the present handicap, for every other mill operating in Canada is suffering in the same way and one mill has recently closed and been dismantled, and the others, like ourselves, are operating with the hope that something will be done; but if nothing is done, it is not reasonable to think that any mill can continue indefinitely to operate at a loss.
Yours truly,
The Brantford Cordage Co., Limited. Jan. 31, 1928.
And this is one of the two remaining industries, and the largest one in the British Empire. That letter practically says " If something is not done we will go out of business too ". And yet we have people who
The Budget-Mr. Boys

suggest that there should be free trade in the case of an industry such as this which is absolutely suited to the country and which could make money under proper tariff conditions.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having regard to the experience of the two hon. members who have preceded me, I do not propose to take up the time of the house or my own time with any introduction, but I shall go directly to the matters which I wish to discuss. Before proceeding with my remarks, let me suggest to the house that, in view of the policy which has been enunciated by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) who has just sat down, it is rather surprising that I can find nowhere in the "swivel-chair" tariff resolution which was passed in Winnipeg any suggestion that either binder twine or cream separators should be made dutiable. I find further that my hon. friends opposite, in passing their resolution, have endeavoured at least to give the impression that:
It is desirable in the national interest that in such revisions of the tariff the cost of living and the cost of the implements used in the production of whatever nature should be given special and attentive study.
Whatever that may mean, it at least would not mean that binder twine, which has been on the free list since 1900, should now have a duty imposed on it, and that cream separators, which I think were put on the free list during the regime of my hon. friends opposite, should have a duty imposed upon them. My hon. friends, if they thought protection was a good thing, have had ample opportunity from 1911 to 1921 to impose a duty on binder twine and cream separators. I rather suspect my good friend who leads the opposition and who comes from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) would not regard that as a sound political move, regardless of the fact that his lieutenant behind him suggests that it may be sound economics.
I wish to discuss just one or two things which have been said in the course of the debate with regard to the position of Canada. Like other hon. members I have felt that there have been a good many sombre reflections in connection with conditions existing in this country and I should like to refer to the matter of the cost of living. Nothing is more important to those who propose to take up their residence in any country than to ascertain what conditions are respecting this thing knowrn as the cost of living. When the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), who I am sorry is not in his place today, suggested that the cost of living is higher in Canada than in the United States, and
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

when, the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) gave figures to indicate that the cost of living had increased since 1921, I hastened to look up the record in order to find out whether either of them was right. I am glad to be in a position to correct the statements made by both of these hon. gentlemen on this very important subject. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said that the government should do everything possible-
-to reduce the average cost of living in this country which is "so high in comparison with the cost of living in the same state of society across the border."
I have secured the figures of a food budget of articles in common everyday use, and I find that in 1925 that budget came to $8.70 in Canada and $10.46 in the United States. I have had that revised in accordance with present day prices and I find that the figures for 1927 amount to $9.63 for Canada and $11.44 for the United States; in other words, a difference in favour of Canada of nearly 20 per cent. The hon. member for Inverness stated in his speech:
"In 1922 the cost of living for a family budget, including foods, rent, clothing, and so forth, was $20.67 per week. In December of last year it was $21.37, a slight increase. In other words, the government have not made happier fireside climes for the poor people of Canada."
My good friend who gave the figure of $20.67 for 1922 had selected the month of July, 1922, and had attempted to compare that with the month of December, 1927. Perhaps my hon. friend missed the column, but I think it would have been better if he had looked at the figures for January, 1922, which show the cost of living for a week as $21.52, and the figure for December, 1927, is $21.37, so that there is a slight decrease. I am not, however, taking months; I think it is much fairer, when we are trying to ascertain the cost of living and to advertise to the prospective immigrant what conditions are in Canada, that we should tell him what the cost of living is for a year. The average for 1921 was $22.70, and for 1927, $21.20; in other words, the cost of living has declined.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
My hon. friend knows,
and there are gentlemen within the sound of my voice who know, that farm products and food products were almost at their lowest ebb in 1922 and there was not very much room for prosperity for either the artisan or the farmer in that particular year. I am pointing out that the period under comparison from

1921 to 1927 shows a marked decrease in the cost of living. An index figure which has been prepared by the bureau of statistics shows that not only for food but for rent, fuel, and everything else that enters into the cost of living, the figure was 167 for 1921 and 152 for 1927, and the general barometer, namely, the general average of wages, which my hon. friend suggested had gone down very materially, was 182.4 in 1922 and 184.3 in 1927. My hon. friends speak a great deal about employment. The index figure for general employment in 1922 was 87.9, bearing out what I have said about conditions which existed then; and in 1927 it was 103.4.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why does the minister take figures for 1922 in relation to employment and wages, and figures for 1921 in relation to the cost of living?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot tell my hon.
friend at the moment what the 1921 figures are. I should be glad to get the other figures or to have my hon, friend give them.
As regards this matter of advertising Canada, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), who is generally an optimist, I think rather threw a wet blanket over this house and1 he certainly did not play the part he generally does in advertising Canada when he made his reference to " thousands of closed plants from the Atlantic to the Pacific." I do not think that is a fair statement. I think the hon. gentleman, perhaps in the heat of his enthusiasm, went further than he intended. But I would point out that these things are not good advertising for Canada, and I think my colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has quite truly said that no better propaganda could be used by United States immigration agents, and more than that by immigration agents from other dominions of the British Empire who are seeking immigrants from the old country. If they are able to show that responsible members of the House of Commons make these statements regarding conditions in Canada, it seems to me we put into their hands an argument Which they cannot fail to use for the benefit of settlement in their own country.
I make these references only in passing because there are one or two matters with which I want to deal in regard to the steel industry, the fishing industry and general tariff matters mentioned in the budget.
Tabulations have been made and issued showing what has been done and what remains to be done under the document known as the Duncan report, and from time to time it has been suggested that a large percentage of the recommendations still remain to be

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
carried out. I am not going into details in connection with that report to-day except for the purpose of introducing a few words that I have to say with regard to the steel industry.
These tabluations have treated every matter mentioned in the Duncan report as of equal value: they have had no regard whatever to any sense of proportion. Now there are major matters dealt with in the Duncan report, and there are minor matters, and I want to point out that the five major matters dealt with in that report are:
1.	Freight rates,
2.	Money grants,
3.	Coking plants,
4.	Statutory harbour commissions,
5.	The steel and coal industry generally.
I want to say to this house and to the
province of Nova Scotia that in so far as the first four subjects are concerned, with the exception of the general financial revision which was suggested in the speech from the throne, they have practically all been dealt with as far as they legislatively can be. There still remains the matter of the steel and coal industry outside of the matter of coking plants, and that is what I desire to deal with now.
A good deal of talk is made in this country and has been heard in this house in regard to blast furnaces and as to the primary activities of the steel industry having gone down remarkably in the last few years. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George the other day read a most doleful statement with regard to blast furnaces. I also heard my hon. friend from Port Arthur-Thunder Bay (Mr. Cowan) make the statement that there were 22 blast furnaces in operation in 1913 and only 4 to-day. I understand that my good friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), speaking in Montreal a day or two ago, referred to the blast furnace industry as having been seriously depleted.

speechtext:
The steel industry, 1
said.
Mr. RALSTON':	But all these gentlemen
failed to note that there were two periods of government between 1913 and 1927, namely 1912 to 1922 and 1922 to 1927, and when I tell them that the blast furnace industry was worse in so far as employment and production was concerned in 1921, I think it will be seen that perhaps my hon. friends have not paid as much attention as they should have to the effect of the argument when it comes to deciding which party should govern this country. The period is 56103-64
taken from 1913 to 1927, the figures are given, and that is all that is suggested. Now I want to give the figures.
In 1913 the number of men employed in that industry was 1,589. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George gave the figure for 1925 as 656, but he did not say that in 1921 there were only 614, and he did not say that in 1927 there was an increase of 20 per cent, or 734.
With regard to production, and that is a very much more important item than how many furnaces are working part of the time,
I find that the annual production of pig iron in 1913 was roughly 1,000,000 tons; in 1921, 593,000 tons; in 1927, 907,000 tons. So our friends, if they want to find out what happened to the steel and blast furnace industry, will have to go back to the years between 1911 and 1921.

speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
will permit me to make my speech; I do not trouble the house very often.
I want to give my hon. friends another figure, and that is with regard to the balance of trade in steel products. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George suggests that we have a very large adverse balance of trade in steel products. In 1912 the adverse balance was $101,000,000; in 1921 that had grown to $169,000,000; and in 1927 it was back again to $106,000,000.
I want to say a word or two for the benefit of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) who knows more about the steel industry I suppose in five minutes than I can hope to know in my lifetime, but I have the temerity to suggest one or two figures and to make one or two statements as to what the records show.
It is suggested that the steel industry has gone to the demnition bow-wows because of the fact that there was a drawback put on the duty on agricultural implements. I want to remind my hon. friend-I know he is fair enough to admit it-that the steel industry in Nova Scotia never got its real foundation until the legislation of 1897 which was introduced by the Hon. Mr. Fielding in this house, and I think he will also agree with me that from that time on the steel industry in Nova Scotia prospered. Mr. Fielding gave assistance to the industry first in 1897 for a period of five years. In 1899 this assistance was made continuous for another five years, but at a diminishing rate. In 1903 he increased

The Budget-Mr. Ralston

the diminishing rate of assistance which was being given, and in 1907 he gave a further extension of that assistance.
I also want to point out to my hon. friends who are very solicitous about the use of Canadian ore that Mr. Fielding was the one who introduced legislation in 1907 providing for special assistance to any industry which would use Canadian ore. But what do we find? Our friends opposite came into power early in 1912, and did they revive the assistance which Mr. Fielding had given? Not a bit of it. Did they repeal the rebate on material used in the manufacture of agricultural implements? Not a bit of it. They left the rebate there; they left the industry without the assistance which the Liberals had given. I make no complaint whatever about their not cancelling the drawback on agricultural implements, but surely they should not complain of Liberal policy when they are the ones who did not raise a finger to help the steel industry in any practical way.
Further than that, I find that they did do something else to the steel industry in 1914. A further drawback was introduced whereby wire rods were practically put on the free list, because a drawback of 99 per cent was given. The result has been that most of the iron for wire fencing of certain gauges has come in and has been used under that drawback, and thousands of tons are being imported at the present time. That was under the Conservative administration. I make no complaint about it whatever. It is along the line of Liberal policy, which is to do the best it can for the industries of this country and at the same time to encourage the primary producers. That was the policy which Mr. Fielding introduced. The steel industry, judging by experience, cannot hope for much help from my hon. friends opposite. A good many tears are being shed, but they amount to nothing more than tears when it comes to the matter of practical assistance.
The other evening one hon. gentleman said that farm tractors were put on the free list in 1918, and the imports of farm tractors have grown tremendously, from $2,000,000 in 1925, to $5,900,000 in 1926, and $8,021,000 in 1927.
I am not complaining about that. It has meant cheap tractors for the farmers, but do not let my friends opposite weep and wail on behalf of the steel industry when they were the party who made these reductions.

speechtext:
I want to say a word with regard to the present situation. The steel industry , as I said, was dealt with in the Duncan report. I do not think anybody in this country regards the steel industry as being absolutely defunct. The records of the price of stock of the Steel Company of Canada do not so indicate, but there are primary industries, in Nova Scotia particularly, which do not enjoy the same advantages which the industries of central Canada have. The Nova Scotia industries are a long way from the market. They constitute the only self-contained British industry on the continent, and you can judge of the importance of the industry to Nova Scotia, when I tell you that 50 per cent of the assessment under the Workmen's Compensation Act is .paid by the coal and steel industry. ^ The Duncan commission heard evidence in connection with that industry and made 'their recommendations, and their recommendation was that the steel industry of Nova Sootia should be given similar assistance to that given the steel industries of central Canada. These steel industries are given a rebate of 99 per cent of the duty on coal used in the melting and smelting of metals. That was their recommendation. There has been a good deal of talk in this house and in the country as to why the government has not implemented that particular recommendation. I would would remind hon. members of what was said at the time. Speaking in this house on March 18 last the Prime Minister said:
. Owing to the existing uncertainty of conditions surrounding the iron and steel industry in the maritimes, the government does not feel in the position to make at present any pronouncement with respect to the commission's recommendations of a renewal of the system granting bounties with respect to steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture.
It will be remembered that for the last year and a half the industry has been in the throes of litigation. To announce that assistance would be given to the steel industry, with two parties contesting for its control, would simply mean throwing something extra into the ring to be contested for; on the other hand, to announce that no assistance would be given would be to throw the industry on the bargain counter. Therefore the government did not make any pronouncement whatever. That position was amply supported, not simply by Liberals but by Conservatives as well, in the press of Nova Scotia. I have in my hand a statement made by the Hon, G. S. Harrington, Minister of Public Works and

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Mines in Nova Scotia, published a day or two after the Prime Minister's statement in this house. Mr. Harrington said:
There will be general regret that the present disturbed condition of the steel and coal industry has led the government to defer beneficial action toward it in keeping with the report. It is no secret, however, that a very general organization of this industry is requisite. At present it appears to be passing through the unsettled stages essential towards that end. It is to be hoped that very shortly it will emerge in a condition that will merit and obtain for it consideration as a great national asset as necessary to the rest of Canada as it is beneficial to Nova Scotia.
The Halifax Herald of the same date said:
It is not necessary to discuss the present litigation affecting the steel industry in support of such an attitude-
Meaning the attitude of the government.
-the necessity for this reservation is selfevident.
A similar statement appeared in the Sydney Post of March 21. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these references amply confirm the soundness of government's position. Only recently has the announcement come that litigation has been terminated and that control of this great industry has definitely passed into the hands of a new and strong financial group. But there still remain certain things to be done. It seems to me that it is in the interest of this industry and in the interest of the Dominion that-first, there should be unity between the coal and the steel businesses. Secondly, there should be a shrinkage of the capital so that the industry will have an opportunity of earning a dividend on some reasonable investment. Thirdly, the unwieldy organization should be simplified. It now consists of some fourteen companies. Fourthly, there ought to be co-operation by the provincial and municipal authorities in the work of building up this great industry. With the litigation ended and these conditions met, the way will be open for serious consideration by the federal government of the presentation of the real and legitimate needs of the industry.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word in respect to the fishing industry dealt with by my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst). I regret that he should have seen fit in the course of the debate to suggest that political considerations dictated the sittings of the commission which is now investigating the fisheries of the maritimes provinces. Let me say to him and other hon. members that the places where the commission was to sit were selected solely with the desire that the commission should get just as close as possible to those engaged in the industry so that every man might have an opportunity of presenting 56103-641
his arguments or views. The idea was that the fishermen of the maritime provinces and a portion of Quebec-which was also included -should have an opportunity of being heard. The commission got tc- work in October, and even though the weather was inclement they proceeded with their inquiry, their desire being to have their report ready for this house at this session. The commission held over forty sittings, travelled sixty days and heard 818 witnesses. Naturally a good deal of expense was incurred, because the commission undertook to pay the expenses of witnesses, delegates elected at meetings of fishermen all over the maritime provinces, in order that their views might be presented. The commission will, I hope, be able to present its report in a very short time, and as one interested in our fisheries I look forward with a great deal of confidence indeed to the findings which it will make, because, as I have said, the fishermen have had as never before an opportunity to present their needs, their problems and their difficulties, and I am sure they will say that they have received a most sympathetic hearing from the commission.
My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg made some suggestions in regard to improving conditions affecting the fisheries. He mentioned the matter of trawlers. I take it from What he said that he is not against the trawler, that his only complaint is .that trawlers which are not really of Canadian register are operating as Canadian trawlers. I assume that if that condition is remedied my hon. friend is favourable to the trawler.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit just one more question?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend must
allow me to proceed. He suggested a constructive policy and urged that there should be efficient inspection. I think he knows that efficient inspection has been inaugurated and in active practice during the past few years, and last year a further advance was made. My hon. friend advocates collection boats. He knows that collection boats wrere put on last year and are working actively, particularly on the eastern shores of Nova Scotia. He speaks of experimental stations, and says that we are only "scratching the surface" in that regard. I think my hon. friend did himself an injustice in that respect, because he knows the experimental station which was started by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) at Halifax is regarded as a model, not simply in North America but in England as well. The empire marketing board has specially mentioned the experimental station started by the government of Canada, and a request has come from the Imperial Economic Commission that the services of Dr. Huntsman -who is in charge of this experimental station-be loaned to Great Britain.
With regard to education, we have already established a fisheries course at Dalhousie university with the degree of bachelor of science in subjects affecting fisheries. I am glad to be able to tell this house that about two weeks ago nineteen young men returned to their homes in Nova Scotia after a six weeks' course under the system of scholarships promoted by this government, in order that they might apply to their work not only practical but scientific knowledge respecting the fishing industry. Those young men returned home convinced that the fishing industry will be best developed if scientific education goes hand in hand with practical work. They will be crusaders in this work.

If I mistake not the idea is to increase the scholarships to fifty for the next course.
As to co-operative marketing, my hon. friend knows, I think, that that is essentially a matter within the jurisdiction of the provinces. I would remind him that years ago a Liberal government in Nova Scotia put upon the statute books of the province an act providing for the free incorporation of fishermen who want to work together co-operatively.
With respect to radio, my hon. friend is quite right. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) was the first one to suggest that the fishing boats be equipped with radio receiving apparatus. Last year, at the hon. member's suggestion, an offer was made to the fishermen of Nova Scotia to broadcast weather reports, but the schooner owners felt that they could not equip their boats. This year, I understand, the offer is being repeated and it is probable that radio broadcasting of weather reports and bulletins will be afforded the fishermen and that the receiving apparatus will be installed on the vessels.
The hon. member also suggests that we should have wider markets. As was suggested last year when the announcement was made by the Prime Minister with regard to the recommendations contained in the Duncan report it does seem unfortunate that our friends should find out so late that after all wider markets are what we need most to encourage all industry. We had an opportunity in 1911 to secure wider markets for Nova Scotia but we did not take advantage of it, and ever since we have been looking for the chance to develop wider avenues of trade. I would remind my hon. friends opposite that in 1923 the then Minister of Finance, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, inserted in our tariff laws a provision that the governor in council might authorize negotiations with any authorized representative of the government of the United States with a view to the making of a commercial agreement between the two countries that might be deemed mutually beneficial. May I also point out that Mr. Fielding also provided that any time the United States reduced their duty on certain natural products, including fish, then the governor in council was empowered to do the same. This constitutes a standing offer in the direction of developing wider markets. I would remind the house further that we have a legation at Washington, and while this is an international question such as one cannot very well discuss here in so short a time, I hope it may be possible eventually to come to some satisfactory arrangement. I do not think it can be questioned for a moment that the

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Liberal party and the Liberal government have done all in their power to secure wider markets not only for the fishery products of Canada but for our other natural products as well. In order to find markets for the products of our fisheries, the Liberal government, in 1908, I believe, undertook to pay one-third of the express rates on fish coming west. That arrangement continued until 1918 when our Conservative friends abolished it. It had proved most beneficial, as shown by the fact that our fisheries products coming west increased 300 per cent in that period. But once again a Liberal government came to the assistance of the fishery industry last session by the 20 per cent freight rate reduction.
Now, may I tell hon. gentlemen what we are doing in the matter of markets. In 1923 our shipments of fresh and frozen fresh fish to points beyond the maritime provinces totalled 35,452,138 pounds, and in 1926, 49,612,366 pounds, or an increase of 40 per cent. The shipments of fresh and smoked fish by the Canadian National Railways have increased from 7,000 tons odd in 1921 to some 15,000 tons in 1926, while by express there has been an increase from 8,000,000 pounds in 1921 to 12,000,000 pounds odd in 1926. It is obvious, therefore, that we are doing something practical for the fishing industry. We cannot discount the problems and difficulties which face the fishing industry of the maritime provinces to-day, and the constructive policies which we have put in force have indicated, I think, how fully we realize the importance of the industry. When I think of these men and of the work to which they have devoted their lives, I do not dolefully picture, as some hon. members have done, village after village of silent streets and boarded windows; rather do I see men working hard and earnestly, endeavouring to do their utmost to earn a living at a vocation which is by no means easy, but at the same time exhibiting the spirit which has characterised generation after generation of our seafaring men. Let me assure the house that it is in the improving of the conditions under which these men labour, and in the effort to help them to overcome their difficulties, that we are seriously engaged at the present time. The adversity of the fishermen is the adversity of the Dominion, and similarly the prosperity of the fishermen is the prosperity of the country as a whole. That is the reason why the government is so earnestly facing the situation and trying by every means in its power to help.
Now I want to say a word with regard to the general provisions of the budget, which has been thoroughly discussed, almost every
hon. member who has spoken having touched upon many phases of it. I should like to gather up a few of the thoughts that occur to me regarding the general effect of the budget from every point of view. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg wanted to know what the budget contained for the fishing industry, for agriculture, and for the various other industries. My reply is that there is in this budget just what has been in every other budget brought down by the Liberal government since it assumed office in 1922: a lessening of the burden of taxation generally; special relief for those engaged in our basic industries and for the implements which they use in production; substantial relief from taxation of those articles which make up the necessaries of life; consideration for those who are least able to bear the burden of taxation; and the recognition that no one section of the community, or no one occupation can claim the benefit of special privileges. I have had necessarily to condense the outstanding results of this government's tariff legislation, and now I may indicate something of what has been done for each of our various industries.
What do we find in the case of agriculture? There has been a 100 per cent reduction of the sales tax on all essential implements for tilling the soil and gathering the crops, and in addition there have been placed on the free list such articles as mowers, harvesters, reapers, cultivators, harrows, manure spreaders and seed drills. Then there is the 90 per cent drawback on materials for the manufacture of general farm implements, besides a 100 per cent reduction of the sales tax and a reduction of from 33 to 75 per cent on labour-saving machinery for modern farming, the tariff rate now being the minimum. There have also been reductions of 100 per cent of the sales tax and of the tariff on fertiliers and spraying preparations, and a cancellation of the sales tax on feeds of all sorts and on general farm products. So much for agriculture.
What about mining? There has been a 100 per cent reduction in the sales tax on all machinery and equipment for the extraction of minerals from their natural state, and a reduction of approximately 40 per cent on all essential machinery.
So far as logging and lumbering operations are concerned, there has been a 100 per cent reduction in the sales tax and a tariff reduction of 33} per cent on machinery and equipment for logging and sawing up to the finished lumber.
As regards fishing, there have been the following reductions:	100 per cent in the sales
tax on all essential materials and equipment;
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

100 per cent in the tariff on fishermen's rope for all purposes up to l j inches; 40 per cent reduction in the tariff on oiled clothing; and 33| per cent reduction in the tariff on motor
engines and parts.
And in the interests of the great mass of our population, including all the others I have enumerated, we find that there has been a complete cancellation of the sales tax on the most essential foods and 50 per cent on others. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Glen) in his admirable speech, gave a list of them. In addition to this, there have been reductions on the following commodities: 35 per cent on raw and refined sugar; 124 per cent on cotton, woollen and flannel fabrics; 33per cent on mitts; 20 per cent on woollen socks and stockings; 25 per cent on heavy woollen underwear; 33^ per cent on cotton blankets; 25 per cent on sheets, table cloths, pillow cases, towels and other household cottons, and 50 per cent in the sales tax on boots and shoes. At the same time, what has happened to our industries. Have they been injuriously affected? Let me give some of the figures in regard to the number of employees engaged, and the value of the products turned out in the year 1922 as compared with the year 1926. In 1922 we find that there were 474,000 employees m all industries in Canada, producing goods to the value of 12,482,000,000, while in 1926 the number of employees had increased to 550,000 and the value of the products of industry to
$3,250,000,000.	.
Some hon. gentleman the other evening complained of the damage done to the agricultural implement industry and he made reference to the extent of our imports under this head. I, on my part, desired to know how many implements we were producing in Canada, because after all that is the barometer: we probably have to import some owing to the extensive activities in our agricultural pursuits. In 1922 we employed in this industry 6,221 workmen and in 1926 10,091; and in the former year we made implements to the value of $18,240,000 while in 1926 the value of these products had increased to $38,269,214. As regards boots and shoes, in 1922 the industry gave employment to 13,702 workmen and in 1926, 15,016; and while the value of the products in 1922 was $45,503,858, in 1926 it was $49,096,000.
So far as mineral production is concerned, my hon. friends opposite have had a good deal to say regarding the present condition of the industry. They declare that there is no mineral production going on.
