Let me inform the
house that the peak of mineral production was reached in 1927, with a total value of $242,000,000. In connection with our estimated surplus for this year I would remind my hon. friends that no less a sum than $14,000,000 has been written off in connection with the revaluation of lands under the soldier settlement scheme, and we still have a balance on the right side of the ledger of $38,000,000; and as regards our foreign trade, there has been an increase in the total from $1,501,731,000, the figure for the year 1922, to $2,298,466,000 in 1927, or an increase of 53 per cent.	[DOT]
Surely the facts I have cited must convince the house that the Minister of Finance has kept faith with the people of Canada. Geography and climate have set for the founders and builders of this nation a great problem; they have created vast difficulties. Scattered along the 3,000 miles of narrow territory are communities of men and women each with difficulties peculiar to their own vocation and locality. To keep faith with all parts of the Dominion requires courage, sympathy, judgment and sincerity. I believe that not only this house but the people of this country as well will agree that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance possesses these qualities to a marked degree.
I want to remind my hon. friend that not only must the government keep faith; not only must the Minister of Finance keep faith, but the people of Canada must keep faith one with the other. There must be mutual tolerance and mutual forbearance regarding the various problems which present themselves in their various callings and localities. To turn over the pages of this budget and simply look for those items which will give a direct and particular advantage to any individual industry or locality is not and never can be the test. I say that a study of this budget and of the budgets which have preceded it will show the same principles in all; consideration for the masses, relief from taxation, stimulation of production and encouragement of industry, and .so long as these principles are maintained in our budgets no class or section of Canada need have any fear. In a word, Mr. Speaker, I think we can regard this budget as a stimulating new chapter in that book of "all-Canada" budgets which have been

The Budget-Mr. Neill
brought down by the Liberal government since 1922; I believe it will be received in that spirit by all parts of Canada and that it will receive genuine support not only in this house but throughout the Dominion as a whole.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will excuse me if I do not appear to address myself so much to you as to the hands of the clock, which haunt me with the ghastly record of how quickly the few minutes allotted to me are passing away. With regard to the budget, if everything which has been said in its favour is true it is indeed a thing beloved of God; if, however, everything which has been said against it is true it is what the man in the street would call a holy terror. After listening to the extreme views on both sides of the question for nearly three weeks, I have decided to believe neither side. At any rate, the budget is a fait accompli now; it has been brought down and the government have a majority with which to pass it, so time will show the result. I would prefer now to discuss one or two points on which the policy of the government has not yet, been declared1, in the hope that when they come to formulate a policy they will at least give some consideration to the views of British Columbia, which I propose to express.
_ The first thing with which I wish to deal is the Australian treaty, and I must say I am surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has not thrown the Australian treaty in our faces and cancelled it long before this, referring particularly to the members from British Columbia. After a great deal of trouble he negotiated a treaty calculated to promote trade for one of the great industries in Ontario, for the paper industry of Canada and particularly for the pulp and paper and fish industries of British Columbia, with the promise that further negotiations would include lumber, which was very desirable. But, with the exception of myself, I cannot recall having heard one word of appreciation of that action of the government, and particularly of the Minister of Finance, coming from hon. gentlemen opposite, whose constituents have been so vitally benefited by this particular treaty. Those benefits will increase in the future, because a treaty does not produoe results in a moment; it takes time for its effects to become fully developed. The hon. members from Vancouver in particular have come here annually opposing that treaty; in fact they voted unanimously in support of a want of confidence motion based primarily on the
Australian treaty. Vancouver is the port through which 92 per cent of the import trade with Australia passes as well as 36 per cent of the export trade; Vancouver is the headquarters of the big interests connected with the fish, lumber and pulp and paper industries, which reckon their investments not in millions but in hundreds of millions oi dollars; but these members, although knowing the benefits which have been derived from the Australian treaty, come here shedding crocodile tears because, forsooth, they say harm is being done to the dairying interests by that treaty. They say that the price of butter has been lower in consequence, although it happens to be a matter of fact that the price of butter has gone up instead of down, due to causes entirely apart from the Australian treaty. But what is a little trifle like that when it is a question of some party advantage? Well, might I paraphrase those well-known words and say, " What can they know of Country, who only Party know?" That is the situation to-day.
Three or four years ago, after a good deal of effort, we succeeded in passing a measure for the protection of the dairying industry by doing away with the sale and manufacture of oleomargarine. I appealed then to hon. gentlemen opposite to vote for the measure on the basis of protection, but did they do so? Not at all; .their concern then was the working man of Vancouver. They said he must have a cheap spread for his children's bread; they were the urban representatives then and must have regard for the working man. Very well; let us apply the same argument to the suggestion that the Australian treaty would reduce the price of butter, although that has not proved to be the case. Let us suppose that the treaty had that effect; according to their argument, would this not be an advantage to those workers for whose welfare they were so solicitous a few years ago? But that does not seem to work. Is it a fact that as far as they are concerned the working man is only entitled to oleomargarine on his children's bread, and should not have butter? Probably it all comes down to this; when it comes to a question of party advantage the workman, the dairyman and everyone else gets the go-by.
That is what these hon. members say here, but what do they say at home? Their speech is very modified there. Probably they will deny having said anything I might attribute to them, but I have with me some statements appearing in the Vancouver Province, the best and biggest newspaper in the west. This is a strong Conservative paper and it is also very
The Budget-Mr. Neill

fair, much more so than the candidates it supports. During the election campaign the Vancouver Province stated that the negotiation of the Australian treaty was the brighest gem in the record of the Ring administration, and one of which they might well be proud. That statement was not published during a time of peace, -but in the midst of an election campaign. I also have another editorial which appeared as late as last January, in which they said that if British Columbia wants the treaty retained, the British Columbia members would do well to make their wishes known emphatically. Have we heard them? I have not. Another Conservative paper in British Columbia states that the cancellation of the treaty would be a disaster. Have we heard that view expressed from the opposition benches? I have not. Party politics become of greater importance than the interests of British Columbia.
The results of the operation of the treaty are alleged to have been unsatisfactory, but in the twenty-four months after that treaty came into operation we increased our exports to Australia by thirty per cent; and as I have said, a treaty does not work like putting a penny into a slot machine; it takes time to reach the maximum benefits. However, we have had an increase of thirty per cent in our export trade; I have not taken the import trade into consideration, because our exports are the more valuable to us. The fish and pulp and paper industries of Canada, which largely means British Columbia exported to Australia in that period $9,500,000 worth of goods, and as most expenditure's of that size naturally do, that resulted in increased work and stimulated industry. In fact, it stimulated the fishing industry so much in the direction of canning the more common grades of salmon, that the government, which had never taken any action in that direction before, were forced to place restrictions on the canners, because the British Columbia waters were being overfished in regard to these grades. That was one instance alone. The pulp and paper towns were busy and the bush was full of workers. Hon. members know how trade acts and reacts. Well, this wave of business extended to the coal industry. We cannot pack $9,500,000 worth of stuff in a canoe and take it to Australia. So it had to be shipped, and the ships carrying those -commodities had to have coal, and the coal was mined in our district. Thus work was given to shipping, to coal miners, to workers in the bush, and in the paper mills and the fishing industry. Then these workers provided a ready and profitable market for vegetables, for fresh butter, for fresh cream and ice cream and for fresh milk Mr. Neill.]
for those engaged in the dairy industry in that particular vicinity, and anybody acquainted with farming knows that that is a far better market than sending butter to Liverpool to compete there with the products of the world.
A great hue and cry was raised by these same hon. gentlemen-in support of this I can quote from the speeches they delivered in my district during the election-to the effect that the egg industry of British Columbia was going to be ruined on account of this disastrous treaty. As a matter of fact I do not believe a single dozen of eggs has come in under the treaty. But that did not prevent the hue and cry that went up at the time. As far as Australian butter is concerned, the danger was not great of hurting the industry in British Columbia or in Canada provided that the dumping duty, of which I will speak later, was maintained. In 1926 the importations of butter into Canada from Australia amounted to 2| million pounds. In 1927 owing to the dumping duty being imposed it had dropped to 800,000 pounds.
The National Dairy Association have presented three' resolutions to the government. The first one asks that the Australian treaty as applied to New Zealand be cancelled. I am heartily in agreement with that and I will give my reasons later. The second resolution asks that the dumping clause be applied, on all butter sent from Australia to Canada either on direct sale or consignment as long as the Paterson scheme' of bonusing exists. I agree with that suggestion and I will go further. I suggest that the dumping clause should be strengthened. I have reason to believe that the Paterson scheme will fail. It created such fictitious prices in Australia that New Zealand also sent its butter into that market, so I believe Australia may abandon the Paterson scheme altogether. I am in favour, I care not who calls me protectionist, of the maintenance and the judicious use of the dumping clause. It may be said that the dumping clause is dangerous. So is a revolver dangerous; in the wrong hands. A revolver is a very handy thing to have in the middle of the night when you hear a burglar moving downstairs. It should be used with discretion and so should the dumping clause. In any event I believe it should be there to be applied when needed. You remember the missionary in the days when Indians used to scalp settlers, who said that he was not afraid because the Lord would take care of him until his time came, but some friend said "Yes, that is all very well, but how is it that whenever you go out

The Budget-Mr. Neill
you take a particularly vicious looking shotgun. with you?" His reply was, "That's all right, I'm not inconsistent. The Lord will take care of me, but supposing I happen to meet an Indian at a time when I had not my shotgun, and his time had come, what would the Lord think of me for not having the machinery to carry out his will?" The same illustration might be applied here. When we need the dumping clause let us have it on the back premises ready to be applied whenever occasion demands. I am strongly in favour of the maintenance of the dumping clause for general use, applied very discreetly, and in favour of its application in the present instance.
The third resolution asked that the Australian treaty be done away with altogether.
I am flatly and entirely opposed to that. You do not burn your house down because there are mice in the basement. Because some phase of the treaty has operated unfairly to Canada the remedy is not to do away with the treaty, which has untold potentialities in the way of trade for the whole of this Dominion. Moreover if the first and second resolutions I have quoted, were brought into effect, there would be no need for the third resolution at all. I repeat that I am entirely against doing away with the Australian treaty.
Coming back now to the first resolution asking for the abolition of the Australian treaty as applied to New Zealand. That feature of the treaty was never introduced into this house; if it had been I should not have supported it. It was put into effect by order in council and I am against it. I understand it was intended as a sort of quid pro quo for the preference they had given us. Well, that is possibly true, but it is too high a price to pay for such a concession, and in any event it is not fair that one industry should have to bear the whole brunt of the effect of the arrangement. The real danger in connection with this Australian treaty is entirely from New Zealand, and I would support the immediate cancellation of the arrangements so far as New Zealand concerned. It may be said, and I have been accused of it before, that I have been making a protectionist speech. I care1 not what epithet is applied, I am only applying the principle of common sense to conditions as they happen to exist. I believe that like the Sabbath, the tariff was made for man and not man for the tariff. So much as regards the Australian treaty. My suggestions in that regard are: that we should keep the treaty for the benefit of the big industries of British Columbia and the workers thereof; that we should
keep the dumping clause and strengthen it if necessary; that we should cancel the treaty as regards New Zealand. These are my own views I think they are the views of my constituents, and I challenge any member from British Columbia to say that the carrying out of such a policy would not inure to the general benefit of the province of British Columbia.
I want now to speak for a moment on the subject of immigration. To begin with, of course, being a British Columbian, I will touch on the oriental question, but briefly. It is true that we were promised oriental exclusion when the oriental resolution was going through this house in 1922. We were told then that the words " effective restriction " would have the same effect as exclusion. That promise has not been carried out in its entirety. I will admit all that has been said by the hon. Minister of Health (Mr. King), when he said the Conservative party had done nothing along those lines, and that the Liberal party were entitled to the credit of having passed the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1924. They also made regulations which have resulted in the control of the fishing industry passing from the Orientals to the white people. Furthermore, they got the Japanese " gentleman's agreement " cut down so that the immigration under it amounted to 150 labourers annually instead of 450. But that is not enough. We want more. We want the abolition of the " gentleman's agreement " altogether or its material alteration. We object to allowing women to come in practically unrestricted, and also to putting the control of immigration into the hands of a foreign nation instead of retaining it in our own hands. I know that negotiations have been going on to amend that " gentleman's agreement ", but I declare here that I am not satisfied that our officials have exhibited the energy they should have in pressing forward our view of the matter. Orientals will stand us off as long as they can, but if we keep the whip hand and exercise the proper amount of pressure I have no doubt we shall achieve a satisfactory result. I give all credit to the statement of the Prime Minister the other day when he said that there were interimperial reasons why we should do nothing that would appear to be offensive, also that we do a large trade with the orient and hope to do more. I admit that, but I do not admit a contention made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) the other day when he spoke in this debate. I agree with much of what that hon. gentleman said, but I do not agree with bis statement that the United States have lost no trade by their somewhat offensive language in con-
101S

The. Budget-Mr. Neill
unction with this matter of oriental immigration. They have lost an enormous quantity of trade. He do not want to lose any trade if we can help it, but nevertheless I take my stand with him that under any consideration we must adhere to our vision of a white Canada and I hope the government will lose no time in having the gentleman's agreement " properly altered.
Now as regards immigration generally, I wish to say, and I am sure that I shall receive small sympathy when I do so, that I am a heretic to the conventional ideas of both sides of the house. I do not agree with the immigration policy of either party. I oppose the policy of the Conservatives which I know. I am not quite so clear as to what the Liberal policy is, but to the extent to which it is indicated by the methods by which they have attempted to carry it out, I do not agree with it. Where does this cry for a vigorous immigration policy come from? It is a sonorous phrase and it sounds very nicely but where does it come from? If we track it down to its origin, it comes from the shipping interests, from the railway interests, and from the big employers of labour, who hope by that means to form a great bank of idle labour, of ignorant alien labour, which by its ignorance of our tongue and its inability to express itself at the polls will be always a cheap, submissive source of supply for them. One would suppose that the very obviousness of their self-interest would largely detract from the strength of their representations, but it does not seem to be so. And forsooth, this class of immigrants is to be assisted to come here at enormous expense. I have been a worker practically all my life; I now represent a large number of workingmen and women, and I fiercely resent the idea that they should be taxed in order to bring in workers to compete with them in the often congested labour market in which they seek to make a living. We talk about protection. Is there protection of the workingman there in regard to the only thing he has to sell? His labour, is it protected? We talk about free trade. Is that free trade in labour? No, it goes far beyond that; it is fifty degrees below the zero of free trade when you ask a man to pay to bring in a competitor to compete with him.
Another method I object to-it is not a method; it is a phantasy-the belief that we can bring labourers in from southern Europe, from the sunny towns of Italy, to work on farms in western Canada. The other day I met in Toronto a man who had come out under this assisted passage scheme to work on a farm in the west. I asked him how he Mr. Neill.]
landed in Toronto and he said: "I got off the train in Montreal and asked a policeman where the train for Toronto was and I got on it. What can you do about it?" I said:	"You
can be deported." He said:	"It would be
hard to find me." He never went near the prairies. I have jKo doubt he figures in a statement made recently by hon. members opposite when they drew a picture of so many agricultural labourers being imported into the prairie provinces in a given period and of how in the next census they were not there, and they immediately jumped to the conclusion that these people had gone to the United States. That is not the case. This man and thousands like him have gone not to the United States, but to Toronto, and1 I presume they are shown there as part of the natural increase. It results in Toronto getting a reputation for fecundity to which it is not entitled. I am against this system, not because it is wrong but because it is impossible and you cannot enforce it. When this investigation into the immigration department is carried out, I venture to predict that it will be found that the heads of the department are not grafters but clean men, and that a good deal of the unpopularity from which they are suffering today is because they have loyally and steadfastly set their faces against political and other pressure from outside seeking to bring in immigrants at so much a head.
It may be said:	Why, this man wants to
stop all immigration! Not at all. My policy is simple and fair and it has the great advantage of being enforceable. I would allow two classes of immigration: I would allow into Canada every white British subject, sound in body and mind, who pays his own passage here. The fact that he has been able to scrape together the money to come here, as I did, as an immigrant, will guaranteee in some sort that he has some stamina and is likely to make good under the different and somewhat difficult conditions in which he will find himself in this country. As regards the continent of Europe,
I would impose a very strict quota, what is known as a family quota; that is, that no one could come in except someone who was an immediate relative of the man in this country who nominated him. An alien who comes here and fails to make good would not likely want to bring in his relations; but when an alien comes here and makes a good citizen, as many of them do, his son or his brother is also likely to make a good citizen, and at any rate the fact that he would be responsible for his maintenance for a certain period and furnish him with work, would guarantee' that the man would not likely be a waster. I would allow that small family quota.

The Budget-Mr. Neill
There is nothing sensational, phenomenal or spectacular about this policy. Sometimes statesmanship consists in doing the obvious and I am asking only that we should imitate our neighbours to the south who have had four or five generations of experience before us in this matter. They have tried the open door and they are now trying the quota system. They wish they had tried the quota system sooner, and I notice that when they deal with the quota, they strengthen it rather than make it slacker.
Another feature of my policy is that the millions that are now being spent in this futile immigration policy we should be able to use in improving the conditions of the farmer, making them more attractive, and especially by research and other methods endeavouring to do away with seasonal unemployment and to promote all-the-year-round work. In addition we would be able, out of those millions to provide old age pensions and unemployment insurance, things that the very best kind of British settler we want in western Canada is accustomed to to-day and is reluctant to leave; and he does not care to go to a country where these advantages are not before him.. If we provided these, we would be more likely to get the best class of immigrant we want.
As regards immigration to the United States, of which we have heard so much nonsense-I think that is a parliamentary word-the large centres will always attract population from the smaller ones and the country districts. That has been the case from the time of Aristotle and it will be so for all time. Let me take Scotland as an illustration. Scotland is a small and in some regards a poor country and it has an enormous export of young men and women. They go largely to England and indeed all over the world. That naturally depletes the population. What do we do about such a situation? Do we howl to the government: Save us; stop the young blood from going away? Not a bit of it. Do we howl to the government about bringing in aliens from somewhere else to fill up the gaps? No. The Scotch take the very sensible method of going in for bigger and better families. In the family of which I was a member and in the families in which my father and mother were respectively members-three families in all- there were thirty-seven children, and that was no exceptional thing at all in Scotland at that time. It was in that way that Scotland dealt with the loss of her young people and the method possesses three virtues beloved of the Scottish race. First of all, it was economical; second, it was profitable and, third, it was pleasant.
I have in my hand a pamphlet called Immigration and Population got up by some of the best scientists in the United States, scientists employed not to secure an ex parte statement as we do out of figures, but to get the truth and nothing but the truth. They went very thoroughly into the whole situation; they took different periods and states and so on, and this is the conclusion they came to. They said that after a certain point had been reached-and I will indicate that point in a minute-this is what they found:
Except for brief periods, immigration will not increase the population-
That is rather startling.
-above the figure it will reach without immigration. .	.	. If we admit those from
other lands we shall decrease by a like number those who will be born of those now here.
They end up with this statement:
The question for cold-blooded consideration by the American of to-day is this: Do you want the soil inherited by your son or by the son of one who now toils in a foreign land?
That question applies with equal force to the Canadian. What happens once that certain point is reached is this: The birth rate of the local people, so to speak, of the people in America or Canada declines in exact proportion to the immigration. What is that certain point? It is proved beyond doubt by statistics that cannot be denied-and I have submitted this to professors and other learned men and statisticians and they say it is true-in the United States the change took place the moment the supply of readily available cheap land which would produce food for practically nothing was exhausted. Of course if you pour immigration into an empty country, it is bound to be good for that country; but when the saturation point is reached, when there is no more good accessible land to be had for nothing, it is like pouring water into a pail; you may change the water in the pail but you will never get it any fuller. It might be said that our conditions are different. Yes, but where have we cheap accessible lands to be had for nothing? Only in the Peace river country and that is not really accessible. In the method I have suggested we would have at first, unlimited immigration from Great Britain, which would meet that situation. If these things are true, and they have not been contradicted, we have been spending millions for immigrants to come to Canada which will not increase our numbers, and will merely change the complexion of our population.
These are my views on the Australian treaty and on the immigration question. I am prepared to support this or any other govern-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

meat which will bring down a policy of that kind. I do not think I have been verbose or wasted much time in discussing these matters. I want to discuss now the biggest problem in British Columbia, and that is in connection with our fishing industry, but I cannot tackle it to-day on account of the forty minute rule. It is surely a bad rule that prevents a representative of the people discussing a matter of great importance to his constituents at the proper time, and this is the proper time. We were told that there was to be a merw heaven and a new earth when this new rule was introduced. We have had two debates since, not particularly contentious, and both have lasted longer than they did before. We have had the spectacle of three or four cabinet ministers cut off in the apex of their arguments, in the very crux of what they were explaining. They had been attacked and they were defending themselves, explaining matters about their department that we had a right to know and which the house and the country had a right to know, and yet they were cut off in the very midst of their argument by this new rule. We also have this situation, that forty or eighty or a hundred men can attack a cabinet minister for forty minutes each, equivalent to eleven days of sitting, and then he has only forty minutes to reply to the one hundred members, or less than half a minute to devote to each. He must be a superman if he can do it. I hope that we shall realize the real dangers of this rale and that with your full consent, Mr. Speaker, it will be relegated to the oblivion from which it came, unwept, unhonoured and unsung.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what a change is here! Time was when the hon. Minister off Finance (Mr. Robb), on making his budget speech could look for, and did get, a pleasant chorus of praise from all the benches to your right, sir, and from those in the far comer on this side of the chamber. In some way or another the burden of that chorus of praise is changing; there is an ever-widening rift within the lute. The hon. minister might have expected from the official opposition searching criticism because sharp differences of principle are involved; but his own supporters, straight-line Liberals, damn this budget with faint praise, and the Liberal-Progressive party-adopted or kidnapped adjunct of the Liberal party-for 
the most part have sat in sullen silence, until this afternoon the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) did essay a few apologetic reasons for supporting the budget; our hon. friends, the contingent from Saskatchewan, never in the house noted for being inarticulate, to say the least, have sat strangely quiet; the group on my left has protested with some force and vehemence-and that, I am afraid, is the " most unkindest cut of all ". My hon. friend will remember how in other days his party and that group were
Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one.
But no'w, Mr. Speaker, that group has torn the mask of smiling friendship from the government's face and at long last has awakened to a true understanding of its methods. Hon. members will recollect how this government once had the habit firmly fixed of being saved in parlous times by the hon. gentlemen, not forgetting the hon. lady, who sit to my left. Have those happy days gone forever?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It looks like it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or are they to return? I rather think the government hope that it is a temporary eclipse only and that the light of favour will shine again. The government has experience upon which to base that hope. But perhaps, to change the simile1; the pitcher has gone once too often to the well.
My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has told the house how the siren voice of the Prime Minister has seduced these Liberals of Manitoba-or Liberal-Progressives, as they call themselves-from their allegiance, how that same voice has lured them to destruction-to destruction that is inevitable when one abandons principle. I am wondering what these Liberal-Progressives are going to say to their ardent free-traders back home. And so with the Saskatchewan contingent, I wonder what they are going to say; are they going to excuse their voting for this " fencemending " budget by declaring that they made themselves, privately, a thorn in the side of the government? Are they going to tell of the desperate struggles in ministers' rooms and behind the closed doors of caucus to get a different sort of budget?
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) is not in his seat. I should like to have him explain the strangeness of the coincidence in regard to his motion to repeal the dumping clause of the Customs Act. It was at the top of the list, called' for hearing time and again, if my memory serves me aright, but in some mysterious way it disappeared from the order paper the day before the budget was brought down, and bv some

The Budget-Mr. Geary
magic reappeared the day after. Had that anything to do with the feelings of Saskatchewan with regard to the budget? Are the Saskatchewan members of the opinion that what they thought were the policies of the Liberal government have been treated fairly in the budget? I should be very much surprised to know that all is unanimity between the government and the Saskatchewan group. I wonder if my friend from North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) will explain his vote on the budget by telling his constituents at some great meeting in the "little red school-house" how opposed he was to it; how, to be sure, he did vote for a 10 per cent reduction in the income tax, but that that was only because he was able to make to this house the brilliant suggestion that the money would be replaced by voluntary contributions towards the extinction of the national debt.
My 'hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) is ipained over ths betrayal of Liberal principles, or so-called Liberal principles. But why shed his few but friendly tears at this stage? The betrayal began in 1897 and was evidenced in the very first budget of a new-coming Liberal government. The Conservative party had been swept from office just one short year before, and "the funeral baked meats were scarcely cold" when the Liberal government espoused the policy of the Conservative party, and has never had the strength to depart in fact from that policy, although it has-notably in convention of 1919, and on platform after platform, as instanced by my hon. friend from Mackenzie-set itself up as being the advocate and proponent of something entirely different. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the groups in this house have come almost to the point of parting with this government, with its actions, its broken pledges, so fresh in their minds?
What is the result, Mr. Speaker, of this wavering by the government from year to year on its tariff policy? Simply that its policy, if it can at all be called a policy, is in a welter of uncertainty, that there is nothing stable, and there can be nothing stable, in such a policy because it is founded on no principle and has not as a basis conviction. There is no sense, there is no stability in a situation such as this, and small wonder it is that not only are murmurs heard but open revolt is seen. Without going over again a situation which has been repeatedly explained in this house, I may cite two familiar instances which will readily occur to the recollection of hon. members. It was in 1924 that the government made a magnificent gesture in the budget speech by reducing
the duty on agricultural implements. There was a great objection to that reduction, a considerable outcry. The matter was the subject of a good deal of discussion between the government and some other people. Ostensibly the reduction in the duty was intended to effect a reduction in the retail price to the consumer, which reduction in price, judging from the illuminating speech which we heard the other night from the hon. member for London (Mr. White), has not at all eventuated. And the object further was to take from the manufacturer the undue profits which it was said he was making. Well, the manfacturers had something to say before that reduction finally passed into law and the result was that the chiefest of all these came from these conferences with the government, perfectly pleased and content, and in due course of time he became a minister of the government and, so far as we know, has lived happily ever after despite that handicap. In the net result, if there was any reduction in price to the consumer-and my hon. friend from London shows that there has been no reduction-it was effected, while ostensibly by a reduction in the tariff, in reality, after negotiation, by a reinstatement of that reduction by other means which placated the manufacturers. There was another magnificent gesture in 1926 at the instance of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), the duty on automobiles being reduced in that year. That reduction was made with a good deal of eclat and considerable support was expected for the government in consequence. Thousands of workmen came to the city of Ottawa to protest and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) struck an attitude:
Come one, come all! this rock shall fly, From its firm base as soon as I.
Or, to use his own words, " I will stick to my guns." Did he stick to his guns? No; more conferences and more meetings in private, and at the end of these conferences the manufacturer emerged with a smile of complete satisfaction. If there has been any reduction in fact in the price to the retail consumer on these particular products that reduction has been effected at the expense of the general funds of the Dominion.
I submit that the same lack of principle is carried into the budget now before us. Hon. members have analyzed that budget with a special knowledge which I myself do not possess and I am glad to be saved any difficulty on that score. Suffice it to say that if you take the case of the big weaving man, any reduction which he has been given-and such reduction does not appear clear in many instances, but if he has been given a reduction
The Budget-Mr. Geary

-he has received it at the expense of a charge upon the spinning man below him. There seems to be no definite principle. A mill in St. Mary, I think it is, the constituency of an hon. member opposite receives a benefit; a mill in Hespeler is sadly damaged; here the axe falls and there a benefit is given. Somebody gets something out of it and somebody else is hurt. Where can the system be found? No one on the government side of the house has attempted to explain the schedules in this budget and probably none of them can. But this fact does stand out, that it is by no means certain that any reduction has been made; there is the certainty that any reduction made will not find its way to the consumer. And this much we gather from the schedules, that if the big man is hurt in one respect he is recompensed by having the load shouldered by some unfortunate below him.
There has been called to my attention an item which I 'think is worth more than a casual glance. There is a salt belt-it may have 'been mentioned before but I apologise for not having been in the house throughout the whole of the session-a belt through the western part of Ontario, beginning, I think, in the riding of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), and extending southerly, bending a little off until it gets into the county of Elgin. Incidentally it passes through several constituencies represented by hon. members in this house, all of which constituencies, if my memory serves me, are by some coincidence represented, with the exception of one or two, by hon. gentlemen on the government benches. An application was made for an increase in the duty on salt. Now that is a staple household necessity and it was a bit thick even for this government to put a duty on salt. But something had to be done, for the government was sorely pressed. And what was done? The same old trick once again-the duty was taken off the coal used in the manufacture of salt.
I instance these matters not for the mere sake of repeating things that have been said before but to make a point which is clear to myself. And I make this point on my own responsibility. It is this: The whole system of taking care of unfortunate industries by drawback reductions in duty, rebate of sales tax and devices of that sort is wrong, and it is wrong no matter who has practised it in the past or who practises it now, because to my mind it is the wrong form for protection to take. If protection is good, if it is a valid and sound proposition, then it should be carried out in the open; protection should

not be got at by devious methods or by devices such as my hon. friends on the government benches practise.
In the framing of a budget, I take it, there are two principles which in the large may be followed. There is in the first place the principle of free trade, and I submit without discussing the matter further that, the late Adam Smith and the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), to the contrary notwithstanding, the principle is unsound. But even admitting it to be sound in general, were conditions untrammelled by circumstances, it is certainly unsound and impracticable in the condition in which Canada finds itself to-day. Apparently that is not the policy of all the members of the government; I have not heard from the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who have been heard in other days to say something quite different, together with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell); they have not spoken this time. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has said he is not a free trader, however, so we may take it that one member at least of the government denies the free trade proposition. Then we have on the other extreme the doctrine of protection, and with that I wish to deal very shortly in a few moments. I may say now, however, that in its national policy the Liberal-Conservative party has protected, does protect and intends to protect where protection is proper under this system, and that protection will be extended where necessary to all branches of industry in this Dominion.
The government have taken neither of these obvious courses, but have chosen to follow what they call the middle course, although it is beyond me how there can be such a thing with any sanity to it. They say they are between the high tariff and the low tariff, but on my assumption no tariff is high which does not protect where protection is justified and no tariff is low which does more than protect in a like case. On those words of low tariff and high tariff, without reason, logic or anything to back them up, the main distinction has been drawn by our opponents between ourselves and other parties throughout this Dominion. To take a middle course with no guiding principle is to veer and shift with the wind and tide, trying to navigate without a compass. In such a case the temptation is strong to take practical politics as a guide, and I submit to you, sir, and to this house that that is just what the government have done; they have succumbed to that temptation, and have even gone further. They have raised practical politics almost to a principle, and I

The Budget-Mr. Geary
think I am not going too far when I say that in their handling of the tariff policy of this country we find the very apotheosis of political expendiency. With the government attempting to drift a course, so to speak, between extremes, as they choose to say, we cannot look for anything certain or anything stable; it will always be that way with this government. They have done so before and they will do it again; we know what they have done and what their ideas are in that respect and we know that the same thing will occur again; the government have their past before them.
We have been criticized perhaps more strongly in the west than in other parts of this country, and in many ways I can well understand the attitude of the western farmer. I can appreciate, although perhaps not quite fully, the difficulties with which he finds himself confronted. In this generation he is a pioneer breaking new ground, two, three or perhaps more generations after our forefathers, those hardy spirits of his own kind who pioneered in the central provinces. From our grandfathers and grandmothers we know the privations and the hardships which must be endured in a new country, and we know that through the initial struggles of our ancestors we in the central provinces have succeeded to a settled and prosperous land, with a diversity of opportunity which was not available to them in their day and generation. The time of transition has been long with us, three or more generations, and by analogy the time of transition in the western provinces would be equally long. I take it, however, that as all in this house have the interests of Canada at heart, they will all use their best endeavours, as they see the light, to make that transition period in the case of our western country shorter than it has been in the central provinces.
While the man who took up his land in the west faced with a light heart and a sense of adventure the development <of that country, and probably for himself alone could continue with great joy the life that it entails, he has others to think of. He is married and there are children, and I can understand the feeling almost of bitterness when he sees that his wife has to face the privations and hardships incidental to land settlement and that his children are deprived of perhaps all the opportunities which the more settled parts of the country afford. It is no wonder that such a man cannot settle himself with patience and resignation to the task he has before him. In the east, in the central provinces he sees what appears to be affluence, while hardship
is his lot and that of his family, and in these circumstances I think the western farmer was an easy prey to misrepresentation of the Conservative policy of protection.
I speak of that policy as having been misrepresented. We have been assailed as a party of high tariff; a tariff high and yet higher; as high as Haman's gallows, if you please, but that is not true. The word "protection" has been used by people who do not want to give the right impression as being protection for some special interest or special person to the end that he may acquire undue profits as the result of his labour. Again, Mr. Speaker, I say that is not true. I am not at all concerned with the manufacturer beyond seeing that he has a fair chance in the struggle to get a fair return for his capital, his energy, his skill and ability. I am concerned for his workmen, that there shall be security in industrial life and a decent living wage. They call us the party of big interests, but to those who know* the texture of the Conservative party in Ontario, for instance, that is not understandable. The people of the province of Ontario would be called radicals by my hon. friends opposite from Quebec; we own the business of generating, transmitting and distributing electrical energy practically throughout the province of Ontario, with the result that we are able to give it to the consumer at cost. We own and operate our own steam railway. In my own city of Toronto we not only control the distribution of electrical energy but we own our own street railway transportation system, our waterworks and even our abattoir, and these services go to the people at cost.
In this house last year, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party made a stronger appeal foi a workable and fair old age pension scheme than did any other party. Because we believe in that principle, and because we believe that old age pensions should come into effect, we suggested and we stand by, the only method which could absolutely ensure fairly and at once the application of the policy, of paying the whole cost ourselves out of the Dominion treasury.
The opposition led, and took a substantial share in, the victory which followed, in the fight for public control of the water rights of the Ottawa river during the last session of parliament. And yet we are called the party of the big interests, whereas through the whole history of the Conservative party the object of its policy has been towards not the big interests, whatever they may be, but towards the amelioration of the lot of the common
The Budget-Mr. Geary

people, and that is what we are standing for to-day. The big interests! St. James street! Do they like the Conservatives of Ontario? They do not. And still one would think we could not be trusted to formulate a proper protective policy that would conserve the interests of the common people.
I have little to add, but to my mind, Mr. Speaker, the only way of distributing the burden of taxation derived indirectly from the customs tariff in this country is under a principle that is definite. I submit to the house that principle is the principle of protection, safeguarded and carried into effect in the way I have suggested-by so controlling the customs duty that no one shall profit unduly. That has been stated time and time again, and was restated the other day by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. An application of that principle could be made in this way-and I am not attempting to discuss it in detail-this is an instance pf what might be done: Supposing it is found during the time parliament is not in session that someone is taking an unfair advantage of the duty. There should be power to the government, on the recommendation of a properly constituted tariff board, to reduce or do away with the duty, just as in the opposite case we have on our statute book a law giving the governor in council power to invoke the dumping clause. That could be done and would be done, and you would then do away with the present system with all the opportunities that call to the government to make use of the tariff to suit the political exigencies of the moment.
I am not one of those who think that the opposition of the farmers to the payment of income tax is based on unworthy reasons. I do agree that if a farmer does not pay income tax it is because he has not got the income which calls for payment. I take it that the farmer is an honest man and in whatever part of the country he may be he desires to pay his fair share towards the upkeep and the management of this country. While the farmer does not pay taxation through the income tax he pays it to perhaps some extent through the sales tax, a tax that we can infer is on its way to abolition, but he pays largely by indirect taxation through the customs tariff. We must have customs duties, and since the farmer must pay his share of taxation through those duties, I take it the question which concerns him is:	Am
I paying my fair share and nothing more? The policy of the Conservative party-that of protection with the safeguards I have indicated-is the only policy I submit that
rVTr. Geary.]
will ensure his paying his fair share and no more. This is a general discussion, perhaps too general, on the subject of the budget, but it goes to a principle. It goes to a principle that has been misrepresented as I have indicated. And can one feel any other desire but that of granting to the farmer his rights? He cannot. Nor can we forget the artisan, the man who works in the shop or in the factory. He surely has his rights. He has the right to stay in this country and earn his living here and not be harried back and forth at the whim of an inconstant government. It is for the working man who depends upon the manufacturer that this party stands when it advocates, as it does advocate, a policy of protection on the lines described.
There is one other phase of this tariff question which to my mind goes deeply to the root of this whole matter, and that is the question of our national life. Customs duties are with us to stay. We have to have them and the burden of taxation should be distributed on some proper and equitable basis. I take it that the house will agree with me that customs duties should be imposed upon some definite principle. This party believes that that principle is the principle of protection. Each man must decide for himself, which policy is best, but in deciding, remember that it has been demonstrated, and fully demonstrated, that lack of protection, where protection is justifiable, means, slowly perhaps, but inevitably, the disintegration of the agricultural and industrial life of this country. What follows? The drift that we see to-day, more and more pronounced, towards the south; the infiltration of United States methods, commercial and political; the substitution of United States ideals, culture, and education, and of their principles of law and justice and order for those principles under which we have lived so happily; the loosening of Canadian national spirit. In short, Mr. Speaker, it means the surrender of our national life so that we will become citizens at large and men without a country. I know well that there are some who think there is nothing but good in such an outcome as that, men who look forward to internationalism. But I am of those, and they are many, who do not want to give up their Canadianism, who cannot give up their citizenship in the British Empire. There are those of us who are even sentimental enough to feel a thrill at the sight of our country's flag, a joy and a pride in being Canadians. To those, Mr. Speaker, it is worth while to struggle and to make sacrifices in order to build up rather than destroy the national life of Canada, worth while to feel, and to think, and to work with heart, and

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
with mind, and with strength, so that this vast and splendid land will be, and will remain for all time to come, our country, ours and our children's.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think when I announce to the house that it is not my intention to make an attempt to deal with the budget in detail, I shall have a special claim for the undivided attention of this assembly. We have listened for a considerable period to the discussion pro and con of the budget. I am not going to discuss it, first, because what I might have said about it has already been said well and often; second, because a tariff policy for this country is a pretty well settled proposition, both parties being agreed that it must be continued, and third, because I have never been able to work up enthusiasm over a discussion of the means of collecting taxation as being any possible solution for an economic problem. So for these reasons I shall turn my attention rather to the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) in his speech the other evening when he made a special attack upon what he called group government and upon the principles which underlie the movement of which I have the honour to be a representative in this house.
I might also make reference to other hon. members opposite who made an attempt to follow the course of the minister in this regard. For instance an attack was made upon the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn). I think I can answer that hon. gentleman's attack by just a single sentence. As I have said, the hon. member for West Elgin attempted to reply to the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I would describe that episode as Ian Maclaren described an insignificant and pompous character in Drumtochty. He said he was the "verra image o' a [DOT] bantam cock fleeing in the face o' judgment." Mr. Speaker, I say, let him flee. The hon. member for Southeast Grey is quite capable of taking care of herself and it is not necessary that I should rush to her assistance, but I cannot let pass the opportunity of making a remark with regard to the speech of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). I think his speech of this afternoon was the most naive, skilful and masterly evasion that it has ever been my humiliation to listen to. After he had declared that he did not know what was in the budget, he indicated that he was going to support it. After having criticized the hon. member for South-*east Grey for having that female type of mind 56103-65
which does not require a reason, he says: "I am going to vote for the budget," and when we inquire why, he says, "Because." I should like to take the time to restate the argument of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I am sorry that it escaped! the attention of the hon. member for Marquette and I think he ought to read it again because, if he can answer the argument of the hon. member for Southeast Grey, he owes it to this house and to his party to do so. The facts which she marshalled from the history of the party are sufficient absolutely to condemn it and I think her argument needs to be answered.
I turn my attention to the minister in question and I shall deal with his argument a little more thoroughly, not because I regard it as being in any manner destructive of the political position which this group holds, but rather because the high position which the minister occupies in this house lends to his argument an authority which a close examination of the subject matter would not warrant. When a minister of the crown is headlined across the country as having wiped out the argument for group government, there are those who may give credence to the announcement. He reminds me of Mzud, who, having got married, went on her honeymoon and elected to go a long sea voyage. She said to herself that she and her husband would act as though they had been for many sea voyages together, but the husband, having noticed a long line of life buoys lashed to the rail, inquired of the skipper why he had taken all these spare tires. The minister posed as a student of political economy and political history; but when w'e come to examine his argument, no matter how well he may have posed, his remarks will spoil the show. I want, however, to congratulate him on his astuteness, for it were better for the Liberal party of this country that the people in general should concentrate their attention upon the alleged dangers of group government than that they should fasten their eyes upon the actual government of the day and the budget which is being discussed at the present time.
I desire also to congratulate him upon his astuteness in another matter. He has discovered that the birth of group organizations constitutes the only formidable challenge that the party system of which he is the protagonist has ever had in this country. I should like to point out to the minister in the terms of Fox that the people of Canada have emerged from the euthanasia of politics; that they have got over their apathy in respect to public matters and that they have given up that acquiescence to things as they are; in short

The Budget-Mr. Irvine

that they have recognized with Disraeli the drollery of the thing called representative government.
I want to confine my remarks to the minister's reference which was a criticism of the United Farmers movement. First of all let me point out that when he charges us, if his statement be regarded on his part as a charge, with believing in group government, I do not know of any single instance when as a group we have proclaimed our belief in group government. I know of no declaration of our annual convention at any time upon which the minister could pin his accusation, if indeed he regards it as being such. In view, however, of our group system of organization, we might regard group government as a fairly logical implication, and if it is, we shall not run away from it. But I merely want to point out that our movement stands for something far more important than group government. The United Farmers movement is an awakening of the people to a sense of personal and collective responsibility in respect to democratic citizenship, and the election of members to this house is only one small phase of that citizenship duty. Deeper and far more fundamental than political action as it is commonly understood, is economic action, and I think that the economic action which has been taken by our movement in the west has been so important and far-reaching in its possibilities, so spectacular in its achievement, as to require no further comment in that regard. We are concerned not less with the social life of our various communities. We are concerned with the securing of that measure of human happiness which alone can make life worth while and which leads us to take an active interest in such matters as education, the health of the people and the moral and social life of the community. Briefly stated, we regard our movement as the means by and through which we shall be able to make our contribution to the building up and developing of an intelligent civilization. There is no democratic action, regardless of the phase of life with which it may be concerned, which is outside of the scope of our movement's interest. That our group may be efficient as a democratic unit in an intelligently organized state, we regard certain things as being of vital importance. These I shall enumerate, and comment upon the most important of them.
First of all, we believe in organization because we do not think that an unorganized people can go anywhere even if they know where they want to go. We believe in organization because a mob can only do one thing, and that is to follow a leader whoever
TMr. Irvine.]
he may be, and the leader as a rule with the most attractive shibboleth and the most money and advertising gets the largest number of votes. We believe that organization is essential, and so we have striven to build up one that is real and alive.
We believe, next, that in order that we may know where we are going it is well to have a little education, and so education is of great importance to our movement in the west.
Next to this comes our principle of cooperation. I notice that some hon. members of this house have indicated by their remarks in this regard that they entertain rather peculiar notions of what cooperation means. I wish I had the time to deal with it as thoroughly as I should like, but I must pass over it speedily with only a few remarks.
We believe in cooperation because we have discovered that competition has become destructive. There was a time, of course, when the competition which to-day has become destructive was the only thing that could be. To-day, however, competition internationally has become so destructive that the nation which wins a war is the one which loses most. Competition has become so destructive in industrial warfare as practically to mean the destruction of the industry concerned, and both organized men and organized capital lose. I refer to one case which has come before this house on several occasions to prove my point- the Besco case. There you had organized capital fighting organized workers,, and they fought with each other until the industry was threatened with destruction, if not actually destroyed. That is what competition does to-day; it has reached the destructive stage. Competition in this house has become destructive. This is a tug of war; this is not a government, and we who are in this corner sometimes grab the coat tails of hon. gentlemen to our right, and sometimes slip across the floor and pull on the coat tails of hon. gentlemen opposite. This is not what I would regard as an intelligent assembly bent on carrying out the business of this country in a cooperative way. If it satisfies hon. gentlemen, I suppose I shall have to take it whether I want it or not, but surely I am permitted to say that it does not satisfy me. Cooperation presupposes a higher common interest than I have ever heard voiced by either party in this house. It presupposes also that the entire civilization of which we form a part should have an intelligent aim. Has our Canadian civilization an intelligent aim? If so, this parliament has not discovered it, for I have not found a pulling of all together towards any common aim. Professor Jacks once gave an illustration which I will use here.

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
He told of looking from a skyscraper hotel down into the streets of Detroit, where he saw a great number of motor cars going north, south, east and west. He realized as he looked down upon them that each one was going some place by itself, but When he took them all together they were not going any place at all. That is a pretty fair picture of our Canadian civilization. We have a great number of groups in this country, despite that hon. gentlemen opposite have not yet recognized that fact. We have organized manufacturers, organized bankers, organized preachers, organized1 farmers, organized bootblacks, and heaven knows how many others we have. Each one of them by itself knows where it is going, or thinks it does, but when we take them all together, can any hon. gentleman tell me where they are going? I say that civilization has to have some intelligent aim so far as Canada is concerned, and that aim cannot be discovered in the spirit of" antagonism and conflict for power which incessantly occupies the attention of this parliament. Cooperation, it is said by hon. members, cannot be practicable because the selfish interests of each group will always force that group to try to gain the masterful position. I want to say that that is a narrow view of the situation. I am not going to deny that selfish interest is there, and that it is the dominating factor, for it is by that selfish interest that we are going to get cooperation.
Let me give another illustration. I want you to think of a mine, a railway company, and a farming community. It is the selfish interest of the mine to get as much wheat for as little coal as possible. It is the selfish interest of the farming community to get as much coal for as little wheat as possible. It is the interest of the railway company to get as much wheat and coal as payment for services, in return for as little hauling as possible. Let us suppose that these three economic groups which we have in our country to-day are fighting amongst themselves and that two of them combine to impose conditions which are insufferable- upon the other. What happens? If they impose on the coal mine, the railway company does not have any coal to supply its power and it has no coal to haul. It cannot, then, haul any wheat either, and the farmer will* freeze to death. So there is a minimum of well being below which no functional group in the community can be allowed to sink without destroying the best interests of all the other groups. So the very selfish interests of each 56103-65$
group is that which I bank upon, if I may be permitted to use that term, to bring about co-operation.
Let me stop here to say that to-day the conflict which exists between parties in this house is the greatest hindrance to the idea of co-operation. It stultifies its very spirit; in fact, it kills it at birth.
Next we believe in the stability of our organization. If we are going to build an organization through which we can function as citizens it will have to become stabilized, and we discovered that the economic interest was the most intimate, the most vital, the most permanent, and the most universal that we could find, and upon that we based our organization. It is because of that very fact that the Alberta organization has withstood the attacks and the shibboleths of the party system for a number of successive elections.
Our next principle is that we invite all other economic groups in the state to do as we are doing-to organize, to equip themselves with the knowledge required for intelligent co-operative effort, to understand the interlocking interests of all, and fix upon some real, intelligent aim for our civilization.
I turn now to deal specifically with our political activities, since they were the centre of the attack by the Minister of Railways. It is only reasonable that a group organized for the purpose of discharging the full duties of citizenship should not neglect its political obligations. What standard of efficiency of citizenship can we expect from people who only mark a ballot once in four years and leave the rest to somebody else? We do not regard that as being a very high ideal of democratic citizenship. But apart from the duty, and apart from the logical course we would have followed anyway, we were forced into this political action by the conditions of the party system. I refer here to the historic sketch given by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). The facts which she placed before the house on that subject cannot be gainsaid. Suffice it to say that if the party system had had sufficient virility, had had thatl resiliency or elasticity which belongs to life so that it could have accommodated itself to the changes which over a centruy of industrial development forced upon the country, the story of our movement might have been a very different one. And so if the party system never did any good thing but this one it has served Canada by forcing economic groups into this parliament.
We are opposed, Mr. Speaker, to the party system. We not only do not wish to play
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

the game; we wish to change the game. I will state briefly why we oppose the party system. We' oppose it, first, because of its failure, as I have just indicated, to adapt itself to a new set of conditions which were not apparent at its inception. I must not stop to develop that thought, but I will give an illustration to make my point clear. I want hon. members to think of a farmer who went out to homestead with a team of old grey mares and a set of double harness. After a few years he found himself with four other horses, but he still has the old set of double harness and no new harness for the new horses. So he just lets the four run around to do as they like while he goes ahead ploughing with the two. That is what we are doing in a parliamentary way, but we are not as handy as the farmer: We hitch our horses up tail to tail; he hitches his so that they both pull the same way. To continue the simile, we started with two old nags, and we still have the old set of double harness, which your honour calls " procedure " and other nice terms. But to-day we find we1 have a number of other horses-some may call them mules- and yet we have only the old set of double harness, with the result that these other horses run free without a fraction of responsibility. I realize that it is easy for any member of the government to tell us we have not any responsibility when we suggest certain legislation. But that is not our fault; we are not shirking it; we are' denied it; and yet we are sent here with the same authority that the hon. ministers on the treasury benches enjoy.
We oppose the party system because so far as we can gather its chief aim is to gain power. We regard power as of such infinite importance that no government or p-oup or party has a right to monopolize it; it is dangerous to place it in their hands, no matter how good they may be.
We oppose the party system because the conflict necessary to gain power is disrupting and inimical to the best interests of the state. We oppose the party system because that very conflict is undermining the confidence of the Canadian people in all government whatsoever, and undermining it to the extent that it is paving the way for a bloody revolution as the only means of redress.

My hon. friends opposite
must accept their share of responsibility for that, and before I am through I think they will be glad to do it silently. The party in power put itself in that position, first of all, by an open disregard of the pledges upon which it secured the support of the people.

Think of the clear statements which party leaders make in respect to each other during elections. Last election and the one before what happened? The leader of the one party went out and told the people of Canada that the policy of the other party was rotten, that its leaders were lacking in integrity and that it was unsafe to entrust the affairs of Canada to that party. The other party leader went out and said the same thing. Now, sir, when the Conservative leader speaks the Conservatives believe him; when the Liberal leader speaks the Liberals believe him. I believe them both. Here are the horns of the dilemma. What these hon. gentlemen say at elections times is either true or not true. If it is true-and they are both truthful gentlemen; I am not referring to the present leader of the opposition, for he has not yet had a chance, I am referring to the former leader of the opposition and the one before that- if what those hon. gentlemen have' said is true, then Canada is in a very bad way. And if what the party leaders said of each other is not true, Canada is in a worse way. There is the position in which you have placed intelligent people. It cannot be denied that party propaganda is laying foundations for a bloody revolution, and while party spokesmen charge that to the bolsheviks, I place the responsibility on your own doorstep. You are the men who are developing the revolutionary spirit in this country, if, indeed, there is such a spirit developing.
Now, let me turn to a positive statement of our political principles. First I lay down a political principle which I do not think any hon. gentleman will challenge for one moment. It is this, that the economic interests form the dominating power in political policy anywhere, any time. In this regard let me give the origin of the two parties whose members are now listening to me. The party to my right was a group organization, an economic group. And what was that group? It was the landlords of England struggling to regain some of the influence lost- at the collapse of feudalism who organized a political party called the Tory party to look after their interests in the House of Commons. Those who might perhaps disagree with that statement I refer to a very definite declaration by Trevelyan in his History of the Nineteenth Century. Referring to 1689, he says: " Power was left in the hands of the landed aristocracy, with the municipal oligarchies as its congenial instruments." Shortly after the industrial revolution the rising manufacturing and merchant classes found that they required representatives in the House of Commons, and they organized the

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
Whig party-a group organization. Now you say, "If that is so, why do you object to them?" That is a very fair question. I will tell you why I object. Because after a century of development with interlocking directorates we find that these two groups came together; but when they merged they did not destroy the two old parties, for they discovered they could handle these parties splendidly for their own interests; in other words, they would not put all the eggs in one basket, but a few eggs in each basket. When one party succeeded the other in office the people	thought	that	they had a	realchange of government, but they had not, because the invisible power controlled both parties. I	instance	this	budget, the	lastbudget, the	budget before	that, and all	thebudgets for	the past	sixty	years as the	outstanding proof of that statement, that both parties seem to be controlled either by a masterly influence in that regard, or else this tariff business is a really good policy. This latter the Liberal party denies, but it must be one or the other. I will leave them to answer which of the two it is.
Next, we believe that if this principle I have laid down is sound, then1 the only true national policy that can be hammered out on the anvil of any parliament must come from the direct representatives of all the economic interests of the state, and not by some single group.
Then we believe in making practical the theory of democratic control which is preached by both parties. As a group we do this because we are a workable unit. The party system is not a workable unit. It is too unwieldy, even if it were a stable organization the people lose control of it because of its very size. At this point I would quote what Warbasse has to say in Co-operative Democracy:
The function of a democracy is to protect itself from the wise men who would save it, the fools that would destroy it, the politicians that would betray it; and retain to itself the right of working out its own salvation.
We finance our political movement, and thus control our policy and our members. I claim no particular morality for our method, and I admit it frankly, there is no more morality in it than in the methods of hon. gentlemen opposite. But I am speaking of a different type of organization, and I owe my allegiance to the farmers movement just as hon. gentlemen opposite owe theirs to a party system.
Now, the application of scientific principles to practical government is another thing which we would seek to establish. I cannot
go into the details of that, but I should like to telll the house that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) will deal with this subject, perhaps to-morrow or the day following, and I invite hon. members to see what suggestions he has to make in that regard.
As regards the application of this economic principle in practical government, perhaps I might give another illustration to support my argument. Let us suppose two chemists in Ottawa studying the contents of a bottle filled with a particular compound-
