Not the kind of stuff you are thinking about. They begin arguing about the actual elements in this compound, and what the result would be if it were applied to the hair of someone's head. One chemist, we shall assume, says the compound is such and such and if you apply it to the head it will remove all the hair; the other chemist says the compound is something very different, and he believes the application of it would cause two hairs to grow where one grew before. And so they argue the point for sixty years; the bottle is still there; and while men's hairs have come and hairs have gone no one knows what the result would be if this remedy were tried. Would anyone dream of calling such men scientists? Yet right in this house we have a state of things similar to this. One of our great political chemists says that the fiscal compound over which the two parties in this country have been arguing for so long will cause prosperity to grow where there was no prosperity before in Canada; the other political chemist affirms the very opposite. Thus they have argued for the past sixty years. But what would genuine chemists do in a case such as I have suggested? They would retire to the laboratory, analyze the compound, element after element, tagging each, and they would put an end to vain argument. Then having arrived at what they considered a sound conclusion, they would look for a dog on which to try this compound; they would make an experiment to see whether the compound would take the hair off the dog or put more hair on it. And so in politics. For sixty years we have argued the question, and there is not a man, woman or child from Halifax to Vancouver who knows what would happen if the tariff policies of the two parties were fully applied. If given a hundred years in which to argue the matter I venture to say that, by this static method, we should be no wiser at the end of that time than we are now. I suggest to my hon. friends that they look for a political dog on which to try their theory to see whether it will work. Let us
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

get down to something decisive and stop arguing, because the argument which has been going on for the last sixty years is certainly not creative; it is not getting us anywhere at all.
I come to the last principle I wish to discuss, the principle of cooperation. We stand for the instituting of cooperation for justice as a substitute for the present party conflict for power. I cannot stop to develop this point because I have something more to say directly to the minister anent his remarks. What I said of cooperation in general a few moments ago will apply in particular to political action. I turn my attention now more directly to the Minister of Railways, taking the order in which he presented his remarks to the house.
In the first place he says that group government is a bad thing because there are groups in Europe. I think the minister went far enough in that connection; indeed he might have been called to order when he termed the leader of the government of Italy a dictator and suggested that other governments in the European countries were not very efficient. I am not, of course, interested in safeguarding the reputation of Mr. Mussolini, nor am I especially interested in any of the governments of Europe. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the minister was not very discreet, to say the least, in his implication. Apart from this, however, the groups of Europe are not analagous to the group I have been discussing to-night; the European groups are hopelessly tied up with the old party idea, just as my hon. friends opposite are. The reason we have trouble in this house is that the government will not recognize we are here. And we are here. One of the first characteristics of a scientific attitude of mind is that it recognizes a fact when it exists, and the existence of this group in this house is an outstanding fact which hon. gentlemen opposite have not yet recognized. That is why the minister has had to roll logs, although I admit that the government has not had any heavy rolling to do this year.
Coming to Europe, let me say that the minister might have found far better examples of the group system if he had been acquainted with the history of the country from which he came. If he is acquainted with that history, as probably he is, then he failed to take note of the groups in the old land. I would refer him to the little group called the Council of London, designated as a group of shopkeepers, who defied both king and parliament and laid the basis of that most popular if nebulous idea of British justice and freedom. I would point
fMr. Irvine.]
to the group that brought a little order out of chaos in the days of Peel; I would point to the Irish group in the House of Commons; I would point to the Labour group in the British parliament-all splendid illustrations which the hon. gentleman might have found had he wanted to look for real examples. But he chose to take Europe because he thinks our people are afraid of Europe. Let me say on behalf of Europe, however, that the governments of France, Germany, Italy and Spain are just as clean, just as democratic and just as efficient as the government of which my hon. friend who spoke is a member.
Let me turn to another point. The hon. gentleman said, "If we allow these economic groups to develop, bless your heart, we do not know where it will end, because we may have a religious group." He was afraid that there might be a Catholic group or a Presbyterian group or a Methodist group. He forgets that the Methodist church is no longer in existence in Canada. However, may I point out to him that there have been religious groups in all parties, and I am not denying them the right, to exist. The clergy of England had a very great deal to do with organizing the party of which my hon. friend is a member-and with the other party as well. I understand also that one of the most potent religious groups in Canada is represented at this moment in my hon. friend's party, and if he considers that group inimical to the best interests of the country I challenge him to throw it out of his party and see what will happen.

I am glad my hon. friend
asks that question because I can tell him that there is a religious group in the other party on this side of the house. And these two religious groups have been on the top of every political fight in this country for years. I say, therefore, to the minister that he is not going to hang any religious groups around the neck of the economic group of this country; those religious groups belong to the party system if they belong to any. Let me remind him that our group is not on the defensive; the party system is. The minister therefore will have to do a lot more defending before he goes much further.
And now I come to the last charge; the minister declares that the group system will lead to log-rolling. This is a term from the lexicon of partyism which I confess I do not understand; I do not know what it means. One hon. gentleman suggested to me that it meant, "If you will scratch my back I

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
will scratch yours." If that is its meaning, I am sure the skin must be off my hon. friend's back by this time. As I say, I do not know what log-rolling means, as used by the minister; but if it means anything bad, evidently he knows what it is, and he does not like it. If the term has reference to the groups in this house, then I will tell him again that it has been necessary for him to practise the art of log-rolling only because the party system has refused to recognize any other method of dealing with honourable men who come here and try to serve the interests of the country as a whole.
Let me conclude by saying this: While I do not expect hon. gentlemen on either side of the house to agree with all I have said to-night, I hope they will go so far as to admit that there is something fundamentally wrong with the system we are practising in this house at the present time, and that if possible they will get together long enough to shade off the most pernicious phases of the party system and give us a chance to work together for Canada. I want to see some great economic principle around which we may all rally in the spirit of co-operation, a principle that will permit us to breathe the spirit of patriotism, a principle that will hold us all by some common appeal, and not this eternal wrangling over nothing and getting nowhere.
Mr. LESLIE G. BELL (St. Antoine): Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the splendid oratory of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine); at least we will all agree that he is an able advocate of the group system of government. But unfortunately he reminds me also of a great orator whom I heard advocating a third party system of government while I was a student at college in Michigan. I do not know what became of the group he was advocating, but I do know that the two great party system in the United States of America, still exists.
The budget debate is the time when we take stock of the affairs of our country. Hon. members opposite have given this house and the country the impression that we are on the crest of a great wave of prosperity, and it is noteworthy that all speeches made by those hon. members have laid strees on the word "prosperity". The Liberal party have sought to broadcast the fact that the policies they inaugurated are meeting with the favourable endorsation of all classes in this country, and we on this side of the house have been chided about the use of the word "protection". I mention this, for fear my hon. friends on the government benches may think
our party are trying to get away from the word, " protection ", used in its proper sense, but nothing is further from our thoughts. We have been criticized for speaking in any other way than that of boosting the present condition of affairs; members who have ventured even a mild criticism have been chastised by hon. members opposite; we have been accused of being responsible for the migration of hundreds of thousands of Canadians to that great neighbouring country to our south, all because of our criticisms of the present inefficient government, and our belief that the country is not prosperous. We are led to believe that the problems facing the country have been solved at last and that a sure remedy has been found in the free trade-low tariff policy inaugurated by hon. members opposite. We have heard some startling revelations concerning our wonderful financial outlook; we have been told that prosperity is no longer around the corner but that at last she has made her smiling presence known, and our native sons, daughters, and relatives are returning to have a share in that prosperity. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), if not aware of the fact and even though his usual modesty forbids his acknowledging it, must surely consider himself the saviour of his country after the flattering remarks concerning him and which hon. members of the government have showered upon him. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) finds Saskatchewan farmers literally rolling in wealth; the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) also sees the golden vision but reluctantly, out of one eye, he also sees a little unemployment, which he calls "seasonal unemployment". The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as Minister of External Affairs, proposes to spend the savings of the budget in Tokyo and Paris, while the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) stands with the bag wide open ready to accept what remains, to spend it recklessly in public works and other institutions throughout the country, not always in keeping, as we know, with the country's needs.
Accepting the statement of the Minister of Finance in the budget as correct, that our prosperity is definitely assured, I would not hesitate to congratulate the Minister of Finance and the government on such an achievement were it not for the fact that certain figures puzzle my admittedly limited capacity in financial matters. I regret that I cannot see my way clear to join in the voluminous though rather discordant chorus of national prosperity. For instance, I find that although we have heard a good deal of

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
boasting about the foreign trade of Canada the total imports and exports for the fiscal year 1927 amount to only $2,298,465,647, whereas for the last two years of the Conservative regime the figures were $2,351,186,832 in 1920 and $2,351,187,332 in 1921, or an increase in both these years of about $52,000,000. Again, if my hon. friends opposite would compare the figures relating to foreign trade for the last six years of Conservative government with the past six years of Liberal government they will find that our total exports from 1916 to 1921 inclusive amounted to $7,310,533,075, while from 1922 to 1927 inclusive the figure is $6,435,621,059. Our total imports for 1916 to 1921 inclusive amounted to $5,542,583,300, while for 1922 to 1927 inclusive they amounted to $5,198,804,217. In other words, during the last six years of Conservative rule our favourable balance of exports over imports amount to $1,867,949,775, while under Liberal rule for the last six years the balance was $1,236,816,842, or a matter of $631,132,933 of a more favourable trade balance under the Conservative regime than under Liberal rule. If we look to the net debt of our country we find another strange thing; we see that when the Conservatives went out of power in 1921 the net debt of Canada amounted to only $2,340,878,984, while by the end of 1927 we find the net debt increased by some $7,000,000, the exact figure of the net national debt being $2,347,834,370. The Minister of Finance has sedulously overlooked the fact that the net debt of the country under the Liberal rule, from the time the Conservatives left power, was increased to the maximum amount of $2,453,776,869 in 1923. The debt was increased by $112,897,885 before they started to reduce it, and yet the one outstanding feature of the budget is the boast of the present government that they are reducing the net debt of the country. Furthermore, it must be borne in mind that this present government have collected from the taxpayers of Canada over a billion dollars in war tax revenue alone and as yet they have not succeeded in reducing the net debt of the country by a single dollar, as I have already pointed out.
Then let us consider the tax reductions outlined in the budget. Hon. members of the government point with some pride to the recent reduction in the sales tax; so let us consider that for a moment. A war time government, Conservative or Union as you will, inaugurated a sales tax of one per cent in 1920, increasing it in 1921 to 3 per cent on certain articles. Like most other war governments they were turned out of office after they had made a good job of their herculean task, and
 *
their successors, the present Liberal government, upon assuming office immediately told the people with a smile that they were increasing the sales tax to 6 per cent. This was in 1922. The people accepted this ultimatum; they had no other choice. In the presentation of the 1923 budget, the rate of the sales tax was adjusted to a uniform 6 per cent, with certain exemptions on raw furs, drain tiles for agricultural purposes, and other articles. In 1924 there was a reduction in the sales tax from 6 per cent to 5 per cent, with certain exemptions on text books and certain articles of production. In 1925 more exemptions were added to the list but there were no reductions in the rates. These exemptions included vegetable plants, shoe lasts, and patterns, dies for boots and shoes, fishing boat engines and well-digging machinery. In 1926 there was no reduction in the sales tax. The reductions in that year in income tax were supposed to be most gratifying to the public, and accordingly there were no reductions. In the present budget the sales tax is reduced another 25 per cent, bringing it down to the rate that prevailed when the present government assumed office in 1921. And yet hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that this government is reducing the sales tax, while we on this side are supposed to accept the statement without question.
I have reviewed the reductions which were made in the sales tax from the year 1922 to the present year 1928 and the facts speak for themselves; the present sales tax rate is the same rate as prevailed when they assumed office. On the other hand the Liberal administration meanwhile has been taking a great deal of money, some hundreds of thousands of dollars in fact, from the people every year through this unjustifiable increase of sales tax and burdening the Canadian consumer, with this extra taxation.
Now, looking to the general conditions which prevail in this country, and the claim which is made with respect to prosperity, I would refer hon. gentlemen opposite to the commercial failures which have taken place in Canada during the present government's term of office. When one considers these figures he is astounded. The high water mark for commercial failures took place when this government assumed office. There were 3,925 commercial failures in 1922, the first year the Liberal government took office, whereas in the previous year, 1921, there were only 1,739. The wave of prosperity which has inundated this country during the Liberal administration of six years has drowned some 15,248 branches of business, compared with 7,939 during the last six years of the Conservative regime from

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
1916 to 1921 inclusive. In 1924 more manufacturers went out of business and double the number of traders succumbed to the great Liberal wave of prosperity ushered in by them in 1922, than under the previous six years of the Conservative administration.
If hon. gentlemen opposite want exact information as to whether business depression or confidence prevails in this country, they should look to the Canada Year Book for 1926. There they will find during every one of the years from 1916 to 1921 inclusive under the heading of "business confidence" the business conducted truly expressed the confidence of the Canadian people. On the other hand if they will look at the succeeding years from 1922 to 1926 inclusive, the latter being the last year given, they will find that business was indicated as being in a depressed state. Only in the year 1926 do we find this is not a fact. This may not appear to hon. gentlemen opposite as a very good barometer for indicating whether or not the country is prosperous at present, but to my mind and sense of reason, when 1827 commercial enterprises covering trade, manufacture, agriculture, logging and fishing, mining, construction, transportation and finance go to the wall, to use the language of the street, a number greater by hundreds than occurred during the previous Conservative regime, and bearing in mind also that there were less in number to go under each year, business conditions at present are not good. However, Providence has been kind to the present government during its term of office. During each year there has been an addition of from 100 to 175 million bushels to the wheat crop. The greatest oat crop in the history of Canada was witnessed in 1922. Likewise, barley had its greatest crop in 1924, and there was the greatest crop of rye in 1922. The enormous amounts realized from these bumper crops should have helped the government a great deal in making business conditions better-and yet, they are worse.
Let us come now to what the government has done for the workingmen of this country. When the present government assumed office it promised that it would do a great deal for the workingmen of Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite chide us about being the rich man's party. We pride ourselves, however, that we are as strongly for the workingman as we are for the manufacturer or any other class of the community. Four questions naturally arise in discussing what this government has done for the workingmen of Canada. They are these: First, has the present government during its term of office reduced the
cost of living? Has it relieved unemployment? Has it raised the workingman's wages? Has it improved the position of the family circle of the working man during its regime? Hon. gentlemen opposite throughout the country at the beginning of an election campaign always claimed that they were going to reduce the cost of living to the workingman, and it was on the strength of this promise that they received the votes of a great many workingmen. Now let us look at the facts. At the outset, let us again recall, the Liberal Government came into power at the beginning of 1922. I have in my hand the last copy of the Labour Gazette of February 28. I have the budget for a family of five covering the staple foods and the average prices in sixty cities in Canada. Let us compare the figures in 1921, or the beginning of January, 1922, with the prices of foodstuffs in January, 1928: Two pounds of sirloin beef in January, 1922, cost the workingman 54.6 cents. In January, 1928, the cost to the workingman was 62.8 cents. Shoulder beef likewise has risen in price from 30.4 to 36.4. There has been a corresponding increase in veal. So it is all down the list. Lard is dearer, cheese, bread, flour, rolled oats, tea and coffee. Pork and eggs are the only things that are cheaper. I assume that eggs are cheaper because of the importation of eggs from foreign countries, such as China. The total cost per week for a family of five under the present Liberal government is $11.19 compared with the cost when the Conservatives left office of $11.03, so that this government has not succeeded in reducing the cost of living for the workingman. These figures given in the Labour Gazette do not include the cost of clothing, recreation, doctor's or dentist's bills, school fees, or contributions for church purposes.
I might as well, at this very moment, although I intended to do so later on. when dealing with unemployment, refer to the serious conditions that the workingman to-day finds himself trying to meet, in this so-called period of prosperity which our hon. friends opposite would lead us to believe is here. How can the workingman believe in prosperity when he is working to-day, on half pay, in many cases, with many months of unemployment and a family to support, and When very few, if any, workingmen can live on this suppositious budget
Nor has the present government raised the workingman's wages. In 1921, the last year of the Conservative regime, the index number giving the average wages for six trades was 186.1. In 1920 it was 192.1. Under the Liberal regime the workingman's wages have

In 1920, wages in miscellaneous factory trades were at their peak, 216.8 and so were lumbering wages, 202.7. Wages of railway-men are to-day lower than they were in 1921, and wages of the coal miners of Nova Scotia, Alberta and Vancouver island have also dropped considerably. Coal mining labourers underground are to-day receiving from 55 cents to 82.64 less per day's work; millers are receiving $10 per week less in the flour mills, and all hands employed in furniture factories are reciving less per day's or per hour's work as compared with 1921. That is the condition of the workingman as regards his wages under this prosperity regime of the present government.
Has the present government relieved unemployment? The present position cf unemployment throughout the Dominion is summarized in the February 1928 issue of the Labour Gazette and I am going to read these extracts for the purpose of having them on record. On page 187 of the February issue of the Labour Gazette I find this statement:
The rnost noticeable recessions occurred among Vancouver workmen, 10.7 per cent of whom were idle in November as compared with 14.3 per cent in December, a change of 3.6 per cent, followed by percentage increases m idleness of 2.9 in St. John, 2.7 in both Edmonton and Halifax, 2.4 in Toronto, 2.1 in Winnipeg, 1.7 in Regina, and 1.1 in Montreal, loronto was the only city to record a slight increase in employment over December, 1926, while in all other cities an adverse situation prevailed.

In Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia there are similar reports as to present conditions in connection with unemployment. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics tabulated returns from 6,177 firms showing a decrease in the payrolls from 886,836 persons on December 1, 1927, to 826,736 persons on January 1, 1928, or a decrease of 60,100, or 6.8 per cent. As regards the city of Montreal I quote from the Montreal Gazette of February 21, as follows:
Unemployment relief is among the most serious problems which the Financial Federation of the Montreal Council of Social Agencies has to face.	_
At the sixth annual meeting the secretary revealed a deficit of $3,000 for the year 1927 over and above the $6,000 appropriated. In 1928, $6,000 was again appropriated for unemployment relief and after two months have passed, over $4,000 had been expended. The deficit this year will be much greater.
The Minister of Railways and Canals spoke of prosperity and I presume he referred to his own province of Saskatchewan. I read from the Montreal Gazette of March 2, 1928, a portion of a report of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Convention held at Saskatoon on the first of March, as follows:

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
G-eorge F. Edwards, director of the organization's research department, had this to say: "From statements made by city officials and those that are responsible for distributing relief throughout this province there is no doubt that the rigorous immigration policy engaged in by the Federal government and transportation companies last year has been the cause of a tremendous amount of suffering and hardships to thousands who were brought to Canada through highly-coloured statements and representations."
As regards the unemployment situation in Montreal, let me refer to the Meurling Refuge.
I find that the number of men cared for in that institution in January, 1928, was 17.218 as compared with 9,193 in January, 1927. The Meurling Refuge is a very fine building maintained by the city of Montreal for homeless, destitute men; how homeless and destitute they are can best be gathered when it is realized that these men go in at 6 p.m. and are given two slices of bread and a cup of coffee. They then have to undress and turn in their clothes to be fumigated, after which they line up and pass in to the shower baths. As each man enters, a man ladles out some soft soap which he slaps on the heads of the destitute men and they stay under the shower until the soap has dissolved. They are then handed a towel, after which they are given a night shirt and retire to their beds, from which they are aroused at an early hour, given two more pieces of bread and a cup of coffee and turned out into the streets for another day. The place is well conducted and is considered by many to be the best thing of its kind on the continent, but it will be understood that no man goes there if he can find any possible method of avoiding it.
Nevertheless, an average of 600 men a night made use of the city of Montreal's refuge at a time when the government index figures for employment were the highest on record for the month of January. These figures illustrate better than anything else that the government's fiscal policy is failing to provide for our population. There can be no true prosperity under conditions where over 17,000 free beds for destitute men have to be provided in one place alone.
In another office, on St. James street, Montreal, crowds of ex-soldiers can be seen daily asking for charity provided through a "tag day," and in another, about a stone's throw away, nearly 400 families have received unemployment relief. In Ottawa, right at the door of parliament, the charitable societies are overburdened with the demands upon them for relief by families in distress through unemployment. In Winnipeg the distress
has been so intense that the government has been asked to contribute to relief work, a request which the Prime Minister has refused.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, in speaking of the unemployment situation, in any way to advertise Canada adversely. I think that what is responsible for the number of unemployed at the present time is the policy which this government has persisted in of not allowing Canadian workmen the opportunity to work in Canadian factories, working up Canadian goods, so that Canadian men and Canadian women, wherever they are situated, may buy Canadian goods made by Canadian workmen at home. I hope it will never be the fate of the Conservative party, because it would also be the fate of a great country, to give way to the demands of any party group or of any section and do away with protection. We look across that boundary of 3,000 miles and see over there a country with a population of 120 millions, a country that is applying a quota law in order to prevent immigrants coming in there and enjoying the fruits of prosperity in that country, and yet Canada under the present Liberal government with its low tariff or free trade policy, or whatever you like to call it, cannot induce immigrants to come to this country even from our own British dominions without paying their transportation charges and practically holding out positions for them when they arrive. What is wrong with this government? What is wrong with Canada? There is nothing wrong with Canada. The trouble is with the fiscal policy of this government, and until that has been remedied, conditions in this country will be no better. What is the use of talking about reducing the war debt, or reducing the national debt of this country? This government is accomplishing neither, and at the same time we are losing every day and almost every hour our own stalwart sons and daughters to a foreign land, from which possibly they will never return. Is there any way in which we can remedy these conditions?

speechtext: Change the government.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Change the government-that seems to be the only way. One would think that the people of the west, whether they belong to the farmers' group or any other group, would realize that until they plant the factory beside the farm there never will be prosperity in this country. I do not know what the farmers want from the Conservative party. The Conservative party have always tried to please the farmers so far
1036	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
as is humanly possible. Railways have been built under the Conservative regime, although our friends opposite would try to make every one believe that they are the only ones who are building all the railroads in the country. The farmers of the west have got the best wheat lands in the world, and they have rereceived them at the cheapest price. We cannot move the wheat lands closer to the ocean or afford to give them much better transportation facilities, and until there is cooperation between the farmer and the manufacturer, and particularly between the farmer and the labouring men in the factories, there is always going to be trouble in solving the problems of this country.
It amuses me sometimes to hear my hon. friends to my left talk about the consumers and producers in this country. To hear them talk you would think that the farmers were the only consumers. But in what way can the farmer compare as a consumer with the workingman in the factory in our big manufacturing cities? These workingmen are the real consumers. They take the products produced by the farmer, the butter, the cheese, the eggs, and all his other products, and they are willing to pay his price provided they have the money in their pockets with which to buy them. When hon. gentlemen to my left speak of poverty and about the farmers being up against it, let me tell them that I could take them to my own constituency in Montreal and show them conditions which no farmer in western Canada or in eastern Canada has ever experienced. I could show them the condition of families who have not 160 acres of land to live on, who have not their own house over their heads, and worse still, who have not even enough to pay one day's rent. I could show them children and whole families living almost wholly on bread without butter; and yet we hear so much from the Progressives to my left of the conditions under which the farmers of this country are living, as if they were the only ones that legislation should provide for. I am the last to advocate the group system of government but if any class requires remedial legislation the first who should have asked for it and received it is the labouring class, who have not experienced under the Liberal government this prosperity which hon. members opposite are trying to demonstrate. Unfortunately the unemployment situation and the conditions of the workingmen avail them nothing under the present government's policy, and there are no indications that for them, prosperity is here.

speechtext: And has not the money to buy.

speechtext:
In reply to the boa. member, I say that the farmer has spent that money; he has not been able to keep it.
I want to refer to an incident that took place in the house this afternoon. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) produced a couple of hammers. I do not know why he bought them in the first place, and I do not know why he produced them in the house. Let me say that in my judgment I do not think he got the worth of his money when he bought them, certainly not so far as regards the effect that he produced in this house. It seemed to me it fell rather flat. If the hon. member proved anything he simply proved that Mr. Drury was an honest man, who, when he found that the evidence he had in his hand did not support the contentions he was making, refused to use that evidence any further. But the fact that Mr. Drury did not have the evidence at his command is no reason to suppose that his contention was not correct. It would be quite possible to produce evidence in abundance to support the contention which I believe Mr. Drury was making. Indeed on one occasion I travelled down from the west in company with a commercial traveller who was well versed in the hardware business and well acquainted with the sale of tools on both sides of the line. He gave me very clear evidence of t'he great difference that prevails in regard to the price of tools on different sides of the line. I myself for a number of years lived in close proximity to the border, and if there is one class of goods on which there is a large difference between the price in the United States and that in Canada it is small hardware, a sample of which the hon. member produced this afternoon. If you want evidence of that fact all you have to do is to go to Woolworth's stores in this city and you will find they are called, five, ten and fifteen cent stores. I think I am

The Budget-Mr. Brown
probably correct in saying that there is scarcely an article in their stores that is sold for fifteen cents that is not sold in the Woolworth stores on the other side for ten cents. That may seem to be a small thing in itself, but remember it is a difference of fifty per cent. Perhaps some of us will remember an incident in this house some years ago when an hon. member produced a teapot in a very dramatic manner, and for many years afterwards he was known as " teapot Blain." I imagine that the hon. member for North Simcoe will in the future be known as " hammer Boys."
The hon. member also dealt with binder twine. I do not know in whose behalf he was speaking, but I would suggest that he also is in need of further light upon the subject. We have sometimes heard it stated in this house that the truth has been told, but not the whole truth. I do not propose to question the accuracy of the figures submitted by the hon. member, but I do assert that he' did not tell us the whole truth; for in his analysis of the problem he omitted one of the most important factors. When he undertook to establish certain facts in regard to the prices of binder twine in former years and to-day, he omitted one of the most essential factors- the price of the raw material. Oh, I have heard the argument before. My opponent in the last election used it in my hearing on one occasion, but it does not make much impression in the west. He used the argument that has been advanced here to-day, that at a certain time there were so many binder twine factories in Canada that binder twine was put upon the free list, and now we have fewer factories and we are paying a higher price than we did then. It is the old fallacy we have to combat-post hoc, propter hoc; a certain thing has happened, and then when another thing happens it is the result of the first. We meet that fallacy again and again from the other side of the house, but particularly was it in evidence to-day when the hon. member used it in regard to binder twine. True, the price of binder twine is higher to-day, and has been consistently higher during the last few years, than it was for a period of years before. But I say the hon. member failed to take into account a very important factor-the price of the raw material. If he wants to investigate the matter further he will find what is familiar to everybody who knows enough about the matter to discuss it in public, that the price of the raw material is controlled by a New York syndicate in conjunction with Central American governments, the latter controlling the raw supply. That may not in itself account for the entire
increase in the price of binder twine, although to-day binder twine is very much cheaper than it was a few years ago, but not of course down to the price at which it was twenty years ago, perhaps. But that very factor will account in very large measure for the increase in price. It is true, of course, that the general scale of prices has been raised, and that the price of labour is also very much higher than it used to be, but in itself the control of the raw material accounts very largely for the increase in the price of binder twine. I shall not go into the matter further. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bancroft) my esteemed deskmate, has made a special study of this question and is in possession of information which will be very valuable to this house and which will refute some of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for North Simcoe.
I am Sony that the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) is not in his seat, because there are three things he hates more than everything else, first, the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), secondly, the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke), and, third, the United Grain Growers. Well, I should like to tell him that the United Grain Growers Company is the controlling factor in _the price of binder twine on the prairies to-day. It handles binder twine to the amount of nine million pounds yearly, and I think even the enemies of that company in the west will be willing to give credit to it for controlling the price of that very necessary article.
I do not propose to deal with the budget at any great length, Mr. Speaker. I do, however, want to refer to the income tax It was a matter of great regret to me when I heard it announced that the income tax was to be reduced. I have expressed myself on that matter in no uncertain terms in the past, and I have not seen fit to change my mind. I have never been able to work up any great feeling of indignation in regard to what is spoken of as the double tax. In many cases, perhaps not all, the corporation tax can easily be charged to overhead and passed on to the ultimate consumer, in which event there is no reason why the individual recipient of dividends from thel company should not also be taxed. Nor have I any particular sympathy for the young unmarried man who has an exemption of $1,500, and further exemptions if he has dependents, who is required to pay income tax on the balance of his salary. And I cannot work up any particular sympathy for the married couple who have an exemption of $3,000 to $500 for every child under eighteen-

-under twenty-one if they also have to pay income tax on their additional income. Even in the case of men who are most easily reached, the salaried men-and we admit they are the most easily reached-I cannot think they are subjected to any particular hardship. If they have no children and are wasting their time on poodle dogs, there is no particular reason to regard them as objects of sympathy when they have an exemption of S3,000.
I am going to make a statement, Mr Speaker, that I think will probably put me in the class of heretics. We hear a great deal said about tax reduction. Honestly I do not think we can properly look forward to tax reduction, certainly not in the volume of taxation. I know our hon. friends across the way do not seem at times to be able to distinguish between volume and rate of taxation; at least they persistently confuse the two. I think it quite possible that the rate of taxation may be reduced in some cases with -advantage to the revenue, but I do not think this country will ever be able to get along with any less revenue than it has today. I believe we shall require more and more revenue as the years go by. When the committee that is now discussing the pensions of returned men makes its report I am satisfied we shall realize we have only begun to touch the pensions problem. I am quite prepared to believe that as the years go by the amount required for soldiers' pensions will increase by very large proportions. I served on that committee the first session I was in parliament in 1922. It was an amazement to me to find that officers of the pension board, medical men, took the view they sometimes expressed in regard to attributability to service. It seems so perfectly evident to a layman that a man who endured the great stress of war must of necessity have suffered to some extent disability for life that I could not understand the position taken even by medical men. I believe there is a change in point of view; I believe it is coming to be recognized that many of these men, men who perhaps were not wounded, are largely to be classed as among the wastage of war. I have in mind one young man who, when I first knew him, was! strong and vigorous, and who when he came back gave every appearance of being a physical wreck; yet he never had a scratch. In my opinion there are many men in the same condition. It seems to me, therefore, that when we come to consider the question of revenue in relation to pensions we shall find that this reduction of taxation 
is nothing more than a pious wish which we should like to have realized but which we shall find among the impossibilities.
I want now to refer to a suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) as to the possibility of forming an alliance with the Conservative party. Such things have not been unknown, Mr. Speaker, when two extreme bodies come together and remain together for a time. Yes, Mr. Speaker, from the time when the Herodians and the Pharisees conspired to destroy the founder of Christianity down to the present time we can find illustrations of extremists coming together to overcome the moderate-minded men. They unite for purposes of destruction, but I wonder whether it would be possible for them to unite for purposes of construction. Let me tell my hon. friends over there that nothing would give the Conservative party greater pleasure than to seduce them into taking the position enunciated by the hon. member for Peace River. It is the one thing I have persistently and consistently tried to warn our farmers against -the temptation to fall for the principle of protection. By and large, the farmer cannot be benefited by a protective tariff. The American farmers have found that out. They succumbed to the temptation to seek higher tariffs and they were under that delusion for years; but they have now begun to find out that it was a delusion-a snare and a delusion. They are therefore seeking relief in such uneconomic measures as the McNary-Haugen bill. I say, nothing would give the Conservative party greater satisfaction than that they should be able to seduce hon. members in the opposite corner into taking the course indicated. I have no doubt that some of them are willing to go. As the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. 'Glen) pointed out this afternoon, there were four of them who in the session of 1926, in the first vote cast in that parliament, gave evidence of a preference for the Conservative party. How many more of them may yet follow I do not know. But what about the lady? Surely they will not forsake the lady member. Her plebeian soul could not stand to be associated with the "snobbish" Conservatives. Surely they cannot forsake her; that would never do. I want Hansard to put that word "snobbish" in quotation marks; otherwise it might give offence to some good Conservatives back home v/ho are my personal friends.
I want now to refer to another item in the tariff, an item upon which some hon. members in the southeast comer have made remarks; I refer to item 267b. Is it not a strange situation to see the hon, member for Rose-

The Budget-Mr. Brown
town (Mr. Evans) and the hon. member for Peace River associated with the Imperial Oil Company in opposition to this particular item? Yet such is the case. But perhaps on second thought it is not so strange; perhaps this is the first step in the direction of that alliance which has been suggested. Who knows? I wish to quote in this connection the hon. member for Rosetown:
Again, under item 167b I find a most amazing thing, the full import of which is not readily discerned. As far as I can see, the government has given notice to all small oil refining companies, and to those contemplating entering the business, to get out and stay out.
I will not quote the hon. member for Peace River in this regard; his remarks were made a day or two ago and they are somewhat lengthy. What he said was part of the general argument in relation to finished products and raw materials. But his position is there stated. Now what is the reason for this change? I have taken some trouble to look into the matter. I find that an application was made to the tariff board by a representative of one of the small oil companies to bring about the change. The situation, as I understand it, is something like this-I will try to give a picture of it. The large oil companies, with their expensive equipment and a good market for the by-products, are able to use the absolutely crude petroleum, while the smaller companies, without that equipment and with a more limited market for their by-products, cannot use such petroleum to advantage. The base of their operations lies in a product which has already passed through one process in refining, the technical term for which I believe is oil tops This particular product has been coming in under a duty of three-tenths of one cent per gallon under the British preference, fourth-tenths	of	one cent	under	the	intermediatetariff, and a half cent under the general. I am informed that in the actual application of the Customs Act they have been paying the same duty as on the finished product, so that instead of this being what the hon. member has depicted it, a notice to the small oil companies	to	"get out	and stay	out." It isabsolutely the reverse. Again, let me express the keen	regret I feel at	seeing the hon.
member for Rosetown associated with the Imperial Oil Company, which I understand has put in a protest recently against this item.

which information we shall no doubt receive

Now just a word in regard to group government or the balance of power theory. These two terms may be synonymous or they may be antagonistic to each other; I do not pretend to know. However, I will discuss the question under the head of the balance of power theory. I am willing to pursue inquiry into the question how far independent members may be given freedom of expression as to when a government should consider itself defeated and when not. This theory of that balance of power seems illogical to me because it cannot be universally applied. It may be very well for one or two to occupy that position and sit on the fence, but everyone cannot do it; some people must assume responsibility. The theory is absurd; and I do not use that term in an offensive way b.ut rather as Euclid used it. when, in pursuing certain lines of reasoning, he arrived at a conclusion which did violence to the axioms he laid down. In such cases the conclusion was absurd, and I use the same term with reference to this particular theory. It is absurd because, in order to make it effective at all, it pre-supposes the existence of two major parties both of which are abhorrent to these who have adopted the theory. I do not want to use any such rough term as bludgeoning, but it does seem to me absurd to think this could be adopted as a permanent principle under which to carry on government, although it might meet a temporary situation. I call to mind a little rhyme we used to say when we were children, which went something like this:
The lion and the unicorn,
Fighting for the crown;
Up jumped a little dog
And knocked them all down.
Who represents the lion and who the unicorn I do not presume to say, but I do know who wishes to take the part of the little dog.
Our friends tell us that the session of 1926 was an ideal session, just what they wanted. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not usually averse to a scrap, but I do not think either this house or the country would consider the session of 1926 to be ideal. It was not ideal to see hon. members opposite at that time; I can scarcely describe their condition. A lioness robbed of her whelps is not to be compared with the attitude of mind exhibited by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I even believe the hon. members with whom I was more intimately associated at that time will not say that the
The Budget-Mr. Brown

conditions within our own ranks were so absolutely ideal that we would have liked to have them remain that way.

speechtext: They are now.

speechtext:
And so are ours, for that
matter. Now they tell us we had a splendid program of legislation that year. Did we? It is true that we had a perfectly honourable arrangement with regard to a legislative program, an arrangement that was well known to the country, and we advanced that legislation to certain stages but we did not get it through. What was the reason? Well, Mr. Speaker, it is well known that when we all voted with the government there was a majority of twelve; when the five members who expressed a Conservative preference in the first vote opposed the government that majority was reduced to two. In addition to that there were always one or two on the ragged edge, so when the test vote came on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) to the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) to the customs report, what was the position? We lost two more votes.
I have no criticism to offer as against the hon. gentlemen who saw fit to take that position. They may have been right or wrong; I am willing to admit that it was a question in which great moral issues were involved, and I am willing to concede that it was a question on which men governed by a high standard of morality might have taken one or the other of two positions. I am quite willing to concede all that, but the fact remains that because these members took that postion we did not get the legislation we desired. But our friends say we got the legislation in 1927. That is true, but we had to run the gauntlet of a general election first, and you are never sure what the result of an election may be. If it had not been for the absolutely stupid tactics of our friends opposite from the time that session opened until it closed they might have been occupying seats on this side of the house and then what would have become of the legislation? I think it hardly safe to count on their following along the same lines. Of course hon. gentlemen opposite may be able to learn; they have reorganized their board of strategy and they may do better than they did before, but it is not a safe thing to bank on. So I say we did not get the legislation in that particular session, and I want to say also that if this much-reviled little group had taken the same position on the budget last year we would not have had the legislation yet; last session would have been as barren as the previous one.

Now, I am told that my time is going very rapidly.

speechtext: Go on.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That would be all very

I know they have given a great deal of consideration. to government in its legislative aspects, but I have never yet heard a single suggestion from those advocating group government as to how an executive is to be formed. Mr. Henry Wood has not told us, and from none of his followers have I heard how they propose to form an executive to carry on the functions of government. If they 'have any ideas on this phase of the question the general public have not been given the benefit of their deliberations. To quote the Ottawa Citizen, however, while the Liberal-Progressive may not be "the last word in political intelligence", at least they have given some thought to this problem. I came across a little book in the library the other day, from which I propose to read a few extracts. I do not say that I agree with this in every respect but it will at least be interesting to hon. members opposite. This little book is one of a series of Chronicles, of Canada, dealing with the winning of popular government in Canada. It deals with the few years immediately following the rebellion of 1837, after Lord Durham had made out his report and Mr. Poulett Thomson, afterwards Lord Sydenham, was sent out to Canada to try to put into effect the principles which Lord Durham had recommended. He speaks of his visit to Lower Canada, where he found no government at all, and then he proceeded to Upper Canada, and at this point I quote:
At Toronto Thomson found a totally different set of conditions. Here was a constitution functioning and a legislature in session; but what a legislature! Split into half a dozen little cliques and factions, it was trying to work with no cabinet, no opposition, no party system-an ideal state of things to which some critics of present conditions would like to return.
In the same connection I read another extract; an election was held, and the result was as follows:
The results were known early in April. They were as follows: For the government, twenty-four members; French, twenty; Moderate Reformers, twenty; Ultra-Reformers, five; Compact party, five; doubtful, seven. The curse of petty faction was not lifted, nor the machinery of two-party government really installed, for it was quite possible for several of these groups to combine in voting down government measures without having sufficient cohesion among themselves to form a ministry and assume control.

Then we have another sentence further:
Mankind has a pathetic faith in the efficacy of political machinery, remade or remodelled, to grind out happiness and bring in the age of gold.
But in order to show that I hold the balance evenly, I am going to give another extract to which perhaps those charged with the responsibilities of government might give heed:
Parliamentary procedure, as they have it in England, was a new thing in Canada. In Great Britain the government does not always resign when defeated on a vote, nor does the opposition defeat the government when it has no power to form an alternative government.
One more quotation. I give this for the benefit of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich)-I am sorry he is not in his place. He delivered an address the other day which was well worth listening to. It is true it had the character or quality of an essay, but seeing that the hon. member's native tongue is not English, he is to be congratulated upon his facility of expression in the English language. The passage I am going to read is not pertinent to the subject under discussion, but I will read it for one reason:
Complete freedom to manage its own affairs should, if logic were strictly followed, separate the colony from the mother country; but the British genius for compromise has met the difficulty in a thoroughly British way by avoiding any precise and rigid definition of the relations existing between the mother country and the daughter state.
This is a little apart from the subject, but I have always felt that our greatest danger lies in attempts at too exact definition. I want to refer to what is spoken of here as "the British genius for compromise". The hon. member for Vegreville read us a lecture on compromise. There should be a distinction between compromise on moral grounds and compromise on questions which are, after all, matters of expediency. When moral issues are involved a man must say: Here I take my stand, I take none else. But the great majority of the questions that we have to consider do not come within that category. They are matters on which there may very well be an honest difference of opinion between men equally anxious to reach a solution of our problems. I have no hesitation in saying that the essence of democratic government is compromise. If there is no willingness to compromise then we find ourselves between autocracy on the one hand and anarchy on the other. If we are going to carry on democratic government there must be a willingness to compromise. That does not mean the renunciation of any great moral principles to which a man commits himself.
There are other things I should like to have said but I find I shall have to refrain from doing so on the present occasion. I wish, however, to conclude with a reference to our position in this parliament. The hon. member for Marquette used words that I heartily endorse, that we should be moved neither by taunts nor by recrimination. We are charged with having forsaken our principles. Hon. members will remember that there is a difference between principles and methods that are employed to give effect to these principles. We may honestly admit that at one time we had in view the formation of a great party that would express our views. But when we talked of that, we got no help whatever from the members representing the United Farmers of Alberta, and absolutely none from the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). I am simply stating facts. They may have been right, we may have been wrong, but I am simply stating the facts. There was another breach in the third session of the last parliament when the "Ginger" group broke away and did not come to our meetings. When I got home, I was told: We sent you fellows down there to work together. I never was reproached for not joining the ginger group, but it was charged against me that we were not able to preserve unity.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that there should be a distinction between principles and the methods that are employed to give effect to these principles. We have taken our position here. W7e are each one of us responsible to our constituents. I have no indication up to the present that I have not been expressing the will of the men who sent me here. I believe the hon. members associated with me are, like myself, anxious to express not only their own views but are anxious to do what their people would like them to do. Happily so far we have been able to make these two duties coincide. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that though there may have been a choice of different means, there is no forsaking of principles.
I am going to close with a somewhat homely illustration. Just before I came away from home I had to sell some pigs. I had them in a pen sixteen feet square. It was not arranged so that I could run them through a chute into my sleigh, so I had to take another method. I got a rope and my method was to try to get a noose round the head of the pig and then a half-hitch round the body. When you have got a pig hitched that way you have got a real hitch. I had a man helping me who was not as experienced as I was, and when I got the noose over the
